block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.note4: The first photograph and the making of ICs share one principle: coat a light-hardening film, expose it, dissolve to leave a pattern. Even the name lithography ('stone printing') comes from printmaking.
block.semiconductor-lab.heliograph.place: Approximation: the image is a fixed picture.
message.semiconductor-lab.heliograph_pla: The light-hardened bitumen stayed - an image appeared! (only the shaded parts dissolved)
Not enough light: all the bitumen dissolved. You got the pewter plate back
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note1: A rubber tree that grows in the jungle. Cut the trunk and white sap oozes out.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note2: Grows in jungles. Right-click with a flint or obsidian flake to tap latex (the flake wears a little). Also works as fuel or for charcoal.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note3: The Para rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) comes from the Amazon. Tubes inside its bark carry a white milky fluid, latex - rubber particles floating in water - which oozes out when cut.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.note4: In 1876 Wickham took seeds out of Brazil; seedlings raised at Kew Gardens were planted in Southeast Asia. Most natural rubber today comes from Southeast Asian plantations.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_log.place: Approximation: latex comes at once (really it drips from slanted cuts into a cup over hours).
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_leaves.no: Rubber tree leaves. Breaking them sometimes gives a sapling.
Rubber tree leaves. Sometimes drop a rubber tree sapling (shears keep the leaves).
Para rubber leaves come in sets of three leaflets. The tree sheds them once in the dry season.
In its native South America a leaf disease (South American leaf blight) made large plantations impossible - one reason plantations succeeded in disease-free Asia.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_sapling.n: Plant it and it grows into a rubber tree.
From rubber tree leaves. Plant on grass or dirt (bone meal works).
A rubber tree can be tapped about 6-7 years after planting.
Rubber seeds are oily and soon lose the ability to sprout, which made carrying them far very hard.
block.semiconductor-lab.rubber_sapling.p: Approximation: grows as fast as an ordinary tree.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note1: White sap from the rubber tree. Add acid and it sets into rubber.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note2: Tap a rubber tree log with a flake. 3 latex + wood vinegar make raw rubber.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note3: Latex is tiny particles of rubber (polyisoprene, (C5H8)n) floating in water. Their surface charges keep them apart; acid cancels the charges, so the particles stick together and set (coagulation).
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.note4: Rubber plantations still set latex with acetic or formic acid. Over 3,500 years ago, Mesoamerican peoples mixed latex with morning-glory juice to make bouncing balls ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.latex.placeholder: Approximation: water content and concentration are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note1: Untreated rubber. Sticky when hot, hard when cold.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note2: 3 latex + wood vinegar (acetic acid). Carry it somewhere hot (jungle, desert) and it becomes 'Sticky Raw Rubber'; somewhere cold (snowy biomes) it becomes 'Stiff Raw Rubber'. Mix with sulfur and bake to vulcanize it.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note3: Raw rubber is just long chain molecules tangled together: warm them and they slide and flow, cool them and they freeze stiff. Old rubberized coats were sticky in summer and cracked in winter.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.note4: Rubber goods boomed in America in the 1820s-30s, but they melted and stank in summer and the craze soon collapsed. Goodyear spent years looking for a cure.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.placeh: Approximation: stickiness and stiffness are shown only in the name (uses do not change). Temperature is the biome's base temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubber_compound.n: Raw rubber with sulfur kneaded in. Bake it to get tough rubber.
Raw rubber + sulfur. Bake in a furnace to get vulcanized rubber.
The sulfur atoms are ready to link the long rubber molecules together here and there when heated.
Modern tyre rubber also contains accelerators to speed up the reaction and carbon black to make it stronger.
item.semiconductor-lab.rubber_compound.p: Approximation: kneading is merged into the crafting table.
item.semiconductor-lab.vulcanized_rubber: Heat rubber with sulfur and it becomes tough rubber that stays non-sticky even when hot.
Bake the rubber compound in a furnace. It does not change in hot or cold places (compare with raw rubber). Used for seals, and the starting point for cyclized rubber, a negative-resist material.

Sulfur bridges (cross-links) turn the rubber molecules into a network, so it no longer flows when warm and springs back when stretched (elasticity). Goodyear is said to have found it in 1839 when he dropped sulfur-mixed rubber on a hot stove.
Goodyear's patent dates from 1844; Hancock in England patented vulcanization in 1843. The name comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
Approximation: sulfur amount, temperature and time are not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.sti: The heat made the raw rubber sticky... (vulcanized rubber does not change)
The cold made the raw rubber stiff... (vulcanized rubber does not change)
message.semiconductor-lab.raw_rubber.nor: The raw rubber is back to normal
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber_m: Raw rubber dissolved with an acid added. Heat it and the rubber turns into a hard resin.

Raw rubber + sulfuric acid + turpentine (the acid bottle is returned). Heat in a furnace to get cyclized rubber. Vulcanized rubber does not dissolve, so it cannot be used. ⚠ GHS: corrosive (sulfuric acid), flammable (turpentine). Treated only as an industrial material.
Rubber molecules (polyisoprene) carry many double bonds. With an acid, neighbouring double bonds join up and six-carbon rings form inside the chain (cyclization).
Vulcanized rubber is a network linked by sulfur bridges, so it does not dissolve. That is why cyclized rubber is made from unvulcanized raw rubber.
Approximation: real processes also use benzene or xylene as solvents. Concentration, temperature and time are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber.n: Rubber changed by acid into a hard resin. It no longer bounces. It is the base of a light-hardening resist.
Heat the cyclization mix in a furnace. Mixed with a sensitizer (a bis-azide) it becomes a negative photoresist ([2-30]).
The rings stiffen the molecules, so the rubber loses its bounce (elasticity). In return it dissolves well in solvents and makes thin, even films - ideal as a photoresist base.
Rubber cyclization was studied from the 1910s; Harries published a sulfuric-acid method in 1919. From about 1957, Kodak's KTFR (cyclized rubber + bis-azide) became the main resist for early ICs.
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclized_rubber.p: Approximation: degree of cyclization and molecular weight are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.limed_wood_liquor: Wood vinegar with lime added. The sour part sticks to the lime, so the rest is easier to distil.
4 wood vinegar + 1 slaked lime make 4. Distil in a furnace to get methanol.

Wood vinegar is water with acetic acid (about 5-10%), methanol (a few %) and more. Slaked lime turns the acetic acid into calcium acetate, a salt that does not evaporate, so methanol comes over first when distilled.
The leftover calcium acetate (grey acetate of lime) was heated to make acetone. In World War I acetone for smokeless-powder solvent ran short and wood distillation was expanded.
Omitted: the calcium acetate is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note1: Distil the liquid from burning wood and you get methanol (wood spirit). Drinking it can make you blind - dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note2: Distil limed wood vinegar in a furnace. Oxidized over hot copper gauze it gives formaldehyde ([2-27]). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acutely toxic, specific target organ toxicity (optic nerve). Never drink it (it cannot be drunk in the game). Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note3: Methanol, CH3OH, is the smallest alcohol. In the body it turns into formaldehyde and formic acid, which damage the optic nerve. It looks just like the ethanol in drinks, so mistaken drinking has long caused accidents.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.note4: In 1834 Dumas and Peligot identified wood spirit; the name methyl comes from Greek for 'wine' + 'wood'. From 1923 BASF synthesised it from carbon monoxide and hydrogen under high pressure.
item.semiconductor-lab.methanol.placehol: Approximation: the rough wood-spirit distillation is merged into one step (really repeated to raise purity).
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.not: Methanol reacts with air on hot copper gauze. The gauze itself is not used up.
4 copper ingots. Put it on a lit campfire and right-click with methanol to get formalin. A cold gauze (not over fire) does nothing. The gauze can be used again and again (a catalyst).

Methanol and oxygen stick to the hot copper surface, react, and leave as formaldehyde and water: 2CH3OH + O2 -> 2HCHO + 2H2O. The copper only speeds the reaction up and stays the same - that is a catalyst.
In 1867 Hofmann confirmed formaldehyde by oxidizing methanol over a hot platinum spiral. Industry later mostly used silver gauze at about 600 C.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.pla: Approximation: gauze temperature and air supply are not modelled (it reacts when over a campfire).
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note1: Formaldehyde dissolved in water. A raw material for plastics. Very harmful.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note2: Oxidize methanol on hot copper gauze. React with phenol to make phenolic resin ([2-28]). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitization, carcinogenicity, mutagenicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note3: Formaldehyde, HCHO, is the smallest aldehyde. It links proteins together and sets them, so it was used to preserve specimens and disinfect. The same linking makes it join with phenol into a resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.note4: Formaldehyde released from building materials caused eye and throat pain (sick building syndrome), so Japan regulated it in building materials from 2003. Butlerov first made it in 1859.
item.semiconductor-lab.formalin.placehol: Approximation: concentration (real formalin is about 37%) is not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.r: Methanol oxidized on the hot copper gauze: formalin! (the gauze is not used up)
message.semiconductor-lab.copper_gauze.c: The gauze is cold - no reaction. Put it on a lit campfire
item.semiconductor-lab.carbolic_oil.note: An oil distilled from coal tar. It contains phenol and more.
Distil coal tar in a furnace. Washed with sodium hydroxide, only the phenol moves into the water (adding acid straight away does not get it out). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion.
Heated coal tar gives, in order of boiling point, light oil, middle oil (about 170-230 C), heavy oil and anthracene oil, leaving pitch. Middle oil is rich in phenol and naphthalene.
Coal tar was a nuisance waste of coal-gas (gaslight) works, but in the 19th century it became a treasure trove of dyes, drugs, explosives and plastics.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbolic_oil.plac: Approximation: the other fractions (light, heavy oil...) and pitch are omitted.
Middle oil washed with alkali: only the phenol dissolved out into the water.
Middle oil + sodium hydroxide. Add sulfuric acid to get phenol back (the acid bottle is returned). ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion.

Phenol is a weak acid, so it reacts with sodium hydroxide to form a water-soluble salt (phenoxide): C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O. Naphthalene and the rest are not acids, so they stay in the oil and can be separated.
Separating things by their acid-base behaviour is a basic trick of chemical plants. The same idea returns in resist development (positive resists dissolve in alkali).
Approximation: the separated oil layer (naphthalene etc.) is thrown away.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note1: Phenol, found in coal tar, was used to disinfect surgery. It burns the skin - dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note2: Sodium phenoxide solution + sulfuric acid. React with formalin to make phenolic resin ([2-28]). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, mutagenicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note3: Phenol, C6H5OH, is a benzene ring with one OH. Acid turns the salt back, and phenol, which dissolves poorly in water, separates out (white needle crystals melting at about 41 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.note4: Runge found it in coal tar in 1834. In 1867 Lister used it to disinfect surgery, and deaths after operations fell sharply. Today it is mostly made by the cumene process (1940s).
item.semiconductor-lab.phenol.placeholde: Approximation: the sodium sulfate by-product is omitted. Purity is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note1: Extra phenol with an acid added. Heat it to get a resin that melts with heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note2: 2 phenol + 1 formalin + hydrochloric acid (the bottle is returned). Heat in a furnace to get 2 novolac. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, carcinogenicity (phenol, formalin).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note3: With acid, formaldehyde links phenol rings with CH2 bridges. With extra phenol there are not enough bridges for a network, so it stops as chains.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.note4: In 1907 Baekeland made both a melting resin and a setting resin just by changing acid/base and the mixing ratio.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac_mix.place: Approximation: the ratio (really about 0.8 formaldehyde per phenol) and temperature are symbolic.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note1: A yellowish phenolic resin that melts with heat. The main material of resists that copy patterns with light.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note2: Heat the novolac reaction mix in a furnace. Mixed with DNQ (a sensitizer) it becomes a positive photoresist ([2-32]). It does not set when heated (it can be melted again and again).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note3: Novolac is short chains of phenol joined by CH2. Many OH groups remain, so it dissolves a little in alkaline water. DNQ makes it dissolve less - until light hits it and it dissolves more: the mechanism of positive resists.
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.note4: From the late 1970s novolac/DNQ positive resists became the workhorse of chip making, through the g-line and i-line era (down to about 0.35 um).
item.semiconductor-lab.novolac.placehold: Approximation: molecular-weight distribution is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note1: Extra formalin with alkali added. Heat it and it sets into a resin that never melts again.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note2: 1 phenol + 2 formalin + sodium hydroxide. Heat it in an autoclave (with water, 150 C and 5 atm or more) to get 2 Bakelite. In a furnace (normal pressure) it comes out foamy. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, carcinogenicity (phenol, formalin).
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note3: With alkali, plenty of formaldehyde attaches to phenol, giving CH2OH arms. With extra formaldehyde, heating joins the arms and the whole thing becomes one network.
item.semiconductor-lab.resol_mix.note4: Baekeland set resol in moulds in a 'Bakelizer' that heated it under pressure so no bubbles formed (patent 1909).
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note1: The first synthetic plastic, made from phenol and formaldehyde. Once set it never melts.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note2: Heat the resol reaction mix under pressure in an autoclave. It does not melt in a furnace (compare with novolac). It does not conduct electricity, so radio and telephone cases and wiring parts were made of it.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note3: Its molecules are bridged in three directions (a thermoset), so it does not flow when hot, hardly burns and does not conduct electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.note4: Invented by Baekeland in 1907, the world's first fully synthetic plastic, called 'the material of a thousand uses'. Radios and black telephones of the 1930s-40s were made of Bakelite.
item.semiconductor-lab.bakelite.placehol: Approximation: no filler (such as wood flour) is added.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_etch.note: A very dangerous acid mixture that dissolves silicon itself. Kept in a lead bottle.

Crafting: 1 hydrofluoric acid + 1 nitric acid + 1 empty lead bottle → 1 (bottles come back). In the etching tank [9-06] it cuts away unwaxed silicon to form mesas. GHS: skull (acute toxicity), corrosive, oxidising.
Nitric acid oxidises silicon to SiO2 and hydrofluoric acid dissolves that SiO2; repeating the two eats into the silicon.
In the 1950s a liquid called CP-4 (HF, nitric, acetic acid and a little bromine) was used to smooth germanium and silicon surfaces.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicon_etch.plac: Approximation: no acetic acid or bromine (not CP-4 itself).
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note1: Warm coal tar gently over a low fire and only the light oil comes out first.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note2: Heat coal tar on a campfire (a furnace heats it so strongly that heavier parts come over too, giving middle oil). Distil it again on a campfire for benzene, or in a furnace for xylene. ⚠ GHS: flammable, carcinogenic (contains benzene).
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note3: When a mixture of liquids is heated, the ones with the lowest boiling points evaporate first. Collecting them by temperature is fractional distillation. In coal tar, the part up to about 170 C is light oil, containing benzene, toluene and xylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.note4: In 1849 Mansfield worked out how to get benzene industrially by fractionating coal-tar light oil. He later died of burns from a benzene fire.
item.semiconductor-lab.light_oil.placeho: Approximation: fractionation is shown as 'campfire = low temperature, furnace = high temperature'. Toluene is separated with the quartz still ([2-59]).
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note1: A molecule of six carbons in a ring. The source of many drugs and dyes. Very harmful.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note2: Distil light oil on a campfire, at low temperature (boiling point 80 C, it comes over first). ⚠ GHS: flammable, carcinogenic (category 1A), mutagenic, specific target organ toxicity (blood), aspiration hazard. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note3: Benzene, C6H6, has six carbons in a regular hexagon with electrons spread around the whole ring (aromatic). Kekule proposed the ring in 1865 (the story goes he dreamt of a snake biting its tail).
item.semiconductor-lab.benzene.note4: Faraday found it in gaslight oil in 1825. It was long used as a solvent until it was found to cause leukaemia; today toluene, xylene and others replace it. In 1856 Perkin made mauve, the first synthetic dye, from coal-tar chemicals, starting the chemical industry.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note1: An oil related to benzene. It dissolves rubber well, so it is the solvent and developer for negative resists.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note2: Distil light oil in a furnace, at higher temperature (boiling point about 140 C). Dissolves negative resists (cyclized rubber type) and is the developer that washes away the unexposed parts ([9-21]). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acutely toxic (inhalation, skin), skin irritant, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note3: Xylene, C6H4(CH3)2, is a benzene ring with two methyl groups (ortho, meta and para forms). It dissolves oils and rubber well but not water.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.note4: Negative resists swell slightly in the xylene developer, so lines finer than about 2 um were impossible. That is why positive resists (developed in alkaline water) took over.
item.semiconductor-lab.xylene.placeholde: Approximation: the three xylene isomers are not separated.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note1: White crystals that smell of mothballs. They appear when tar oil is cooled.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note2: Middle oil + ice (crystals come out on cooling). Sulfonate it to start on the road to DNQ. ⚠ GHS: flammable solid, acute toxicity, carcinogenicity (category 2), aquatic hazard.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note3: Naphthalene, C10H8, is two benzene rings joined. It is the most abundant compound in coal tar; cooling middle oil makes it separate as white plate crystals.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.note4: It was once used as mothballs. As a dye raw material it carried the 19th-century chemical industry, and sensitizers like DNQ belong to the naphthalene family.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalene.place: Approximation: the remaining oil is thrown away.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthalenesulfon: Naphthalene with a sulfuric-acid arm (sulfo group) attached.
Naphthalene + sulfuric acid (the bottle is returned). With 2 sodium hydroxide and baking it gives 2-naphthol. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, serious eye damage.
The SO3H of sulfuric acid replaces a hydrogen on the naphthalene ring (sulfonation). At high temperature it prefers position 2.
Sulfonation is a basic reaction of the chemical industry, for detergents and dyes.
Approximation: the position change with temperature is not modelled (only the 2-acid).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol_melt.not: Naphthalenesulfonic acid mixed with strong alkali. Bake it to get 2-naphthol.
Naphthalenesulfonic acid + 2 sodium hydroxide. Bake in a furnace for 2-naphthol. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (alkali).
In molten sodium hydroxide the sulfo group is swapped for OH (alkali fusion).
The same reaction as the old way of making phenol (sulfonate benzene, then alkali fusion).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol_melt.pla: Approximation: the sodium sulfite by-product is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note1: White crystals: naphthalene with an OH. A dye raw material.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note2: Bake the alkali fusion mix in a furnace. With sulfuric acid, ammoniacal liquor and sulfur dioxide it gives Tobias acid. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, aquatic hazard.
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note3: 2-Naphthol, C10H7OH, is the naphthalene version of phenol, a material for azo dyes (reds and oranges).
item.semiconductor-lab.naphthol.note4: The late-19th-century German dye industry made thousands of colours from tar compounds such as naphthols.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note1: Naphthalene carrying a sulfo group and an amino group. The last raw material before DNQ.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note2: 2-Naphthol + sulfuric acid + ammoniacal liquor + sulfur dioxide. With potassium nitrite, hydrochloric acid, ice and bleaching powder it gives DNQ. ⚠ GHS: eye and skin irritant.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note3: 2-Amino-1-naphthalenesulfonic acid. The OH of naphthol is turned into NH2 with the help of ammonia and sulfite (the Bucherer reaction, 1904).
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.note4: Named after the German chemist Tobias, who patented its preparation in the 1890s. It was originally a dye raw material.
item.semiconductor-lab.tobias_acid.place: Approximation: sulfonation and amination are merged into one step.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note1: Saltpeter mixed with lead. Heated, the lead takes one oxygen and leaves potassium nitrite.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note2: Saltpeter + lead ingot. Bake in a furnace for potassium nitrite. ⚠ GHS: oxidizer (saltpeter), reproductive toxicity (lead).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note3: KNO3 + Pb -> KNO2 + PbO. In molten saltpeter the lead steals one oxygen and becomes lead monoxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.note4: An old way to make nitrites. Today nitrogen oxides are absorbed in alkali instead.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrite_mix.place: Approximation: the lead monoxide by-product is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_nitrite: Saltpeter with one oxygen less. Used for diazotization.
Bake the saltpeter-lead mix in a furnace. With hydrochloric acid it gives nitrous acid, which diazotizes Tobias acid into DNQ. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid, acute toxicity, aquatic hazard.
Nitrous acid, HNO2, is unstable, so it is made from a nitrite and an acid just before use. It turns an amino group NH2 into N≡N+ (a diazo group): diazotization (Griess, 1858).
Tiny amounts of nitrite keep the colour of ham and sausages. Too much is poisonous.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note1: A yellow powder that breaks down in light - the 'eye' of a resist that copies patterns with light. Carry it into the sun and it decomposes.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note2: Tobias acid + potassium nitrite + hydrochloric acid + ice (diazotize while cold) + bleaching powder (alkaline hypochlorite oxidizes it, replacing the sulfo group with O-). If you stand in sunlight (day, open sky above) holding it, it turns into 'Light-Decomposed DNQ'. Safe in a chest or indoors. Mixed with novolac it makes a positive resist ([2-32]). ⚠ GHS: self-reactive (decomposes easily with heat or light), skin sensitizer. Treated only as an industrial material (a sensitizer).
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note3: In light, DNQ loses N2 and rearranges (Wolff rearrangement) into an indene carboxylic acid, which dissolves in alkaline water. So a film of novolac + DNQ dissolves only where light fell: a positive resist.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.note4: Invented by Suss at Kalle in the 1940s for diazo copying paper. Clean-room lights in chip fabs are yellow because they leave out the UV-to-blue light that DNQ and other sensitizers react to.
item.semiconductor-lab.dnq.placeholder: Approximation: converting it to the sulfonyl chloride and binding it to novolac is omitted. Decomposition shows only in the name (uses do not change).
message.semiconductor-lab.dnq.decomposed: Sunlight decomposed the DNQ! (nitrogen escaped) Carry sensitizers in the shade
item.semiconductor-lab.positive_resist.n: A liquid that, where light hits it, later dissolves in alkaline developer. Carrying it in sunlight ruins it.

In a glass bottle (the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 novolac + 1 DNQ + 1 xylene + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Spread on wafers with the spin coater [9-19]. Holding it in sunlight (daytime, open sky above) exposes it and spoils it (chests and indoors are safe). GHS: flammable (solvent).

Novolac resin alone dissolves a little in alkali, but DNQ mixed in holds it back. Ultraviolet light breaks DNQ down into an acid, so exposed areas dissolve readily: what light touches disappears, hence 'positive'.

Süs at Kalle devised it in the 1940s for diazo copying paper. It became the main IC resist only in the late 1970s with projection printing (before that, negative KPR and KTFR). ⚠️ The game uses positive resist first to match the v0.3 lithography flow (LITHO_DESIGN). Fab lighting is yellow so the resist is not exposed.
item.semiconductor-lab.positive_resist.p: Approximation: the solvent is xylene (real positive resists use cellosolve acetate and others). Resist made from exposed DNQ is not told apart at the crafting table.
message.semiconductor-lab.positive_resis: Sunlight exposed the resist! (keep it indoors or in a chest)
item.semiconductor-lab.cation_exchange_r: Resin beads that catch metal ions (such as sodium) in water and swap them for hydrogen ions.
Bakelite + sulfuric acid (the bottle is returned) make 2. With anion exchange resin and glass it makes an ion exchange column. ⚠ GHS: eye irritant (acidic).
A phenolic resin with sulfuric-acid arms (sulfo groups, SO3H): R-SO3H + Na+ -> R-SO3Na + H+. When every site is taken it is saturated; running acid through turns it back to H+ (regeneration).
In 1935 Adams and Holmes in Britain made ion exchange resins from Bakelite-type resins. Before that, natural minerals (zeolites) were used.
Approximation: sulfonation conditions are not modelled. Modern resins are polystyrene-based (D'Alelio, 1944).
item.semiconductor-lab.anion_exchange_re: Resin beads that catch chloride and other ions in water and swap them for hydroxide ions.
Novolac + ammoniacal liquor (ammonia) + formalin make 2. ⚠ GHS: skin irritant (alkaline).
A resin with amino groups: R-OH + Cl- -> R-Cl + OH-. The H+ from the cation side and the OH- from this side combine into water, H2O, so the ions disappear.
Adams and Holmes also made anion exchangers from phenylenediamine-formaldehyde resins.
Approximation: made with ammoniacal liquor (ammonia) instead of an amine.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_exchange_col: A column packed with resins related to Bakelite. It removes the last salts from water to make it very pure.

6 soda-lime glass + cation exchange resin + anion exchange resin. Right-click with distilled water to get deionized water (8 times). When the cation side is spent, right-click with sulfuric acid; when the anion side is spent, with sodium hydroxide, to regenerate.
Cation exchange swaps metal ions for H+, anion exchange swaps chloride and others for OH-, and H+ and OH- become water. It removes even the traces of ions that distillation leaves.
From the 1950s chip factories rinsed wafers with water purified by ion exchange. Today's ultrapure-water plants stack reverse osmosis, ion exchange, UV and more ([2-18]).
Approximation: water volume, flow rate and resin amount are symbolic (1 use = 1 bottle).
item.semiconductor-lab.deionized_water.n: Very pure water with almost no salt or ions.
Pass distilled water through an ion exchange column (in a glass bottle). The starting point for ultrapure water [2-18] and wafer cleaning.
Pure water hardly conducts electricity. The fewer ions, the higher the resistance; 18.2 MOhm-cm at 25 C is the theoretical limit (water itself splits slightly into H+ and OH-).
In chip factories a single stray ion such as sodium can spoil a transistor, so wafers are rinsed with huge amounts of ultrapure water.
message.semiconductor-lab.ion_exchange_c: The cation exchange resin is spent (%s / %s / %s) - regenerate with sulfuric acid
The anion exchange resin is spent (%s / %s / %s) - regenerate with sodium hydroxide
Regenerated the cation exchange resin with sulfuric acid (%s / %s / %s)
Regenerated the anion exchange resin with sodium hydroxide (%s / %s / %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.calcium_acetate.n: The grey powder left when limed wood vinegar is boiled down. The source of acetic acid and acetone.
Boil limed wood vinegar down on a campfire (distilling it in a furnace gives methanol instead). + sulfuric acid -> glacial acetic acid; bake in a furnace -> acetone ([2-40]).
The salt formed when the acetic acid in wood vinegar meets lime: 2CH3COOH + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(CH3COO)2 + 2H2O. Driving off the water and wood spirit leaves a powder (grey acetate of lime).
Around 1850 Turnbull in the USA ran the first successful works making acetate of lime from wood distillation. Until the early 20th century most industrial acetic acid and acetone were made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note1: The sour part of vinegar, concentrated. It freezes when it is just a little cold - hence 'glacial'.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note2: Calcium acetate + sulfuric acid make 2 (the bottle is returned). Take it somewhere cold (snowy biomes, mountain tops) and it becomes 'Frozen Glacial Acetic Acid', melting again where it is warm. ⚠ GHS: flammable, skin corrosion.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note3: The strong acid (sulfuric) drives the weak acid (acetic) out of its salt: Ca(CH3COO)2 + H2SO4 -> 2CH3COOH + CaSO4 (gypsum). Acetic acid with almost no water freezes at about 17 C.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.note4: Vinegar is about 4-5% acetic acid. It is a raw material for cellulose acetate ([2-18] reverse-osmosis membranes, photographic film) and vinyl acetate (glues). Today it is mostly made from methanol and carbon monoxide (Monsanto process, 1960s).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.place: Approximation: the gypsum by-product is not collected. Freezing is shown by biome temperature.
message.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.fr: The cold froze the glacial acetic acid (it sets at about 17 C)
message.semiconductor-lab.acetic_acid.me: The glacial acetic acid melted again
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note1: The main part of nail-polish remover. It dissolves many things and dries fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note2: Bake calcium acetate in a furnace. A raw material for bisphenol A (epoxy resin [2-41]) and a solvent for stripping resist and cleaning equipment. ⚠ GHS: flammable, eye irritant, specific target organ toxicity (drowsiness).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note3: Heated calcium acetate breaks down into calcium carbonate and acetone: Ca(CH3COO)2 -> CaCO3 + (CH3)2CO. Acetone is the smallest ketone and mixes with both water and oil.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.note4: In World War I acetone, the solvent for cordite (smokeless powder), ran short; Weizmann developed a way to make it by bacterial fermentation (ABE fermentation, 1915). He later became the first president of Israel.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetone.placehold: Approximation: the calcium carbonate by-product is not collected.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note1: Fat from cows, pigs and sheep. Used to make soap and candles.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note2: Sometimes dropped by cows, pigs and sheep. 3 of them with sodium hydroxide and water make a soap batch.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note3: Fats are molecules of one glycerol with three fatty acids attached (triglycerides). Animal fat is rich in saturated fatty acids (such as stearic acid) that are solid at room temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.note4: In 1823 Chevreul showed that fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol. Tallow candles were later replaced by stearin and paraffin candles.
item.semiconductor-lab.tallow.placeholde: Approximation: rendering fat from meat is skipped (the fat itself drops).
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note1: Fat, strong alkali and water in a pot. Boil it to make soap.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note2: 3 tallow + sodium hydroxide + water bucket (returned). Boil on a campfire to get saponified tallow. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (alkali).
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note3: Alkali cutting the links (esters) in a fat is called saponification - 'soap-making'.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap_batch.note4: Long ago the alkali came from potash in wood-ash lye plus slaked lime. In the 19th century industrial soda became cheap and soap became everyone's.
item.semiconductor-lab.saponified_tallow: Boiled into soap, with glycerin still mixed in. Add salt and only the soap floats up.
Boil the soap batch on a campfire. With salt it gives 3 soap and leaves the spent lye (glycerin water) in the grid (salting out).
(C17H35COO)3C3H5 + 3NaOH -> 3C17H35COONa (soap) + C3H5(OH)3 (glycerin). Plenty of salt makes the soap insoluble, so it sets and floats off (salting out).
Soap works long made soap by 'kettle boiling + salting out'.
Approximation: repeated salting and washing is merged into one step.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note1: Mix fat with strong alkali and you get soap. It lets water wash away greasy dirt.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note2: Saponified tallow + salt make 3 (made with sodium hydroxide, so it is hard soap; potassium hydroxide would give soft soap). The first step into cleaning equipment.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note3: A soap molecule has a water-loving head (-COO-) and a long oil-loving tail. The tails surround grease in tiny balls (micelles) that float in water and wash away.
item.semiconductor-lab.soap.note4: The oldest evidence of a soap-like substance is from Babylon around 2800 BC ⚠️. Chip wafers are not washed with soap but with RCA cleaning (1965, ammonia and hydrogen peroxide etc., [9-14]).
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note1: The liquid left after the soap is separated. Sweet glycerin is dissolved in it.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note2: Left in the grid when making soap from saponified tallow. Bake in a furnace to get glycerin.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note3: Spent lye contains glycerin, salt and a little alkali. Evaporating and distilling it yields glycerin.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.note4: It used to be thrown away; from the 19th century the glycerin was recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_lye.placeho: Approximation: the salt is not recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note1: A sweet, syrupy liquid. Used in skin lotions and medicines too.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note2: Bake spent lye in a furnace. Reacted with hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide it gives epichlorohydrin (a raw material for epoxy resin [2-41]).
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note3: Glycerin, C3H5(OH)3, is an alcohol with three OH groups. It dissolves in water and holds moisture, so it is a humectant.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerin.note4: Scheele found it in 1779 by boiling oil. Today it comes in huge amounts as a by-product of biodiesel.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note1: A weak alkaline water that dissolves only the resist that light has hit.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note2: About 1% sodium hydroxide in water (glass bottle; the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 sodium hydroxide + 1 water bucket + 3 empty glass bottles → 3 (the bucket comes back). Used in the developer bench [9-21]. GHS: corrosive (eyes, skin).
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note3: In exposed positive resist the DNQ has turned into an acid, which reacts with the alkali and dissolves. Unexposed resist stays.
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.note4: Sodium that gets into oxide upsets MOSFETs, so later fabs switched to metal-free TMAH (2.38% solution is standard).
item.semiconductor-lab.developer.placeho: Approximation: made from a water bucket (really from pure water).
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note1: White crystals: two phenols joined by acetone. One half of epoxy resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note2: 2 phenol + acetone + hydrochloric acid (the bottle is returned). ⚠ GHS: serious eye damage, skin sensitizer, reproductive toxicity.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note3: With acid, two phenol rings join onto one carbon of acetone: 2C6H5OH + (CH3)2CO -> (HOC6H4)2C(CH3)2 + H2O. The 'A' stands for acetone.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.note4: First made by Dianin in Russia in 1891. It is also the raw material of polycarbonate (CDs, glasses); because it acts somewhat like a hormone, its use in food containers is regulated.
item.semiconductor-lab.bisphenol_a.place: Approximation: heating conditions and purity are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.dichlorohydrin.no: Glycerin with two OH groups swapped for chlorine. One step before epichlorohydrin.

Glycerin + 2 hydrochloric acid (bottles returned). + sodium hydroxide -> epichlorohydrin. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitizer, carcinogenic (category 1B), flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
Two of the OH groups of glycerin, C3H5(OH)3, are replaced by Cl from hydrogen chloride.
Making it from glycerin is an old route; for a long time it came from propylene (petroleum). Since the 2000s glycerin from biodiesel is used again.
item.semiconductor-lab.epichlorohydrin.n: The other half of epoxy resin. It has a triangular ring (an epoxy group). Very harmful.

Dichlorohydrin + sodium hydroxide. React with bisphenol A and NaOH for epoxy resin. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion, skin sensitizer, carcinogenic (category 1B), flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
When the alkali pulls off one hydrogen chloride, a three-membered ring of oxygen and two carbons (the epoxy group) forms. The ring opens easily and links to other molecules.
First made by Berthelot in 1854. A raw material for epoxy resins, synthetic rubbers and water-treatment chemicals.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note1: A sticky resin that has not set yet. Mix in a hardener and heat it to make it hard (like two-part glue).
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note2: Bisphenol A + 2 epichlorohydrin + sodium hydroxide make 2. With novolac (the hardener) it becomes a molding compound. Heated alone it does not set. ⚠ GHS: skin irritant, skin sensitizer.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note3: Bisphenol A with an epoxy group at each end. The OH of a phenolic hardener (or NH2 of an amine) opens the epoxy rings and links them into a network.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.note4: Around 1936 Castan in Switzerland (working on dental fillings) and Greenlee in the USA made it independently. Used for glues, paints and encapsulating electronics.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_resin.place: Approximation: molecular weight (degree of polymerization) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.epoxy_molding_com: A black mix of epoxy resin and hardener. It becomes the case that wraps an IC.
Uncured epoxy resin + novolac (hardener). Heat in a furnace to get cured epoxy. Material for IC encapsulation ([9-34]).
The black case of an IC is epoxy resin + phenol-novolac hardener + silica powder (so it barely expands with heat) + carbon black (to block light), heated and set in a mould.
In the 1960s-70s IC packages moved from costly ceramic to cheap moulded epoxy (transfer moulding), so ICs could be made cheaply in huge numbers.
Approximation: no silica powder or carbon black.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note1: Set epoxy resin. It keeps out water and electricity and protects the IC.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note2: Heat the epoxy molding compound in a furnace. It does not melt when heated (a thermoset).
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note3: Epoxy groups and the novolac OH groups have linked into a 3D network, so it is hard, resists heat and chemicals, and does not conduct.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.note4: Almost every IC today sits inside this black epoxy, which protects the chip and its fine gold wires from moisture and knocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_epoxy.place: Approximation: shaping in a mould is not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.fermentation_cro: Put sugar water with yeast in it, and it slowly turns into alcohol.

2 earthenware pots + a wooden slab. Right-click with sugar wash to fill it. While it bubbles it is fermenting. When it is done, right-click with an empty hand for 2 fermented wash + 1 yeast. Put in fermented wash (alcohol) and acetic acid bacteria from the air make 2 vinegar ([11-10]). Pasteurized wine is refused.
With little oxygen, yeast gets energy by splitting sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide: C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. The bubbles are CO2.
In Georgia, traces of wine survive in clay jars from about 6000 BC. Wine is still made there in big buried clay jars called qvevri.
Approximation: temperature does not change the speed, and yeast stopping at high alcohol is not modelled.
message.semiconductor-lab.fermentation_c: The crock is already in use
Empty crock. Put in sugar wash
You took out fermented wash and the yeast that grew
item.semiconductor-lab.wild_yeast.note1: Tiny living things (yeast) from fruit skins, grown up. Used for bread and alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.wild_yeast.note2: Sweet berries or an apple + sugar + water bucket. When you empty a fermentation crock, one yeast comes back because it grew.
item.semiconductor-lab.wild_yeast.note3: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It lives on fruit skins and in nectar, so crushed fruit left alone starts fermenting by itself.
item.semiconductor-lab.wild_yeast.note4: In 1857 Pasteur showed fermentation is the work of living yeast. In 1897 Buchner found that juice from ground-up yeast (no cells) still ferments: the discovery of enzymes (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1907).
item.semiconductor-lab.wild_yeast.placeh: Approximation: yeast strains (wild or selected) are not distinguished.
item.semiconductor-lab.sugar_wash.note1: Sugar water with yeast in it. Goes into a fermentation crock.
item.semiconductor-lab.sugar_wash.note2: 3 sugar + wild yeast + water bucket. In a fermentation crock it becomes fermented wash.
item.semiconductor-lab.sugar_wash.note3: Yeast enzymes split sucrose into glucose and fructose, which then become alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.sugar_wash.note4: Fermented sugarcane molasses becomes rum. Brazil still makes huge amounts of fuel ethanol from sugarcane.
item.semiconductor-lab.sugar_wash.placeh: Approximation: the wheat (starch) route, which needs malt to make sugar, is not implemented.
item.semiconductor-lab.fermented_wash.no: A liquid with a little alcohol (about 10%). Distilling makes it stronger.
Taken from a fermentation crock. 3 + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle -> ethanol.
Above about 15% alcohol the yeast itself weakens, so fermentation alone cannot make strong alcohol.
Beer and wine are drinks at this stage. Whisky and shochu are made by distilling it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fermented_wash.pl: Approximation: alcohol strength is fixed at about 10%.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note1: The alcohol in drinks. Used to disinfect and to make other chemicals. Burns easily.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note2: 3 fermented wash + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle. Raw material for ethylene [2-36] and chloroform [2-38]; a solvent. ⚠ GHS: flammable, eye irritant.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note3: Ethanol, C2H5OH, boils at 78 C, below water (100 C), so distilling collects it. But at 95.6% the vapour has the same makeup as the liquid (an azeotrope), so distilling cannot make it any stronger.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note4: To get 100% ethanol you use something that takes only the water (quicklime, molecular sieves), or distil with benzene added.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.placehold: Approximation: making it 100% (anhydrous) is not implemented.
block.semiconductor-lab.alumina_catalyst: Pass alcohol vapour over hot white powder (alumina) and it turns into a gas called ethylene.

6 iron + 3 alumina. Put it on a lit campfire and right-click with ethanol -> 1 bag of ethylene (the bottle is returned). The tube (catalyst) is not used up. A cold tube does not react. Right-click with a bag of hydrogen sulfide for sulfur (Claus process [2-11]).
The hot alumina surface pulls water out of ethanol (dehydration): C2H5OH -> C2H4 + H2O. Alumina only helps the reaction and is not used up (a catalyst).
Before oil became cheap, ethylene was made from alcohol this way. Brazil and India still make 'bio-ethylene' from sugarcane alcohol.
Approximation: temperature is only 'over a fire or not'. The water by-product is not collected. The old route of dehydrating with concentrated sulfuric acid is not implemented.
message.semiconductor-lab.alumina_cataly: The tube is cold. Put it on a lit campfire
The ethanol lost water and became ethylene
item.semiconductor-lab.ethylene_gas.note: A sweet-smelling, very flammable gas. The source of polyethylene (plastic bags).
Made from ethanol in an alumina catalyst tube. Becomes polyethylene [2-37] in a high-pressure reactor. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure, specific target organ toxicity (drowsiness).
In ethylene, C2H4, the two carbons share a double bond. When it opens and links to the next ethylene again and again, you get polyethylene.
In 1795 four Dutch chemists called it 'oil-making gas' (with chlorine it makes an oily liquid) ⚠️. Ethylene is also a plant hormone that ripens fruit; it is used to ripen bananas.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethylene_gas.plac: Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The petroleum (naphtha cracking) route is not included (this mod has no crude oil).
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene.note: A light plastic that keeps out water and electricity; used for plastic bags and buckets.
Made from ethylene in a high-pressure reactor. Used for chemical containers and wire insulation. Softens when heated (thermoplastic).
A long chain of tens of thousands of -CH2-CH2- units. Made of only carbon and hydrogen, it resists acids, alkalis, and even hydrofluoric acid.
In World War II it insulated the cables of airborne radar. In chip fabs today, hydrofluoric acid bottles are polyethylene too.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene.plac: Approximation: molecular weight and density are not distinguished.
block.semiconductor-lab.high_pressure_re: A machine that squeezes a gas with huge force and turns it into plastic (polyethylene).
8 steel + compressor. 4 bags of ethylene + oxygen (1 bag lasts 16 runs) -> 1 polyethylene (20 s, 5 kW). Without oxygen it does not start.
Very high pressure (about 1400 atm) packs ethylene molecules close together; a tiny trace of oxygen starts it off (initiator), the double bonds open and link one after another.
In 1933 Fawcett and Gibson at ICI were studying a different reaction and found a white waxy solid in the vessel. Only in 1935 did they learn that oxygen leaking in had started it.
Approximation: pressure and temperature are not given as numbers. Unreacted ethylene is not recycled, and low- vs high-density polyethylene is not distinguished.
A white powder that smells of chlorine. It whitens cloth and disinfects water.
Slaked lime + a bag of chlorine. With ethanol it makes chloroform. ⚠ GHS: oxidizer, skin corrosion, harmful to aquatic life. Mixed with acid it releases chlorine (never mix).
Slaked lime absorbs chlorine and becomes a powder containing calcium hypochlorite. The hypochlorite ion ClO- oxidizes and breaks down dye and germ molecules.
Patented by Tennant in Scotland in 1799. Before that, whitening cloth meant months of laying it in the sun; now it took days.
Approximation: the chamber where lime absorbs chlorine is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note1: A heavy, sweet-smelling liquid. It was once used to put patients to sleep for surgery, but it is harmful, so it is no longer used.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note2: Ethanol + 2 bleaching powder + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle (the ethanol bottle is returned too). Raw material for PTFE [2-38] (the next step cannot be made yet); a solvent. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin irritant, carcinogenic (category 2), reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note3: Chlorine from the bleaching powder oxidizes ethanol and adds chlorine to it; at the end, the one-carbon CHCl3 is split off (the haloform reaction).
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note4: In 1831 Guthrie (USA), Soubeiran (France) and Liebig (Germany) each made it independently. Simpson used it as an anaesthetic in 1847. Today it is a raw material for refrigerants and Teflon.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.placeh: Approximation: conditions are not described (DESIGN). By-products (calcium formate, calcium chloride) are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.placehol: Approximation: real Scottish kelp ash held only a few percent sodium carbonate, mostly potassium salts (here the liquor yields soda). ⚠️
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene_bott: A plastic bottle that hydrofluoric acid cannot eat through.
HF dissolves glass, but polyethylene (a chain of -CH2- only) has nothing for it to attack.
Before polyethylene, HF was kept in lead, wax (ceresin) or gutta-percha bottles. Polyethylene was found at ICI in 1933; HF bottles of it came in the 1950s. ⚠️ the exact year is not confirmed.

Polyethylene resists most acids and bases at room temperature, but strong oxidisers (hot concentrated nitric acid) and some solvents soften it. Today very pure HF for chips is shipped in PTFE or high-purity PE.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus_trichl: A sharp-smelling liquid of phosphorus and chlorine. A tool for putting chlorine onto other things.

White phosphorus (the water jar is returned) + 3 bags of chlorine. Used for acetic acid -> acetyl chloride and cinnamic acid -> cinnamoyl chloride. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material.
P4 + 6Cl2 -> 4PCl3. PCl3 swaps the OH of an acid for Cl: 3RCOOH + PCl3 -> 3RCOCl + H3PO3.
First made in 1808 by Gay-Lussac and Thenard. Still made in large amounts for pesticides, flame retardants and medicines.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetyl_chloride.n: Acetic acid with its OH swapped for chlorine. Very reactive.

3 acetic acid + phosphorus trichloride make 3 (no phosphorous acid). + sodium acetate -> acetic anhydride. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material. Flammable.
The Cl next to C=O leaves easily, handing an acetyl group CH3CO- to other molecules.
In 1852 Gerhardt in France made acetic anhydride for the first time, from acetyl chloride and a salt of acetic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetyl_chloride.p: Approximation: the phosphorous acid by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_acetate.no: A white salt from neutralizing acetic acid with sodium hydroxide. The filling of reusable hand warmers.
Acetic acid + sodium hydroxide. Material for acetic anhydride and cinnamic acid (the Perkin reaction).
CH3COOH + NaOH -> CH3COONa + H2O. In the Perkin reaction it acts as a weak base that starts things by pulling a hydrogen off acetic anhydride.
Its melted solution can cool without setting (supercooling), then sets all at once when disturbed, giving off heat: that is how reusable hand warmers work.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_acetate.pl: Approximation: hydrate water (the trihydrate) is not distinguished.
Two acetic acids with one water taken out. It puts acetyl groups onto other things.

Acetyl chloride + sodium acetate (no salt by-product). Material for cinnamic acid (Perkin reaction) and cellulose acetate (the [2-18] membrane). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Treated only as an industrial material.
CH3COCl + CH3COONa -> (CH3CO)2O + NaCl. With water, (CH3CO)2O turns back into two acetic acids.
First made by Gerhardt in 1852. Today it goes into cellulose acetate (cigarette filters, photo film) and aspirin.
Approximation: the modern ketene route is not included. The salt by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note1: Benzene with one CH3 attached. Smells like paint thinner.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note2: 2 light oil + quartz still (returned): finely separating the cut between benzene and xylene (rectification). + 2 chlorine -> benzal chloride. ⚠ GHS: flammable, aspiration hazard, reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note3: Boils at 111 C, between benzene (80 C) and xylene (about 140 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note4: Named after Tolu balsam from South America; Deville found it in 1841 by distilling that resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.placehold: Approximation: the number of rectifying stages and purity are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzal_chloride.n: Toluene with two hydrogens of its CH3 swapped for chlorine. One step before benzaldehyde.
Toluene + 2 bags of chlorine. + slaked lime + water bucket -> benzaldehyde. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin and eye irritant, carcinogenic (category 1B). Treated only as an industrial material.
With light or heat, chlorine replaces hydrogens on the CH3 (the side chain), not on the ring: C6H5CH3 + 2Cl2 -> C6H5CHCl2 + 2HCl.
Since the later 19th century this has been a route for making benzaldehyde industrially.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzal_chloride.p: Approximation: light and heat conditions are not modelled. The hydrogen chloride by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzaldehyde.note: A liquid with a sweet almond smell. Raw material for cinnamic acid.
Benzal chloride + slaked lime + water bucket (the empty bucket is returned). + acetic anhydride + sodium acetate -> Perkin mixture. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (oral).
C6H5CHCl2 + H2O -> C6H5CHO + 2HCl (the lime takes up the hydrogen chloride).
It was taken from bitter almond oil in 1803; in 1832 Liebig and Wohler studied its structure and spread the idea of the 'radical'.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzaldehyde.plac: Approximation: the calcium chloride by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note1: Benzaldehyde mixed with acetic anhydride. Heat it in a furnace to get cinnamic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note2: Benzaldehyde + acetic anhydride + sodium acetate; heat in a furnace for cinnamic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note3: Sodium acetate pulls a hydrogen off acetic anhydride, which then adds to the C=O of benzaldehyde and forms a carbon-carbon double bond: C6H5CHO + (CH3CO)2O -> C6H5CH=CHCOOH + CH3COOH.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note4: Perkin found the purple dye mauve at 18 (1856). In 1868 he used this reaction to make coumarin (the scent of fresh hay).
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.placeh: Approximation: conditions are not described (DESIGN). The acetic acid by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamic_acid.not: White crystals related to the smell of cinnamon. They stick together when light hits them.
Heat the Perkin reaction mixture in a furnace. 3 + phosphorus trichloride -> 3 cinnamoyl chloride (material for the KPR negative resist).
C6H5CH=CHCOOH. When UV hits the crystal, neighbouring C=C bonds open and join into a four-carbon ring ([2+2] dimerization).
Kodak's 1950s negative photoresist KPR put many of these 'light-sticking' groups onto chains of polyvinyl alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamic_acid.pla: Approximation: cis and trans are not distinguished (treated as trans).
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamoyl_chlorid: Cinnamic acid with its OH swapped for chlorine. A tool for attaching cinnamic acid to other molecules.

3 cinnamic acid + phosphorus trichloride make 3. Attached to polyvinyl alcohol it gives polyvinyl cinnamate (KPR material, not makeable yet). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material.
C6H5CH=CHCOCl. The Cl leaves easily and links with the OH of an alcohol to form an ester.
Minsk and colleagues at Kodak made polyvinyl cinnamate from polyvinyl alcohol and cinnamoyl chloride (1950s) ⚠️.
Approximation: the phosphorous acid by-product is not produced.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note1: Seal the lid tight and heat the water inside, and the steam squeezes everything. Heating under that squeeze sets things without bubbles.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note2: 7 steel + copper cable (pressure gauge omitted). 10 kW. Material top-left, water bucket bottom-left (4 runs). As it heats, steam pressure rises (about 5 atm at 150 C, up to 20 atm at the safety valve, up to 300 C). Resol mixture -> 2 Bakelite at 150 C and 5 atm or more. Without water or with too little pressure you get foamy Bakelite.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note3: Water heated in a closed vessel stays liquid above its boiling point, and the steam pressure (saturated vapour pressure) climbs steeply with temperature. Same idea as a pressure cooker.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note4: Baekeland solved the problem of resol foaming from its own water vapour by holding it down with pressure ('heat and pressure': filed 1907, patented 1909). The vessel was called a 'Bakelizer' ⚠️. ⚠ Accident: a pressure vessel bursts if the safety valve fails or the walls are too thin (the many 19th-century boiler explosions led to safety valves and inspection rules).
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.placeh: Approximation: temperature and pressure use a simple model (same form as the Acheson furnace; saturated vapour pressure from the Antoine equation). Mould shapes are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.foamy_bakelite.no: Heated without pressure, so it is full of bubbles and brittle. A failure.
Made by heating resol mixture in a furnace (normal air pressure), or in an autoclave without enough pressure. Not usable for anything else.
As resol sets it gives off water (and a little formaldehyde). Without pressure these turn to gas, make bubbles, and get frozen in.
People before Baekeland had made phenol-formaldehyde resins too, but they came out foamy and brittle and were useless.
item.semiconductor-lab.foamy_bakelite.pl: Approximation: how foamy it is is not modelled (it either works or not).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetylene_gas.not: A very flammable gas that comes off when water hits carbide. The light of old lamps.

Calcium carbide + water bucket (the empty bucket is returned). + acetic acid + mercuric sulfate (catalyst) -> vinyl acetate. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas (category 1), gas under pressure, may decompose explosively even without air.
CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. Its carbons share a triple bond, so many things can be added onto it.
Willson made carbide by accident in 1892. In the first half of the 20th century, before petroleum, acetylene was a key raw material for plastics and synthetic rubber (acetylene chemistry).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetylene_gas.pla: Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The slaked lime by-product is not produced.
A white powder that helps things add onto acetylene. A very strong poison.

Mercury (the iron flask is returned) + 2 sulfuric acid. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (category 1-2), specific target organ toxicity, hazardous to the aquatic environment (long-term). Treated only as an industrial material.
Mercury ions attach to acetylene's triple bond and make it easier to add acetic acid or water.

Lesson: Minamata disease. The Chisso factory in Minamata, Kumamoto, used mercuric sulfate as a catalyst to make acetaldehyde from acetylene and released the methylmercury formed in the reaction into the sea. Many people who ate the fish developed a severe nerve disease (officially recognized in 1956), and some still suffer today. Factories now use methods without mercury.
Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out (the real one is slowly lost). Modern vinyl acetate uses no mercury (zinc or palladium catalysts).
item.semiconductor-lab.vinyl_acetate.not: Acetic acid added onto acetylene. Linked up it becomes polyvinyl acetate (the stuff in wood glue).

Acetylene + acetic acid + mercuric sulfate (catalyst, returned). 4 + hydrogen peroxide (initiator, bottle returned) -> 2 polyvinyl acetate. ⚠ GHS: flammable, specific target organ toxicity, carcinogenic (category 2).
HC≡CH + CH3COOH -> CH2=CHOCOCH3. A C=C double bond remains, so it can be linked into a polymer.
First made by Klatte in Germany in 1912 (Griesheim-Elektron).
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_acetate: A soft resin behind wood glue and chewing gum.
4 vinyl acetate + hydrogen peroxide make 2. + methanol + sodium hydroxide -> polyvinyl alcohol.
Radicals (fragments with an unpaired electron) from hydrogen peroxide open the double bond and link vinyl acetate one after another (radical polymerization).
The white liquid of wood glue is fine particles of polyvinyl acetate spread in water (an emulsion).
Approximation: polymerization temperature and molecular weight are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_alcohol: A white resin that dissolves in water. In laundry starch and liquid glue.
Polyvinyl acetate + methanol + sodium hydroxide (methyl acetate is not produced). + 2 cinnamoyl chloride -> polyvinyl cinnamate (KPR negative resist material). Also for polarizing film [B-06].
'Vinyl alcohol' itself is unstable and cannot be linked up, so vinyl acetate is linked first and then its acetate parts are swapped for OH (saponification).
Made by Herrmann and Haehnel in Germany in 1924. In Japan the PVA fibre vinylon (Sakurada and others, 1939) went into production in 1950.
Approximation: the degree of saponification is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_cinnama: A resin that hardens only where light hits it. Material for one of the earliest photoresists used to copy chip patterns.
Polyvinyl alcohol + 2 cinnamoyl chloride. Material for the negative photoresist ([2-30], E's process).

UV makes the C=C of the many cinnamate groups on the chain join with cinnamate on a neighbouring chain into a four-carbon ring ([2+2] dimerization). The chains become bridged, so lit areas no longer dissolve in solvent: a negative resist.

KPR, the photoresist made by Minsk and colleagues at Kodak in the 1950s, was used to pattern the earliest transistors and ICs ⚠️. Later, cyclized rubber + bis-azide resists took over. (Bis-azides explode easily with shock or heat, so this game does not make them and uses the earlier KPR instead.)
Approximation: pyridine (reaction solvent and base) is omitted. Sensitizers that raise the speed are handled in E's process.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_dichrom: Bright orange crystals. Very harmful (hexavalent chromium).

2 sodium chromate + sulfuric acid (bottle returns) + potassium carbonate. Heated in a furnace it decomposes to chromium(III) oxide. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing, acute toxicity, skin corrosion, respiratory and skin sensitization, carcinogenicity (category 1B), mutagenicity, reproductive toxicity, aquatic hazard. Handled only as an industrial material.
Adding acid joins two yellow chromate ions into orange dichromate (2CrO4²⁻ + 2H⁺ -> Cr2O7²⁻ + H2O). The potassium salt dissolves poorly, so it crystallizes out easily.

Mixed into gelatin, dichromate hardens where light falls (dichromated gelatin [2-31], an ancestor of photoengraving). A strong oxidizer once used for cleaning lab glassware (chromic acid), now avoided because of its toxicity.
Approximation: really made by double decomposition of sodium dichromate with potassium chloride (potassium carbonate stands in here).
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony_pentachl: A fuming liquid that smells of chlorine. It helps reactions that add fluorine.

Antimony + 3 bags of chlorine. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). Used for chloroform + 2 hydrofluoric acid -> R-22. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, hazardous to aquatic life. Reacts violently with water. Treated only as an industrial material.
Antimony acts as a 'carrier' that swaps fluorine from hydrogen fluoride for chlorine on the other molecule (the Swarts reaction).
In the 1890s Swarts in Belgium found how to put fluorine on organic compounds with antimony fluorides. The later refrigerant (CFC) industry grew from this.
Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out. Really, part of the SbCl5 turns into fluorides (SbCl3F2 etc.) that do the work.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorodifluoromet: A gas once used as an air-conditioner refrigerant. Raw material for PTFE.

Chloroform (bottle returned) + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + antimony pentachloride (catalyst, returned). In a pyrolysis furnace it becomes TFE. ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure. Damages the ozone layer.
CHCl3 + 2HF -> CHClF2 + 2HCl. Two of chloroform's chlorines are swapped for fluorine.
A member of the CFC family (an HCFC). Because it damages the ozone layer, the Montreal Protocol (1987) led to phasing out its use as a refrigerant; its use as a feedstock continues.
Approximation: the hydrogen chloride by-product is not produced. 1 bag = about 1 mol.
item.semiconductor-lab.tetrafluoroethyle: Ethylene with every hydrogen swapped for fluorine. Linked up, it becomes Teflon (PTFE).

Made from 2 bags of R-22 in a pyrolysis furnace. 4 bags -> PTFE in an autoclave (with water, 80 C or more). ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure, carcinogenic (category 1B). It can polymerize by itself or decompose explosively. Treated only as an industrial material.
2CHClF2 -> C2F4 + 2HCl (about 700 C). When its C=C double bond opens, it links up again and again.
In 1938 Plunkett at DuPont stored TFE in cylinders for refrigerant experiments. Opening the valve gave no gas, yet the cylinder weighed the same. Cut open, it held a slippery white powder: PTFE.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note1: A white plastic that is very slippery, sticks to almost nothing, and dissolves in nothing. The coating of non-stick pans.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note2: Polymerize 4 bags of TFE in an autoclave (with water, 80 C or more). It resists hydrofluoric acid, aqua regia and almost every chemical. Used for chemical pipes and containers in chip fabs.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note3: Long -CF2-CF2- chains. Fluorine wraps the carbon tightly and the C-F bond is very strong, so other molecules cannot get at it.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note4: Plunkett found it by accident in 1938 when another experiment went wrong. In the Manhattan Project it was used to handle corrosive uranium hexafluoride gas for enriching uranium.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.placeholder: Approximation: real polymerization runs at TFE's own pressure (about 10-30 atm) with a persulfate initiator. This vessel's pressure is only steam, so temperature is the only condition.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrolysis_furnac: A furnace that sends gas through a platinum tube and heats it until its molecules rearrange.
6 steel + platinum + copper cable. 8 kW. 2 bags of R-22 -> 1 bag of TFE + 2 bags of hydrogen chloride (10 s).

At about 700 C hydrogen chloride leaves chlorodifluoromethane, and two leftover CF2 fragments join into TFE. The tube is platinum, which resists attack even when hot (real ones use platinum, silver or nickel alloys).
Rearranging molecules with heat ('pyrolysis' or 'cracking') is also the heart of making ethylene from petroleum in today's chemical industry.
Approximation: temperature is not given as a number. By-products (such as hexafluoropropylene) are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative_resist.n: A liquid that hardens and stays where light hits it. Carrying it in sunlight ruins it.

In a glass bottle (the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 polyvinyl cinnamate (from D) + 1 xylene + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Coated in the spin coater [9-19] it becomes a negative resist, developed in xylene [9-21]. Holding it in sunlight spoils it. GHS: flammable (solvent).

The cinnamate groups on the polyvinyl cinnamate chains join in pairs under ultraviolet light ([2+2] photodimerisation). Cross-linked chains no longer dissolve; unexposed areas wash away in xylene, hence 'negative'.

Minsk and colleagues at Kodak made it as KPR around 1954; it was the resist when Bell Labs and the US Army applied photoengraving to semiconductors in 1955–57. From 1957 KTFR, based on cyclized rubber, became the main IC resist. Both swell in the developer and cannot print lines much finer than about 2 µm, so positive resist took over in the late 1970s. ⚠️ Real KPR contained a sensitiser so ordinary mercury lamp light exposed it well (no sensitiser here).
item.semiconductor-lab.negative_resist.p: Approximation: no sensitiser (real KPR used one to respond to longer wavelengths). Solvent is xylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrofluoric_acid: The same very dangerous acid, now in a light plastic bottle that will not break.
Pour lead-bottled HF into an empty polyethylene bottle (the lead bottle comes back). Machines take HF in either bottle.
From the 1950s polyethylene bottles replaced lead, wax and gutta-percha for HF: HF dissolves glass but cannot attack the -CH2- chain. ⚠️ the exact year is not confirmed.

HF goes through skin and takes calcium from the body; burns may not hurt at first. Hazard (GHS): fatal on skin contact or if swallowed or inhaled, causes severe burns. Calcium gluconate gel is the first aid.
item.semiconductor-lab.cellulose_acetate: A white powder: wood fibre with acetic acid attached. Used for photo film and cigarette filters.
Wood pulp + 2 acetic anhydride + acetic acid + sulfuric acid (catalyst, bottle returned). 2 + acetone + water bucket -> RO membrane.
Acetic anhydride puts acetyl groups on cellulose's OH groups (esterification). With fewer OH groups it dissolves in solvents like acetone.
First made by Schutzenberger in 1865. It became 'safety film', replacing flammable celluloid movie film.
Approximation: the degree of substitution is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note1: A very fine membrane that lets only water through and holds back dissolved salts.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note2: 2 cellulose acetate + acetone (dissolve and spread) + water bucket (set it). A part of the ultrapure water system.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note3: Normally water moves by itself toward the stronger solution (osmosis). Push the strong side harder than the osmotic pressure and only water is squeezed back the other way (reverse osmosis).
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note4: Around 1960 Loeb and Sourirajan at UCLA made an 'asymmetric' membrane, very dense only at the surface and porous below, which passed water fast enough to make fresh water from seawater.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.place: Approximation: the partial drying time and additive (magnesium perchlorate) in casting are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water.n: The cleanest water, with almost no ions or germs. Used to wash chips.
Made from deionized water in the ultrapure water system (filled into a polyethylene bottle). Resistivity 18.2 MOhm·cm (25 C). Used for wafer cleaning and rinsing ([9-14]).

Water molecules themselves split very slightly into H+ and OH- (10^-7 mol/L each). Only that conducts, so resistivity cannot go above 18.2 MOhm·cm. In a glass bottle, sodium and other ions would leach out of the glass.
Ion-exchanged pure water was used in chip plants from the 1950s, and the term 'ultrapure water' spread from the late 1970s-80s ⚠️. Today a fab uses thousands of tonnes a day.
item.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water.p: Approximation: resistivity is fixed at 18.2 MOhm·cm (its drop over time as CO2 from the air dissolves is not modelled).
block.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water_: A three-stage system (ion exchange, filtering, UV) that removes almost every impurity from water.

4 polyethylene + mercury lamp tube (UV) + 2 ion exchange columns + RO membrane + copper cable. 1 kW. Deionized water (glass bottle) + empty polyethylene bottle -> ultrapure water + empty glass bottle (5 s). Plain distilled water is not accepted (run it through an ion exchange column first).
Water goes through distillation -> ion exchange (ions) -> reverse osmosis (organics, particles, germs) -> UV at 254 nm (kills germs, breaks down organics).
Real systems keep water circulating nonstop: if it stands still, germs grow in the pipes and CO2 from the air dissolves, lowering the purity.
Approximation: membrane fouling, recirculation and resistivity measurement are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_sulfate.no: Bright blue crystals. Pass electricity through their solution and copper comes out.
Malachite + 2 sulfuric acid (bottles returned) + water bucket make 2. The liquid for the electroplating bath. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (oral), eye irritant, hazardous to aquatic life (long-term).
Cu2CO3(OH)2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2CuSO4 + CO2 + 3H2O. The blue comes from water molecules attached to the copper ions (CuSO4·5H2O); dried, it turns white.
Long called blue vitriol, it went into Bordeaux mixture (1885) against mildew in vineyards. Today's chip copper wiring is plated out of copper sulfate solution too.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_sulfate.pl: Approximation: the carbon dioxide by-product is not produced. Dissolving copper in concentrated sulfuric acid is not included.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_wax_moul: A beeswax impression brushed with graphite powder so it conducts electricity.
Honeycomb (beeswax) + graphite. Goes in the cathode slot (where copper deposits) of the electroplating bath.
Wax does not conduct, so copper will not deposit on it. Coating it with graphite (conductive carbon) makes the whole surface a cathode.
Around 1840 Murray in Britain coated wax and plaster moulds with graphite, so anyone could do electrotyping ⚠️.
Approximation: the mould's shape (what it copies) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_electrotyp: Copper deposited by electricity that copies the mould's shape exactly.
Made in the electroplating bath. Each one is 63.5 g of copper (1 mol) and takes 193 kC of charge (= 2 x 96485 C).
Faraday's law: the amount deposited is proportional to the charge passed. Each Cu2+ ion needs two electrons, so 1 mol (63.5 g) needs 2F (about 190,000 coulombs).

In 1838 Jacobi (German-born, working in Russia) announced electrotyping ('galvanoplastics'). It led to printing plates, copies of medals and sculptures, and later electroplating and chip copper wiring.
Approximation: 1 item = 1 mol of copper. Voltage is fixed at about 1 V.
block.semiconductor-lab.electroplating_b: A tank that deposits copper onto a mould by passing electricity through copper sulfate solution.

7 soda-lime glass + copper cable. 2 kW (about 1 V, 2000 A). Top: copper ingot (anode), middle: copper sulfate, bottom: graphite-coated wax mould (cathode). One electrotype per 63.5 g of copper. The copper sulfate is not used up (the anode dissolves by the same amount). Watch the screen: copper mass rises in step with the charge.
Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu; anode: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-. Copper in the liquid is only carried from anode to cathode, so the copper sulfate is not consumed.

In 1840 the Elkington brothers patented silver plating, and plating tableware became an industry. In 1997 IBM switched chip wiring from aluminium to copper plated into trenches from copper sulfate (the damascene process).
Approximation: voltage is fixed; bath concentration, temperature and additives are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.solvay_tower.not: A tower that makes soda from salt and limestone. The ammonia inside goes round and round and is used again and again.

6 iron + soda-lime glass + copper cable + furnace. 5 kW. 2 salt + 1 calcite (limestone) -> 1 sodium carbonate (15 s). Add ammonia water first (4 units per bottle; the empty bottle comes out). The ammonia comes back each run; only 1 unit is lost every 16 runs. The calcium chloride by-product liquid is thrown away.

NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 (precipitates, as baking soda barely dissolves in cold water) + NH4Cl. Heating the baking soda gives sodium carbonate. Lime turns NH4Cl back into NH3. Overall 2NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2, with no ammonia used up.

Ernest Solvay of Belgium patented it in 1861 and started a plant in 1865. It replaced the Leblanc process, which fouled the air with hydrochloric acid gas; in the 20th century almost all soda was made this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.solvay_tower.pla: Approximation: the whole plant is one block. The calcium chloride by-product ([2-13], on hold) is not produced. Ammonia amounts are symbolic units.
item.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.note1: A very strong acid mixture that even dissolves gold. Make it right before you use it.
item.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.note2: 3 hydrochloric acid + 1 nitric acid + 4 empty glass bottles -> 4 (bottles returned). + gold ingot + empty bottle -> chloroauric acid. It cannot be stored: while you carry it, sooner or later (about 5 minutes on average) it turns into spent aqua regia. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, serious eye damage, acute toxicity (inhaled), oxidizer. Gives off toxic chlorine and nitrosyl chloride. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.note3: Nitric acid slowly oxidizes gold, and chloride ions immediately pull it into solution as the complex ion [AuCl4]-: Au + HNO3 + 4HCl -> HAuCl4 + NO + 2H2O. Nitric acid alone, or hydrochloric acid alone, cannot dissolve gold.
item.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.note4: A 13th-century alchemical text (Pseudo-Geber) describes it ⚠️. In 1940 George de Hevesy dissolved the gold Nobel medals of von Laue and Franck in aqua regia so the Nazis could not seize them, and left the jar on a lab shelf. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals were recast.
