item.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.placeh: Approximation: it does not decay inside a chest (time only counts while you carry it). The year 1300 is ⚠️.
message.semiconductor-lab.aqua_regia.dec: The gases escaped from the aqua regia; it has lost its power
Aqua regia that has lost its power to dissolve gold over time.
Aqua regia turns into this while you carry it. It cannot dissolve gold. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (dilute acids).
Nitrosyl chloride and chlorine escape as gases, leaving dilute hydrochloric and nitric acids. Aqua regia is always mixed just before use.
In chip fabs and precious-metal plants too, aqua regia is mixed on the spot and never stored.
Approximation: the exact contents are not modelled.
A yellow liquid with gold dissolved in it. Gold can be recovered from it.
Aqua regia + gold ingot + empty glass bottle (the aqua regia bottle is returned). + a bag of sulfur dioxide -> gold powder. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, skin sensitizer.
HAuCl4. Gold is dissolved as the complex ion [AuCl4]-.
Used for recovering and refining gold (the electrolyte of the Wohlwill process).
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_powder.note1: Brown gold powder taken out of the liquid. Melt it and it turns back into shiny gold.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_powder.note2: Chloroauric acid + a bag of sulfur dioxide (bottle returned). Smelt it into a gold ingot.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_powder.note3: Sulfur dioxide gives electrons to the gold ions and turns them back into gold atoms (reduction): 2HAuCl4 + 3SO2 + 6H2O -> 2Au + 3H2SO4 + 8HCl. Very fine gold particles absorb light and look brown.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_powder.note4: Gold was recovered this way after the war from the aqua regia holding Hevesy's medals, and the Nobel Foundation recast them.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_powder.place: Approximation: the by-product acids are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.borosilicate_batc: Sand, boron powder and soda mixed together. Melt it in a strong fire for heat-resistant glass.
6 sand + boron trioxide + sodium carbonate make 6. Melt in a blast furnace (fire strengthened by bellows, about 1300 C or more) for borosilicate glass. A plain furnace cannot melt it.
About SiO2 80%, B2O3 13%, Na2O 4% (almost no lime). It melts less easily than soda-lime glass, so it needs a strong fire.
In Jena, Germany, Schott worked with Abbe and Zeiss, trying glass compositions one by one until he found it.
Approximation: the alumina (about 2%) is left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.borosilicate_glas: Glass that hardly cracks over a flame. The beakers and flasks of the science room.
Melt the batch in a blast furnace. It does not crack on a campfire (soda-lime glass cracks into cullet; compare them).
It expands with heat by about 3.3x10^-6 per K, a third of soda-lime glass (about 9x10^-6 per K). When suddenly heated, hot and cold parts stretch by nearly the same amount, so it hardly cracks.

Made by Schott in Germany in 1893; Corning in the USA sold it as Pyrex from 1915. It was essential for glass apparatus that gets hot, like vacuum pumps (Gaede's mercury diffusion pump [5-05]) and vacuum tubes ⚠️.
Approximation: thermal expansion is only explained; the game shows it as cracking or not.
item.semiconductor-lab.cracked_glass.not: Glass that cracked and broke when put on a fire.
Soda-lime glass on a campfire turns into this. Remelt it in a furnace to get soda-lime glass back.
Only the part touching the flame expands quickly while the cold parts around it do not, so pulling forces build up in the glass and it breaks (thermal shock).
Glassworks mix broken glass (cullet) back into the batch. It melts more easily and saves fuel.
item.semiconductor-lab.cracked_glass.pla: Approximation: it always cracks on a campfire.
block.semiconductor-lab.chromatography_c: A thin tube packed with powder. Run mixed colours through it and they separate colour by colour.

2 soda-lime glass + calcite (calcium carbonate). Right-click with leaf pigment extract to soak it into the top. Right-click with benzene to wash it through: orange carotene (comes out first) and green chlorophyll (stays as a band) come out. Without the running liquid nothing separates.

Carried by the running liquid, substances that stick to the powder more move more slowly. Carotene, which sticks least, leads; then xanthophyll (yellow), chlorophyll a (blue-green) and b (yellow-green) form bands.

In 1906 Tsvet in Russia separated leaf pigments into coloured bands in a tube of calcium carbonate and called it chromatography, 'colour writing'. It grew into Martin and Synge's partition chromatography (1941, Nobel Prize 1952) and gas chromatography (1952), now used to measure tiny impurities left in trichlorosilane and noble gases.
Approximation: xanthophyll and chlorophyll a and b are lumped together. The column packing is not used up.
message.semiconductor-lab.chromatography: The pigments soaked into the top. Now run the liquid (benzene)
Pigments are already loaded. Wash them through with benzene
Bands formed: orange (carotene) came out first at the bottom; yellow, blue-green and yellow-green (chlorophyll) above
item.semiconductor-lab.leaf_pigment_extr: A dark green liquid: the colours of leaves dissolved in alcohol.
4 leaves + ethanol (bottle returned) + empty glass bottle. Put it into a chromatography column. ⚠ Ethanol is flammable.
Hidden behind green chlorophyll are yellow and orange pigments too (carotene, xanthophyll). Autumn colours appear when chlorophyll breaks down and these show through.
With this extract Tsvet showed that leaf colour is not one pigment but several.
Approximation: the kind of leaf does not change the pigment amounts.
item.semiconductor-lab.carotene.note1: The orange colour of carrots. Leaves have it too.
item.semiconductor-lab.carotene.note2: In the chromatography column it is washed out first by the benzene.
item.semiconductor-lab.carotene.note3: A long molecule of only carbon and hydrogen; it barely sticks to calcium carbonate (low polarity), so it moves fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.carotene.note4: The body turns it into vitamin A. The name comes from carrot.
item.semiconductor-lab.carotene.placehol: Approximation: beta-carotene and other carotenes are not separated.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorophyll.note1: The green of leaves. It gathers light that plants use to make food.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorophyll.note2: Stays in the chromatography column as a green band (dug out).
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorophyll.note3: A ring molecule with magnesium at its centre. With many O and N atoms it sticks to calcium carbonate (high polarity) and moves slowly.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorophyll.note4: Willstatter won the 1915 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for chlorophyll research. Solar-cell researchers also study how it gathers light.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorophyll.place: Approximation: chlorophyll a and b and xanthophyll are lumped together.
Salt with sulfuric acid poured on it. Heated, it gives off a choking gas (hydrogen chloride).

2 salt + sulfuric acid (bottle returned). Roast it in a furnace for salt cake (the gas goes into the air). Or combine it with a water bucket + empty glass bottle on the crafting table: the gas is absorbed into hydrochloric acid and the salt cake stays in the grid (absorption tower). ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion. Hydrogen chloride is toxic.
2NaCl + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2HCl. Hydrogen chloride dissolves readily in water as hydrochloric acid.

Lesson: Leblanc works at first dumped hydrogen chloride gas from their chimneys, killing nearby fields and woods. In 1836 Gossage absorbed it in water in a coke-packed tower, and Britain's Alkali Act of 1863 (an early air-pollution law) required 95% of the gas to be captured.
Approximation: the heating stages (low and high temperature) are not separated.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt_cake.note1: A white salt made from salt and sulfuric acid. An intermediate of the Leblanc process.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt_cake.note2: Roast the salt cake charge in a furnace, or it is left over from the absorption-tower crafting. + calcite + charcoal -> black ash charge.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt_cake.note3: Na2SO4. Also used in glassmaking and paper pulp (the kraft process).
item.semiconductor-lab.salt_cake.note4: It is the same substance (as a hydrate) as 'Glauber's salt', sold as a medicine by Glauber in 17th-century Germany.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt_cake.placeho: Approximation: the hydrate (Glauber's salt) is not distinguished.
Salt cake, limestone and charcoal mixed. Roasted in a furnace it becomes black ash.
Salt cake + calcite + charcoal. Roast in a furnace for black ash.
Na2SO4 + 2C + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaS + 2CO2. Carbon takes the oxygen from the sulfate, and the leftover sulfur pairs with calcium.
In the late 18th century France ran short of soda from plant ashes, and the Academy of Sciences offered a prize for making soda from salt.
Approximation: the revolving furnace is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.black_ash.note1: A black lump of soda mixed with smelly waste. In water only the soda dissolves out.
item.semiconductor-lab.black_ash.note2: Roast the black ash charge in a furnace. + water bucket -> sodium carbonate (the insoluble calcium sulfide waste, galligu, stays in the grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.black_ash.note3: Sodium carbonate dissolves in water but calcium sulfide (CaS) does not, so washing with water separates them (leaching).
item.semiconductor-lab.black_ash.note4: Lesson: the calcium sulfide waste ('galligu') was piled in heaps and, in the rain, gave off foul, toxic hydrogen sulfide. Leblanc devised the process in 1791, but his works were seized in the Revolution and he died in poverty in 1806.
item.semiconductor-lab.black_ash.placeho: Approximation: sulfur is recovered from the waste via [2-11] (hydrochloric acid -> hydrogen sulfide -> Claus process).
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminosilicate_b: Sand, alumina and soda mixed. Melted in a strong fire it becomes glass that can be strengthened.
5 sand + alumina + sodium carbonate make 6. Melt in a blast furnace for aluminosilicate glass (a plain furnace cannot).
Aluminium opens up the glass network so ions move more easily, letting ion exchange strengthen it deeply.
Smartphone cover glass is made of aluminosilicate glass like this.
Approximation: minor components such as magnesia are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminosilicate_g: A hard glass containing alumina. Not strengthened yet, so it breaks if struck.
Melt the batch in a blast furnace. 4 + saltpeter -> glass in a potassium nitrate bath. Cracks when struck with a hammerstone.
It holds plenty of sodium ions, which are later swapped for potassium ions.
Corning's 1960s strengthened glass 'Chemcor' used glass like this, but it did not sell at the time.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_in_salt_bat: Glass ready to be dipped in a melted salt (potassium nitrate).
4 aluminosilicate glass + saltpeter make 4. In a furnace (the salt melts at about 400 C) it becomes chemically strengthened glass. ⚠ Saltpeter is an oxidizer (GHS).
In molten KNO3 at about 400 C, Na+ at the glass surface trades places with K+ from the bath (ion exchange). The glass does not melt, so its shape stays the same.
Real glass is soaked for hours; the longer it soaks, the deeper the strengthened layer.
Approximation: soaking time and layer depth are not modelled; the bath uses one saltpeter per batch.
item.semiconductor-lab.strengthened_glas: Glass whose surface is squeezed tight, so it hardly breaks when struck.
Made from glass in a potassium nitrate bath in a furnace. A hammerstone does not crack it (ordinary, borosilicate and unstrengthened glass do; compare them).
Big K+ ions are pushed into spaces left by small Na+ ions, leaving the surface squeezed (compressive stress). Cracks grow by pulling, so they cannot start until they beat that squeeze.

S. S. Kistler reported strengthening by ion exchange in 1962. In 2007 an improved strengthened aluminosilicate glass was used for smartphone screens; today nearly every smartphone face is this kind of glass ⚠️.
Approximation: shown only as cracks or not (real glass still breaks under a big enough blow).
A soft metal: indium with a little tin. Material for transparent electrodes.
8 indium + tin ingot make 9. Deposit it on borosilicate glass in the vacuum evaporator.
About 9:1 indium to tin. Oxidized later, it becomes ITO: In2O3 with about 10% SnO2.

Reich and Richter found indium in 1863 by the indigo line in the spectrum of Freiberg sphalerite. Most indium is still a by-product of zinc smelting (the same indium the roasting furnace gives from sphalerite).
Approximation: the melting step for making the alloy is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.indium_tin_coated: Glass with a thin metal film. Still silvery; you cannot see through it.
Made in the vacuum evaporator from borosilicate glass + indium-tin alloy. Bake in a furnace (oxidized by air) for ITO glass.
A metal's free electrons reflect light, so a metal film is opaque. As an oxide it has fewer electrons and lets light through.
Depositing a metal film and then oxidizing it by baking in air was one early way to make transparent electrodes. Today ITO is sputtered on directly ([9-26]).
Approximation: film thickness is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.ito_glass.note1: Glass you can see through that still conducts electricity. Used in smartphone screens and touch panels.
item.semiconductor-lab.ito_glass.note2: Bake indium-tin coated glass in a furnace. Plain glass does not conduct, but this surface film does. ⚠ Inhaled indium compound dust damages the lungs (GHS: specific target organ toxicity).
item.semiconductor-lab.ito_glass.note3: Sn4+ in the In2O3 crystal leaves a spare electron, so it conducts like an n-type semiconductor. But it has far fewer electrons than a metal, so visible light passes instead of being reflected.
item.semiconductor-lab.ito_glass.note4: In 1907 Badeker first reported a 'transparent, conducting film' of thin cadmium oxide. Indium oxide films were studied in the 1950s, and ITO became the electrode of LCDs, touch panels and solar cells (the first year of ITO varies by source ⚠️).
item.semiconductor-lab.ito_glass.placeho: Approximation: resistance and transparency figures are not modelled. The year is ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus_under_: White phosphorus sealed in glass with non-burning nitrogen gas. With no air, it does not burn when heated.

White phosphorus (water jar returned) + a bag of nitrogen. Furnace (about 250 C) -> red phosphorus. ⚠ White phosphorus is highly toxic and ignites by itself in air (GHS: pyrophoric, acute toxicity, skin corrosion).
White phosphorus is made of small tetrahedral P4 molecules. Heated without air, the molecules open up and link into the long chains of red phosphorus.
Schrotter heated it in carbon dioxide or nitrogen instead of air, changing it without burning it.
Approximation: the sealed glass container is not returned.
item.semiconductor-lab.red_phosphorus.no: A reddish-brown powder. The same element as white phosphorus, yet it does not burn in air and needs no water jar. It coats the striking side of a matchbox.

Bake white phosphorus under nitrogen in a furnace. Compare with white phosphorus: it needs a water jar, and heated in air it burns to white smoke (phosphorus pentoxide). ⚠ GHS: flammable solid (ignites with friction or heat), hazardous to aquatic life.

Phosphorus atoms are linked into long chains and networks, so it is more stable and less toxic than P4 molecules. Forms of the same element with different structures are allotropes (like diamond and graphite).

Lesson: in white-phosphorus match factories, workers got 'phossy jaw', their jawbones rotting from the vapour. In 1855 Lundstrom in Sweden made the safety match by moving red phosphorus to the box; later white-phosphorus matches were banned (Berne Convention, 1906).
item.semiconductor-lab.red_phosphorus.pl: Approximation: the match head (potassium chlorate) is not made.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus_pentox: A white, smoke-like powder made when white phosphorus burns in air. It soaks up water very strongly.
Made by heating white phosphorus in a furnace as it is (without nitrogen): it burned. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, serious eye damage. Reacts violently with water to form phosphoric acid.
P4 + 5O2 -> P4O10. It takes water from its surroundings so strongly that labs use it as a drying agent.
Dissolved in water it becomes phosphoric acid, used in fertilizer, food and chip etching (etching aluminium).
Approximation: the water jar burns and is not returned.
item.semiconductor-lab.alkali_waste.note: Smelly grey waste left after the soda is washed out. Sulfur can be recovered from it.
Left in the crafting grid when black ash is washed with water (making sodium carbonate). + hydrochloric acid -> hydrogen sulfide.
Mostly calcium sulfide, CaS. The sulfur from the sulfuric acid is locked up here.

Lesson: the waste was heaped around the works and, in the rain, gave off foul, toxic hydrogen sulfide. In 1882 Chance drove hydrogen sulfide out of it with carbon dioxide, and with the Claus process (1883) sulfur could be recovered.
item.semiconductor-lab.alkali_waste.plac: Approximation: hydrochloric acid (the lab method) releases the hydrogen sulfide instead of Chance's carbon dioxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_sulfide_: A very harmful gas that smells of rotten eggs. Carrying it, a little may leak and make you feel sick.

Alkali waste + hydrochloric acid (bottle returned). Right-click an alumina catalyst tube over a fire -> sulfur (Claus process). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled, category 2), flammable gas, hazardous to aquatic life. At high levels it numbs the nose so you cannot smell it. Treated only as an industrial material.
CaS + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2S. Claus process: 2H2S + O2 -> 2S + 2H2O (on hot alumina, with oxygen from the air).
Described by Scheele in 1777. Hydrogen sulfide from oil and natural gas is still turned into sulfur by the Claus process; most of the world's sulfur is made this way.
Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. Leaks do not use up the bag.
message.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_sulfi: Rotten-egg smell... hydrogen sulfide leaked from the bag (at high levels your nose goes numb and you cannot notice)
message.semiconductor-lab.alumina_cataly: The hydrogen sulfide reacted with oxygen in the air and became sulfur (Claus process)
block.semiconductor-lab.bottle_machine.n: A machine that keeps making bottles as long as it has glass. Nobody had to blow them by mouth anymore.

6 steel + bellows + copper cable + furnace. 2 kW. 1 soda-lime glass -> 1 glass bottle (1 s; running nonstop, 60 a minute). Hand-making on the crafting table (3 glass -> 3 bottles) is done one batch at a time by a person. Compare them.
It sucks molten glass up into a mould (by vacuum), moves it to a second mould and blows air in to shape the bottle. Breath and hands were replaced by vacuum, compressed air and moulds.

In 1903 Owens in the USA built a fully automatic bottle machine (ASME Landmark #86), replacing work done by glassblowers and child helpers (it also helped reduce child labour ⚠️). The 1926 ribbon machine (ASME #81) made up to about 2000 light-bulb envelopes a minute, making bulbs cheap.
block.semiconductor-lab.bottle_machine.p: Approximation: bottles per minute is a game value; real speeds varied greatly by machine and year ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_alloy.note1: Nickel mixed with aluminium. Dissolve out only the aluminium and you get a spongy nickel catalyst.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_alloy.note2: Nickel + aluminium ingot. + sodium hydroxide -> Raney nickel.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_alloy.note3: Aluminium dissolves in sodium hydroxide but nickel does not; the aluminium leaves fine pores behind.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_alloy.note4: Devised by Murray Raney in the USA in 1926.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_alloy.place: Approximation: the melting step for the alloy is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_nickel.note: Black nickel full of tiny pores. A catalyst that helps add hydrogen to things.

Alloy + sodium hydroxide. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). Used for phenol -> cyclohexanol and adiponitrile -> hexamethylenediamine. ⚠ GHS: pyrophoric (burns in air when dry), suspected carcinogen, skin sensitizer.
Its huge surface holds lots of hydrogen and hands it on to other molecules.
Still used in large amounts to hydrogenate nylon precursors, medicines and edible oils.
item.semiconductor-lab.raney_nickel.plac: Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out. The fire risk when dry is only explained.
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclohexanol.note: A thick liquid: phenol with hydrogen added. One step before one of nylon's two raw materials.
Phenol + 3 bags of hydrogen + Raney nickel (returned). + 2 nitric acid -> adipic acid. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin irritant.
C6H5OH + 3H2 -> C6H11OH. Hydrogen adds to the ring's double bonds, turning the flat ring into a chair-shaped one.
1930s nylon was made from coal-tar phenol; today it comes from benzene (petroleum).
item.semiconductor-lab.cyclohexanol.plac: Approximation: temperature and pressure are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.adipic_acid.note1: A white powder. One of nylon 66's two raw materials.
item.semiconductor-lab.adipic_acid.note2: Cyclohexanol + 2 nitric acid (bottles returned). + 2 ammonia water -> ammonium adipate. + hexamethylenediamine -> nylon salt. ⚠ GHS: serious eye damage.
item.semiconductor-lab.adipic_acid.note3: Nitric acid splits the ring open into a six-carbon chain with COOH at each end: HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH.
item.semiconductor-lab.adipic_acid.note4: This oxidation gives off nitrous oxide (N2O, a strong greenhouse gas), so modern plants capture and destroy it.
item.semiconductor-lab.adipic_acid.place: Approximation: the nitrous oxide by-product is not produced.
A salt of adipic acid and ammonia. Heated, it loses water and becomes adiponitrile.
Adipic acid + 2 ammonia water (bottles returned). Furnace -> adiponitrile.
COOH forms a salt with NH4+, and heat removes water twice to give -CN (a nitrile).
Really it is vaporized and passed over a catalyst at about 350 C.
Approximation: the catalyst (such as boron phosphate) is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.adiponitrile.note: A liquid with nitrogen at each end. Adding hydrogen makes nylon's other raw material.
Bake ammonium adipate in a furnace. + 4 bags of hydrogen + Raney nickel (returned) -> hexamethylenediamine. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
NC-(CH2)4-CN. Four hydrogens added to C≡N give -CH2NH2 (an amine).
Today it is made by electrolysis (electrohydrodimerization of acrylonitrile, 1965) or from butadiene.
item.semiconductor-lab.hexamethylenediam: White crystals with NH2 at each end. Nylon 66's other raw material.
Adiponitrile + 4 hydrogen + Raney nickel. + adipic acid -> nylon salt. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, acute toxicity.
H2N-(CH2)6-NH2: six carbons. Paired with adipic acid (six carbons), hence 'nylon 66'.
Nitrogen from ammonia, made from the air's nitrogen, ends up here.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_salt.note1: A salt pairing adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine one to one. Heated, it forms long chains.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_salt.note2: Adipic acid + hexamethylenediamine. In an autoclave (with water, about 270 C and 15 atm or more) it becomes nylon 66. With too little pressure it comes back as salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_salt.note3: Making a salt first locks the acid and amine at exactly 1:1 (if one is in excess, the chains stay short).
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_salt.note4: Carothers' team realized that exact balance was the key to long chains.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_salt.placeh: Approximation: solution strength is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_66.note1: Strong and light: the material of the first fully synthetic fibre.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_66.note2: Made from nylon salt in the autoclave. Melt it in a furnace and draw it into 4 nylon fibre.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_66.note3: The acid's COOH and the amine's NH2 join by giving off water (an amide bond, the same link as in the proteins of silk and wool), repeated hundreds of times into a long chain.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_66.note4: Made by Carothers' team at DuPont in February 1935. It was advertised as made from coal, air and water. The work also confirmed Staudinger's idea that polymers are long-chain molecules.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_66.placehol: Approximation: molecular weight is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_fiber.note1: Thin, strong, stretchy thread. Used for stockings and fishing line.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_fiber.note2: Melt nylon 66 in a furnace and draw it into 4. Compare with linen thread ([0-06] flax): linen is strong but does not stretch, creases and soaks up water; nylon stretches and springs back, absorbs little water and is not eaten by moths.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_fiber.note3: Melted, pushed through tiny holes, cooled and then stretched, the chains line up in one direction and get strong (drawing). Team member Julian Hill found in 1930 that fibres could be pulled from molten polymers.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_fiber.note4: Sold as stockings from 1939, replacing silk. In World War II it went into parachutes and ropes.
item.semiconductor-lab.nylon_fiber.place: Approximation: thread thickness and strength figures are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.acrylic_acid.note: A sharp-smelling liquid. Linked up, it becomes acrylic resin.

3 acetylene + 3 carbon monoxide + water bucket + nickel carbonyl make 3 (Reppe process). Glycerin + 3 acrylic acid -> triacrylate. ⚠ GHS: flammable, skin corrosion, acute toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
HC≡CH + CO + H2O -> CH2=CH-COOH. Nickel attaches the carbon monoxide to acetylene. A C=C double bond remains, so light or heat can link it up.
In 1930s Germany, Reppe found ways to handle acetylene safely under pressure and opened up acetylene chemistry ('Reppe chemistry'). Acrylic acid is now made from petroleum propylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.acrylic_acid.plac: Approximation: conditions are not described (DESIGN). The nickel carbonyl is used up.
item.semiconductor-lab.glycerol_triacryl: A liquid with three acrylic 'arms'. Light joins the arms into a hard network.
Glycerin + 3 acrylic acid + sulfuric acid (catalyst, bottle returned). The main material of light-curing resin. ⚠ GHS: skin irritant, skin sensitizer.
One acrylic acid is esterified onto each of glycerin's three OH groups. With three arms, linking makes a 3D network (one arm would give soft chains).
Light-cured adhesives, dental fillings, nail gels and 3D-printer resins all use acrylics with two, three or more arms like this.
Approximation: real stereolithography resins mix many acrylics (oligomers).
item.semiconductor-lab.aluminium_chlorid: A dry white powder. It helps attach other things to a benzene ring.
Aluminium + 3 bags of chlorine. Material for benzophenone. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride.
2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3. It craves electrons (a Lewis acid), pulling off chlorine to make a positive carbon that attacks benzene.
Friedel and Crafts discovered this reaction (the Friedel-Crafts reaction) in 1877.
Approximation: it is used up (really more than a catalytic amount is needed too).
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_tetrachlor: A heavy liquid: carbon with four chlorines. Once used in fire extinguishers and dry cleaning.

Chloroform + a bag of chlorine. Material for benzophenone. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, carcinogenic (category 2), specific target organ toxicity (liver), damages the ozone layer. Treated only as an industrial material.
It damages the liver and the ozone layer, so its use was phased out under the Montreal Protocol.
Approximation: the hydrogen chloride by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzophenone.note: White crystals that, hit by UV light, start other molecules linking up.
2 benzene + carbon tetrachloride + aluminium chloride + water bucket. The photoinitiator of light-curing resin. ⚠ GHS: suspected carcinogen (category 2), hazardous to aquatic life.
Two benzenes attach to the carbon of CCl4 by the Friedel-Crafts reaction, and water turns it into C=O. Absorbing UV, it pulls a hydrogen from an amine and makes radicals.
Because it absorbs UV, it is also used in sunscreens and to keep things from fading in sunlight.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzophenone.plac: Approximation: two reaction steps are combined into one.
item.semiconductor-lab.photopolymer_resi: A liquid that hardens only where light hits it. The material of light-curing 3D printers. Carry it into the sun and it sets.

3 triacrylate + benzophenone + hexamethylenediamine (amine) make 3. Standing in sunlight (day, open sky above) while holding it turns it into cured resin; shade or a chest keeps it liquid. Like the negative resist [2-30], lit areas link up and stop dissolving.
UV -> benzophenone takes hydrogen from the amine -> radicals -> acrylic C=C bonds link one after another -> three arms make a network and it sets (radical photopolymerization).

In 1981 Hideo Kodama in Nagoya reported building solid objects by curing resin layer by layer with light, and in 1984 Hull in the USA filed a stereolithography patent ⚠️. Chip photoresists and 3D-printer resins work the same way.
Approximation: wavelength and intensity are not modelled (sunlit or not). The years are ⚠️.
message.semiconductor-lab.photopolymer_r: UV in the sunlight set the resin
item.semiconductor-lab.cured_photopolyme: Resin set by light. It will not melt again.
Made by holding light-curing resin in sunlight. It does not melt when heated (it is a network).
The three acrylic arms have linked into a 3D network (crosslinked).
A 3D printer picks where to cure with light, one layer at a time, to build a solid ([P-04]).
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrite_ore.note1: An ore that glitters like gold, so it is called 'fool's gold'. Really it is iron and sulfur.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrite_ore.note2: FeS2. Found all over the overworld (height -32 to 80). Mine with a stone pickaxe or better. Leave the raw pyrite in water and it turns into green vitriol.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrite_ore.note3: It readily forms cube-shaped crystals. It has too much sulfur to be a good iron ore.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrite_ore.note4: Struck against flint it throws sparks, so it was once used for fire-making and in wheel-lock guns. The name comes from the Greek for 'fire'.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrite.note1: A golden mineral. Left in water, it slowly turns into green crystals (green vitriol).
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrite.note2: Drop it in water and wait (about 2 minutes; nothing happens on land) for green vitriol. ⚠ The weathering water turns strongly acidic (acid mine water is pollution).
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrite.note3: 2FeS2 + 7O2 + 2H2O -> 2FeSO4 + 2H2SO4. Water and oxygen from the air turn the sulfur into sulfate.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrite.note4: England's 16th-19th century 'copperas' works left heaps of pyrite in the rain for years, then boiled the seepage with scrap iron to make green vitriol. Lesson: acid water from old mines (acid mine drainage) still pollutes rivers today.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrite.placeholde: Approximation: years of weathering take minutes.
item.semiconductor-lab.green_vitriol.not: Pale green crystals. Roasted, they give off a thick, strong acid (oil of vitriol).

Made by weathering pyrite in water. + quartz still (glass retort, returned) + empty glass bottle -> oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid). Colcothar stays in the crafting grid. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (oral), eye irritant.
FeSO4·7H2O. Roasted: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3; SO3 absorbed in water gives H2SO4.
It was also an ink ingredient (with oak galls for black 'iron gall ink'); much of the medieval world's writing used this ink.
item.semiconductor-lab.green_vitriol.pla: Approximation: water of crystallization is not modelled; no sulfur dioxide is produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.colcothar.note1: A red rust powder. Old paint, and the 'rouge' for polishing lenses.
item.semiconductor-lab.colcothar.note2: Left in the crafting grid when green vitriol is roasted for oil of vitriol.
item.semiconductor-lab.colcothar.note3: Fe2O3. Its very fine, hard grains polish glass and metal to a shine (jeweller's rouge).
item.semiconductor-lab.colcothar.note4: In Japanese it is called 'bengara', after a red pigment from Bengal; it coloured the red houses of Fukiya.
item.semiconductor-lab.colcothar.placeho: Approximation: it has no polishing use yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_fluorid: A white powder that lets current flow in the electrolysis that frees fluorine.
Potassium carbonate + hydrofluoric acid (the lead bottle returns). Electrolyte of the fluorine cell (not used up). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, eye irritation.
Hydrogen fluoride alone barely conducts electricity. Moissan dissolved potassium fluoride in it so current could flow.
Plants today electrolyse a molten KF and HF salt (KF·2HF) at about 100 C.
item.semiconductor-lab.triethylaluminium: A very dangerous liquid that bursts into flame just by touching air. A catalyst ingredient.

Aluminium + a bag of hydrogen + 3 bags of ethylene (Ziegler's direct process). + titanium tetrachloride -> Ziegler-Natta catalyst. ⚠ GHS: pyrophoric liquid, releases flammable gas with water, skin corrosion. Treated only as an industrial material.
2Al + 3H2 + 6C2H4 -> 2Al(C2H5)3. An 'organometallic' with aluminium bonded directly to carbon.
In the 1950s, studying aluminium and ethylene, Ziegler noticed by chance that a trace of nickel changed the reaction (the 'nickel effect'); he then tried metal after metal and arrived at titanium.
Approximation: handling in sealed containers under nitrogen is only explained.
item.semiconductor-lab.ziegler_natta_cat: A titanium-aluminium catalyst. Linking ethylene one by one on it makes stiff polyethylene at ordinary pressure.

Titanium tetrachloride + triethylaluminium. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). 4 ethylene -> high-density polyethylene. Also used for polyacetylene [2-55]. ⚠ GHS: pyrophoric, skin corrosion.
Ethylene binds at an open site on a titanium atom and is inserted one at a time at the root of the growing chain, giving straight, unbranched chains.

Ziegler in Germany made polyethylene this way in 1953, and Natta in Italy made ordered polypropylene in 1954 (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1963). A little earlier, in 1951, Hogan and Banks at Phillips Petroleum in the USA had made similar stiff polyethylene with a chromium oxide catalyst.
Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out. The chromium-oxide Phillips catalyst is not implemented.
item.semiconductor-lab.hdpe.note1: Stiff white polyethylene. Buckets, bottle caps, kerosene cans.
item.semiconductor-lab.hdpe.note2: 4 ethylene + Ziegler-Natta catalyst (returned). No electricity and no high pressure needed. Compare with polyethylene from the high-pressure reactor [2-37] (soft, plastic bags).
item.semiconductor-lab.hdpe.note3: Straight unbranched chains pack neatly (more crystalline), so it is denser (about 0.95), stiffer and more heat-resistant. High-pressure polyethylene has many branches that leave gaps, so it is less dense (about 0.92) and softer.
item.semiconductor-lab.hdpe.note4: PET bottles are a different plastic, but their caps are this kind (or polypropylene).
item.semiconductor-lab.hdpe.placeholder: Approximation: molecular weight and density figures are only explained.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyacetylene_fil: A silvery, shiny plastic film. As it is, it hardly conducts electricity.
4 bags of acetylene + Ziegler-Natta catalyst (returned). + iodine -> doped polyacetylene. With the continuity tester, the bulb does not light.
(CH)n: a long chain of alternating single and double bonds (conjugated). Electrons can move a little along it, so it behaves like a semiconductor.
Around 1967, in a lab at Tokyo Institute of Technology, someone added 1000 times too much catalyst and got a silvery film instead of black powder.
Approximation: cis and trans are not distinguished; the 1000x catalyst is only explained.
item.semiconductor-lab.doped_polyacetyle: A plastic that conducts electricity like a metal after iodine was added.
Polyacetylene film + iodine. The continuity tester's bulb lights (compare with before doping). ⚠ Iodine irritates skin and eyes (GHS).
Iodine pulls electrons from the chain, leaving positive 'holes' that carry current (p-type). Like semiconductor doping [9-11], it adds charge carriers. Conductivity rose over a hundred million times.

In 1977 researchers from Japan and the USA (one was Alan MacDiarmid) showed that adding iodine makes it conduct (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2000). Lithium-ion battery research also began with attempts to use polyacetylene as an electrode.
Approximation: conductivity is fixed at roughly the 1977 value (about 30 S/cm); degradation in air is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.continuity_tester: A battery-and-bulb tool. Touch its wires to something to see if electricity flows.

Zinc + graphite rod (dry cell) + copper cable + soda-lime glass (bulb). Hold it in your main hand and the thing to test in the other, then right-click: it shows the conductivity (S/cm) and whether the bulb lights. Copper, iron, gold, graphite and doped polyacetylene light it; glass, polyethylene, PTFE and ultrapure water do not.
Conductivity (S/cm) ranges over 23 orders of magnitude, from 10^-18 (PTFE) to 10^5 (copper).
Whether something conducts depends on how many charge carriers (electrons or holes) can move: the difference between metals, semiconductors and insulators.
Approximation: rough room-temperature values; items not in the table cannot be measured.
message.semiconductor-lab.continuity_tes: Hold the thing to test in your other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.diethyl_ether.not: A strong-smelling liquid that evaporates quickly. Very flammable. The refrigerant of the first refrigerator.

2 ethanol (bottles returned) + sulfuric acid (bottle returned) + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle. Refrigerant for the hand-cranked ice machine. ⚠ GHS: flammable liquid (category 1), acute toxicity (oral), drowsiness. Forms explosive peroxides in air. Treated only as an industrial material.
2C2H5OH -> (C2H5)2O + H2O (the sulfuric acid takes the water). It boils at 34.6 C, evaporates very easily and takes a lot of heat from its surroundings as it does.
Cordus in Germany made it around 1540 as 'sweet oil of vitriol'. In 1846 Morton in the USA used it as a surgical anaesthetic, transforming surgery.
item.semiconductor-lab.cfc12_gas.note1: A gas called the dream refrigerant: non-flammable and non-toxic. But high in the sky it was destroying the ozone layer.
item.semiconductor-lab.cfc12_gas.note2: Carbon tetrachloride + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + antimony pentachloride (catalyst, returned). A refrigerant for the hand-cranked ice machine (unlike ether it never leaks away). But every ice made leaks a little into the sky and lowers the world's ozone (check with a Dobson meter). ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure, hazardous to the ozone layer.
item.semiconductor-lab.cfc12_gas.note3: CCl4 + 2HF -> CCl2F2 + 2HCl. It is so stable that it rises intact to the stratosphere, where strong UV breaks it apart and frees chlorine atoms; one chlorine atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules (it repeats like a catalyst).
item.semiconductor-lab.cfc12_gas.note4: In 1928 Midgley and colleagues at GM chose it to remove the poison and fire risks of ammonia and sulfur dioxide refrigerants. Lesson: in 1974 Molina and Rowland warned it destroys the ozone layer, and the Antarctic ozone hole was found in 1985. Under the 1987 Montreal Protocol every country stopped making it, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
item.semiconductor-lab.cfc12_gas.placeho: Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. Leak amounts and ozone loss/recovery are game values. During an ozone hole (below 220 DU), players in sunlight sometimes get sunburned (decision Q3-11).
item.semiconductor-lab.dobson_meter.note: An instrument that measures the ozone overhead. Right-click to read it.

Quartz tube (passes UV) + 2 iron + copper cable. Right-click for the world's ozone (Dobson units, DU). It starts at 300 DU; below 220 DU counts as an ozone hole. CFC leaks lower it; without leaks it recovers 1 DU per day. While there is an ozone hole, standing in sunlight sometimes gives sunburn (brief weakness).
It compares UV wavelengths that ozone absorbs strongly and weakly to work out how much ozone is overhead. 300 DU means all the ozone, squeezed to ground-level pressure, would be 3 mm thick.
Built by Dobson in Britain in 1924. In 1985 Farman and colleagues at the British Antarctic Survey found the Antarctic ozone hole with this instrument.
item.semiconductor-lab.dobson_meter.plac: Approximation: one value for the whole world, unchanged by place or season.
message.semiconductor-lab.fermentation_c: Pasteurized wine has no germs, so it will not turn to vinegar
item.semiconductor-lab.hfc23_gas.note1: A refrigerant made so as not to harm the ozone layer. But it is very good at warming the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.hfc23_gas.note2: Chloroform + 3 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + antimony pentachloride (catalyst, returned). Works as a refrigerant in the hand-cranked ice machine and does not lower the ozone (compare with CFC). ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure. A strong greenhouse gas.
item.semiconductor-lab.hfc23_gas.note3: CHF3. With no chlorine, it releases none in the stratosphere and does not destroy ozone. But it absorbs infrared strongly, warming the Earth over ten thousand times more than the same amount of carbon dioxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.hfc23_gas.note4: Lesson: HFCs replaced CFCs to save the ozone layer, then turned out to drive global warming. The 2016 Kigali Amendment set HFCs to be cut too (in force 2019). HFC-23 is also a large by-product of making R-22, which was a problem in itself.
item.semiconductor-lab.hfc23_gas.placeho: Approximation: the greenhouse effect is not tracked as a number in the game (explained only).
message.semiconductor-lab.ozone.sunburn: Strong UV through the ozone hole... you got sunburned (weakness)
item.semiconductor-lab.hydroxyacetopheno: The first material for the chemically amplified resist's resin.
Resist reactor: phenol + acetic anhydride + aluminium chloride → this + acetic acid. Hydrogen (Raney nickel) turns it into 4-hydroxystyrene.
An acetyl group is put on phenol (phenyl acetate), then aluminium chloride moves it across the ring (Fries rearrangement, 1908).
Also an industrial starting material for the painkiller paracetamol.
item.semiconductor-lab.protected_phs.not: The resin of chemically amplified resist, capped so that alkali cannot dissolve it.
Resist reactor: polyhydroxystyrene -> this (capped with t-BOC). With photoacid generator + xylene + glass bottle -> chemically amplified resist.
The phenol OH groups wear a t-BOC cap (protecting group). Acid plus heat removes the cap, the OH reappears and the film dissolves in alkali.
Polyhydroxystyrene absorbs little 248 nm light (novolac absorbs too much), so KrF light reaches the bottom of the film.
item.semiconductor-lab.protected_phs.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ the capping reagent (di-tert-butyl dicarbonate) is not made (it needs phosgene; decision Q3-16). The reactor is assumed to put the cap on.
item.semiconductor-lab.diphenyl_sulfoxid: The starting point of the photoacid generator: two benzene rings joined by sulfur.
Resist reactor: 2 benzene + sulfur dioxide + aluminium chloride → this.
Ph2SO. Adding one more benzene ring gives triphenylsulfonium (Ph3S⁺).
Attaching groups to benzene with aluminium chloride is the Friedel–Crafts reaction (1877).
Omitted: ⚠️ really made from thionyl chloride (SOCl2); sulfur dioxide stands in here.
item.semiconductor-lab.photoacid_generat: A powder that releases a strong acid when light hits it — the heart of chemically amplified resist.
Resist reactor: diphenyl sulfoxide + benzene + aluminium chloride + potassium hexafluoroantimonate -> this.
Triphenylsulfonium hexafluoroantimonate (Ph3S⁺ SbF6⁻). Light breaks it and releases HSbF6, an extremely strong acid. Found by Crivello in the 1970s.
IBM's 1982 chemically amplified resist used this salt. One acid made by light removes hundreds of caps when heated, so little light is needed.
item.semiconductor-lab.chemically_amplif: A resist that prints with short light such as the KrF laser (248 nm). Acid made by light is multiplied hundreds of times by heat.

Protected polyhydroxystyrene + photoacid generator + xylene + glass bottle (crafting). Spin-coat (positive) → expose → bake on the hot plate (PEB) → develop in alkali. Without the bake nothing dissolves.
Novolac (the older positive resist) absorbs too much light below 250 nm, so it never reaches the bottom. Chemically amplified resist absorbs a little and then the acid works as a catalyst.
Announced by IBM researchers in 1982; every KrF, ArF and EUV generation uses resists built on this idea.
Omitted: ⚠️ the real solvent is PGMEA or similar; xylene stands in here.
block.semiconductor-lab.resist_reactor.n: Makes the materials of chemically amplified resist (resin and photoacid generator). The combination you put in picks the reaction.

1.5 kW, 15 s each. Four inputs plus a catalyst slot. ① phenol + acetic anhydride + aluminium chloride ② 4-hydroxyacetophenone + acetic anhydride + hydrogen (Raney nickel) ③ 1-(4-acetoxyphenyl)ethanol ④ 4 4-acetoxystyrene ⑤ poly(4-acetoxystyrene) + ammonia water + methanol ⑥ polyhydroxystyrene ⑦ 2 benzene + sulfur dioxide + aluminium chloride ⑧ antimony trioxide + 2 potassium fluoride + 4 hydrofluoric acid + hydrogen peroxide ⑨ diphenyl sulfoxide + benzene + aluminium chloride + potassium hexafluoroantimonate. Anything extra stops it.
The resin (protected polyhydroxystyrene) comes from ①–⑥ (the real route: cap the OH with acetate, polymerize, then uncap), the photoacid generator (Ph3S⁺ SbF6⁻) from ⑦–⑨.
Hydrofluoric acid is used only as an industrial material, in lead or polyethylene containers (GHS: skull, corrosive). Benzene causes cancer.
block.semiconductor-lab.resist_reactor.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power, time and amounts are game values. The t-BOC reagent (not made: it needs phosgene) and thionyl chloride (approximated with sulfur dioxide) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetoxyphenyl_eth: One step before the styrene. Heat it to remove water and get the styrene.
In the resist reactor: 4-hydroxyacetophenone + acetic anhydride + hydrogen (Raney nickel catalyst) -> this + acetic acid. Once more in the reactor (dehydration) -> 4-acetoxystyrene.
The OH is capped with acetyl, and the ketone is hydrogenated to an alcohol over nickel. Heating removes water to form a double bond (vinyl group).
The OH is capped because it would interfere with polymerization; it is taken off again at the end.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetoxystyrene.no: A small molecule (monomer) that links up into a plastic.
Made in the resist reactor from 1-(4-acetoxyphenyl)ethanol (dehydration). 4 polymerize into poly(4-acetoxystyrene).
A styrene relative. The vinyl groups link one after another (radical polymerization). Styrenes start to polymerize from heat alone.
It links the same way as the polystyrene in foam packaging, with an OAc group on each ring.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetoxystyrene.pl: Approximation: really polymerized in solution with an initiator. The reactor polymerizes it from the monomer alone.
item.semiconductor-lab.poly_acetoxystyre: Resist resin with the OH still capped.
In the resist reactor: 4 4-acetoxystyrene -> this. + ammonia water + methanol (reactor) -> polyhydroxystyrene.
Each ring of the polymer carries an acetate (OAc). Ammonia and methanol remove it (hydrolysis), restoring the OH.
This detour (cap, polymerize, uncap) is needed because hydroxystyrene itself polymerizes poorly.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyhydroxystyren: A plastic that dissolves in alkaline water. The body of a chemically amplified resist.
In the resist reactor: poly(4-acetoxystyrene) + ammonia water (bottle returned) + methanol. Capped with t-BOC in the reactor -> protected polyhydroxystyrene.
With OH (phenol-like) groups on the rings, it dissolves in alkaline developer (as in [2-32]). It lets shorter wavelengths (KrF 248 nm) through better than novolak.
Novolak absorbs too much 248 nm light for it to reach the bottom of the resist, so PHS took over from KrF on.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_hexaflu: A salt with six fluorines on antimony. A very weakly binding anion.

In the resist reactor: antimony trioxide + 2 potassium fluoride + 4 hydrofluoric acid (containers returned) + hydrogen peroxide -> 2. A material for the photoacid generator. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, harmful to aquatic life.
Hydrogen peroxide turns Sb(III) into Sb(V), and six fluorides make SbF6-. Because SbF6- hardly holds on to anything, its acid HSbF6 is extremely strong (a superacid relative).
Antimony- and arsenic-based anions give strong acids, but they are toxic, so today metal-free fluorinated anions are more common.
Approximation: reaction conditions and filtering are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetaldehyde.note: A pungent liquid made by adding water to acetylene.
Acetylene (bag) + water (bucket returned) + mercuric sulfate (catalyst, returned). 2 + sodium hydroxide -> crotonaldehyde. ⚠ GHS: flammable liquid, suspected carcinogen.
HC≡CH + H2O -> CH3CHO over a mercury catalyst (Kucherov 1881). Before petroleum, many chemicals were made from acetylene.

Failure record: at Chisso's Minamata plant in Japan, methylmercury from this reaction's mercury catalyst flowed into the sea and caused Minamata disease (confirmed 1956). Today it is made from ethylene by another route.
item.semiconductor-lab.crotonaldehyde.no: A liquid of two acetaldehyde units joined.
2 acetaldehyde + sodium hydroxide. + 2 hydrogen + Raney nickel (returned) -> 1-butanol. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, flammable.
Alkali joins acetaldehyde molecules (aldol condensation) and water leaves, giving CH3CH=CHCHO: from two carbons to four.
Before petroleum, butanol was made from acetylene this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.crotonaldehyde.pl: Approximation: sodium hydroxide is really a small catalytic amount; the game uses one.
item.semiconductor-lab.butanol.note2: Crotonaldehyde + 2 hydrogen (bags) + Raney nickel (returned). + potassium dichromate + sulfuric acid -> butyric acid. ⚠ GHS: flammable liquid, serious eye damage.
item.semiconductor-lab.butanol.note3: Hydrogen adds to both C=C and C=O, giving CH3CH2CH2CH2OH.
item.semiconductor-lab.butanol.note4: Around World War I, Weizmann made acetone and butanol by microbial fermentation (ABE fermentation).
item.semiconductor-lab.butyric_acid.note: An acid that smells of rancid butter.
1-Butanol + potassium dichromate + sulfuric acid (bottle returned). 3 + phosphorus trichloride -> 3 butyryl chloride. ⚠ GHS: corrosive.
Dichromate oxidizes the alcohol to a carboxylic acid (orange chromium turns green).
The name comes from the Latin for 'butter'. It is also one of the smells of feet.
Butyric acid with its OH swapped for chlorine; very reactive.
3 butyric acid + phosphorus trichloride -> 3. + benzene + aluminium chloride -> butyrophenone. ⚠ GHS: corrosive, reacts violently with water.
3 RCOOH + PCl3 -> 3 RCOCl + H3PO3. Acid chlorides attach carbon chains to other molecules.
Moisture in the air turns it back into butyric acid and hydrogen chloride, and it fumes.
Approximation: the phosphorous acid is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.butyrophenone.not: A liquid with a four-carbon ketone chain on a benzene ring.
Benzene + butyryl chloride + aluminium chloride. + zinc + mercury + hydrochloric acid -> butylbenzene.
Aluminium chloride pulls Cl off butyryl chloride and the cation attaches to the ring (Friedel-Crafts acylation, 1877).
Attaching the chain directly would rearrange it into a branched one, so the trick is to attach a ketone and then reduce it.
item.semiconductor-lab.butylbenzene.note: A liquid with a straight four-carbon chain on a benzene ring.
Butyrophenone + zinc + mercury (iron flask returned) + hydrochloric acid. + nitric acid + sulfuric acid -> 4-nitrobutylbenzene. ⚠ GHS: flammable.
Zinc amalgam (zinc + mercury) and hydrochloric acid turn C=O into CH2 (Clemmensen reduction, 1913).
This straight chain helps make the liquid-crystal molecule long and rod-like.
item.semiconductor-lab.butylbenzene.plac: Approximation: really only a little mercury on the zinc surface; the game uses one.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrobutylbenzene: Butylbenzene with an NO2 group; a yellow liquid.
Butylbenzene + nitric acid + sulfuric acid (bottles returned). + iron + hydrochloric acid -> 4-butylaniline. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity.
Strong nitric and sulfuric acids make NO2+, which attaches to the ring (nitration). The isomer opposite the chain (4-position) is used.
Nitration is the starting point of the dye and drug industries.
Approximation: some goes to the neighbouring 2-position too; separating it is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.butylaniline.note: NO2 changed to NH2 (an aniline relative); a liquid.
4-Nitrobutylbenzene + iron + hydrochloric acid (bottle returned). + anisaldehyde -> the liquid crystal MBBA. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity.
Iron and hydrochloric acid reduce NO2 to NH2 (Béchamp reduction, 1854), the method that fed the aniline dye industry.
In 1856 Perkin made the first synthetic dye, mauveine, from aniline, and the chemical industry began.
item.semiconductor-lab.anisole.note1: Phenol with OH changed to methoxy; a sweet-smelling liquid.
item.semiconductor-lab.anisole.note2: Phenol + methanol + alumina (approximate catalyst). + carbon monoxide + hydrogen chloride + aluminium chloride -> anisaldehyde. ⚠ GHS: flammable.
item.semiconductor-lab.anisole.note3: PhOH + CH3OH -> PhOCH3 + H2O over hot alumina.
item.semiconductor-lab.anisole.placehold: Approximation: alumina is really a catalyst that is not used up; the game uses one.
item.semiconductor-lab.anisaldehyde.note: A liquid with an anise scent. Half of the liquid-crystal molecule.
Anisole + carbon monoxide (bag) + hydrogen chloride (bag) + aluminium chloride. + 4-butylaniline -> MBBA.
CO, HCl and AlCl3 put a CHO group on the ring (Gattermann-Koch reaction, 1897), opposite the methoxy group.
It is also used in perfumes and food flavourings.
item.semiconductor-lab.tributylamine.not: A basic liquid that stops acid. A little goes into EUV resist.
3 1-butanol + ammonia (bag) + Raney nickel (catalyst, returned). A material for EUV resist. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, corrosive.
(C4H9)3N: ammonia with all three H replaced by butyl groups (alcohol and ammonia reacted over nickel with hydrogen). In the resist it neutralizes acid that drifts into unexposed areas (a quencher).
During baking the acid drifts sideways by a few nm. With EUV lines only a dozen or so nm wide, that drift blurs the lines, so tuning the base is important.
item.semiconductor-lab.tributylamine.pla: Approximation: really reacted at about 200 °C with hydrogen. The water by-product is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_resist.note1: Resist printed with EUV (13.5 nm) light. Made to print even with few particles of light.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_resist.note2: Protected polyhydroxystyrene + 2 photoacid generator + tributylamine + xylene + glass bottle. Positive, alkaline developer (coating, post-exposure bake and developing are E's process).
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_resist.note3: One EUV photon carries about 92 eV, about 14 times an ArF photon (193 nm, about 6.4 eV), so the same dose holds about 1/14 as many photons. Each photon knocks electrons loose in the film, and those electrons break the photoacid generator to release acid. Extra photoacid generator is added, and acid that spreads too far is stopped by the quencher (base).
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_resist.note4: With few photons, the number landing in each spot varies (shot noise), and now and then a line breaks or two lines join (stochastic defects). This is EUV's biggest headache; since the 2010s, metal-oxide resists (tin and others, which absorb the light strongly) have also been studied.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_resist.placeh: Approximation: ⚠️ real EUV resists use metal-free photoacid generators (fluorinated sulfonates and others) to avoid contaminating chips; the game keeps the antimony salt. The solvent is xylene (really PGMEA and others).
item.semiconductor-lab.phthalic_anhydrid: White crystals. A material for blue pigment and plastics.
Naphthalene + vanadium pentoxide (catalyst, returned). 4 + 2 urea + copper(I) chloride + ammonium molybdate -> copper phthalocyanine. ⚠ GHS: respiratory and skin sensitizer, serious eye damage.
C10H8 + 4.5 O2 -> C8H4O3 + 2CO2 + 2H2O, passing naphthalene vapour and air over hot V2O5 (from 1916).

At first, in 1896, BASF made it by oxidizing naphthalene with sulfuric acid and mercury sulfate (said to come from the accident of a thermometer breaking and mercury falling in ⚠️). Today's method uses no toxic mercury.
Approximation: the air and heating to about 400 °C are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.urea.note2: 2 ammonia (bags) + carbon dioxide (bag). The nitrogen source for copper phthalocyanine.
item.semiconductor-lab.urea.note3: 2NH3 + CO2 -> (NH2)2CO + H2O (Bosch-Meiser process, 1922). In 1828 Wöhler made urea from ammonium cyanate, showing that substances of living bodies can be made in the lab.
item.semiconductor-lab.urea.note4: Today it is the world's most-used nitrogen fertilizer.
item.semiconductor-lab.urea.placeholder: Approximation: really reacted at high pressure and temperature; the water is omitted.
A whitish copper salt. The copper source for copper phthalocyanine.
Copper + 2 hydrochloric acid (bottles returned) -> 2. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, harmful to aquatic life.
CuCl, copper in the +1 state. Air and moisture slowly turn it into green Cu(II).
In a flame, copper chlorides burn blue-green (the blue of fireworks).
Approximation: really made from copper with copper(II) chloride or hydrochloric acid and air; hydrogen evolution and the like are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_molybdat: White molybdenum powder. Speeds up the reaction that makes copper phthalocyanine.
Molybdenum trioxide + ammonia water (bottle returned). Returned after crafting (a catalyst).
(NH4)6Mo7O24. In the Wyler process it helps phthalic anhydride and urea close into the phthalocyanine ring.
It is also a reagent for measuring phosphorus (the yellow phosphomolybdate precipitate).
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_phthalocya: 4 phthalic anhydride + 2 urea + copper(I) chloride + ammonium molybdate (catalyst, returned). The blue for colour resists (C's [9-45]).
Copper sits in the middle of a big ring of four phthalic units linked by nitrogen. It stands up very well to light, heat and chemicals.

A blue substance found by accident in Switzerland in 1927 is said to be the first; it turned up again at a Scottish factory in 1928, and sold as 'phthalocyanine blue' from about 1935. The 1936 Wyler process made it cheap. It colours bullet-train blue, ballpoint ink and the blue filters of camera sensors.
Approximation: really reacted in a solvent at about 200 °C. The proportions are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.howto: Put the material and water on the left and connect power. Water turns to steam and the inside gets hot and pressurised, then it reacts (Bakelite, PTFE, nylon, pulp...). Too little heat or pressure gives a failed product.
block.semiconductor-lab.bottle_machine.h: Put in soda-lime glass and connect power: glass bottles come out quickly, far faster than glassblowing by hand.
block.semiconductor-lab.electroplating_b: Put in a copper ingot and a mould (wax coated with graphite) and connect power. Copper travels through the liquid onto the mould, making a copper electrotype.
block.semiconductor-lab.high_pressure_re: Put in ethylene bags and a little oxygen and connect power. At very high pressure you get polyethylene.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrolysis_furnac: Put in chlorodifluoromethane bags and connect power. Heat splits it into tetrafluoroethylene (the PTFE raw material) and hydrogen chloride.
block.semiconductor-lab.solvay_tower.how: Put in salt, calcite and ammonia water and connect power. You get sodium carbonate (soda). The ammonia mostly goes round and comes back.
block.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water_: Put in deionized water and a polyethylene bottle and connect power. You get ultrapure water for washing chips.
block.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_still.ho: Insert ammoniacal liquor, slaked lime, empty glass bottles and a water bucket → ammonia water (bottled). Electric heating.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_retort.howto: Insert coal and heat with fuel → coke, ammoniacal liquor and coal tar. No electricity.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_retort.howt: Insert fluorite, sulfuric acid, lead or polyethylene bottles, a water bucket and fuel → hydrofluoric acid (bottled). Fuel-heated.
block.semiconductor-lab.peroxide_cell.ho: Insert sulfuric acid, platinum (anode, kept), a water bucket and empty glass bottles → hydrogen peroxide (bottled). Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.resist_reactor.h: Four inputs for materials, catalyst below. The combination picks the reaction for the resist resin or photoacid generator. Anything extra stops it. 1.5 kW.
item.semiconductor-lab.difluoroethane_ga: Acetylene with fluorine added - the first step toward fluororubber.

Acetylene + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + antimony pentachloride (catalyst, returned). + chlorine -> 1-chloro-1,1-difluoroethane. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure. Hydrogen fluoride sometimes leaks while making it (brief weakness).
HC≡CH + 2HF -> CH3CHF2, with antimony chloride as the catalyst that adds HF to acetylene.
This gas itself is also used as HFC-152a, a refrigerant and spray propellant.
Approximation: catalyst amount and temperature are omitted; no bag is tracked (a gas item).
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorodifluoroeth: A gas carrying fluorine and chlorine. Cracked by heat, it becomes vinylidene fluoride.
1,1-Difluoroethane + chlorine (bag). Furnace (cracking) -> vinylidene fluoride. ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure. Chlorine sometimes leaks while making it (brief nausea).
CH3CHF2 + Cl2 -> CH3CClF2 + HCl (chlorination by light). Heated to about 600 °C it loses HCl to give CH2=CF2.
As HCFC-142b it harms the ozone layer slightly, so it is no longer used as a refrigerant ([2-48]).
Approximation: the HCl given off is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinylidene_fluori: The first building block (monomer) of fluororubber.
Crack 1-chloro-1,1-difluoroethane in a furnace. 3 + hexafluoropropylene + hydrogen peroxide + water -> raw fluororubber. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure.
CH2=CF2, which links up through its double bond. Linked alone it becomes a stiff crystalline plastic (PVDF).
PVDF is also a binder in battery electrodes and a pipe material in chemical plants.
item.semiconductor-lab.hexafluoropropyle: The second building block (monomer) of fluororubber; its bulk makes the rubber soft.
Crack tetrafluoroethylene in a furnace. With 3 vinylidene fluoride it makes fluororubber. ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure, acute toxicity (inhalation).
CF2=CF-CF3. The sticking-out CF3 stops the chains packing into crystals, so the mixed polymer is soft like rubber.
It is made by rearranging tetrafluoroethylene, the Teflon (PTFE) monomer, with heat.
Approximation: really 3 TFE -> 2 HFP; 1 -> 1 in the game.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_raw_rubber.no: 3 vinylidene fluoride + hexafluoropropylene + hydrogen peroxide (initiator, bottle returned) + water (bucket returned). + magnesium oxide + bisphenol A -> 4 compound.
It is polymerized as tiny droplets in water (emulsion polymerization), the two monomers linking together (copolymerization).
DuPont brought it out as 'Viton' in the 1950s (1957 ⚠️).
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_raw_rubber.pl: Approximation: the real initiator is a persulfate.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_compound.note: Fluororubber mixed with curing agents. Baked, it becomes O-rings.
Raw rubber + magnesium oxide + bisphenol A -> 4. Furnace (curing) -> fluororubber O-ring.
Bisphenol links the chains (cross-linking) and magnesium oxide neutralizes the hydrogen fluoride released - a different method from sulfur vulcanization of ordinary rubber ([2-29]).
Rubber's properties change greatly with how it is cross-linked and what is mixed in.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_compound.plac: Approximation: really bisphenol AF (fluorinated) and an accelerator.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_o_ring.note1: A black ring that seals gaps. Resists heat, oil and chemicals.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_o_ring.note2: Bake the compound in a furnace (curing). A sealing material for C's EUV vacuum enclosure.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_o_ring.note3: Chains loaded with fluorine last a long time at 200-250 °C and in oil, fuel and many chemicals, and give off little gas in vacuum.
item.semiconductor-lab.fkm_o_ring.note4: A cousin of Teflon frying pans. Ordinary rubber O-rings harden with heat and let the vacuum leak.
message.semiconductor-lab.difluoroethane: Hydrogen fluoride leaked... you feel a little weak
message.semiconductor-lab.chlorodifluoro: Chlorine leaked... you feel a little sick
item.semiconductor-lab.refractory_brick_: Mostly quartz sand, shaped into a brick. It still has to be fired very hot.

Silica sand (SiO2) bound with a little slaked lime (about 2%, as milk of lime), pressed into shape. An ordinary furnace (~1000 C) is not hot enough: fire it in a blast furnace (~1450 C). During firing, quartz slowly turns into other crystal forms (tridymite, cristobalite), which is why silica bricks grow slightly instead of shrinking.
Ordinary bricks melt in a furnace. Only bricks full of quartz can take the heat.

Silica brick, about 95% SiO2. Fire-clay bricks soften around 1600 C, but silica bricks stay hard almost up to their melting point (~1700 C), so they were used for the roofs of steel furnaces. Silica is acidic: it is the right lining for an acid Bessemer converter.

1822: William Weston Young made bricks from the quartz-rich 'Dinas' rock of the Vale of Neath in Wales, so silica bricks are still called Dinas bricks. They made the hot open-hearth furnaces of the 1860s possible.

Silica bricks are acidic and are eaten by basic slag (CaO, MgO). That is why the Thomas converter (1878) needed a basic dolomite lining to remove phosphorus. Quartz changes crystal form near 573 C with a sudden size change, so silica bricks crack if heated or cooled quickly at low temperature.
Bake charcoal with electricity way too hard and it turns into graphite.

Resistance furnace where the charge itself is the heater: current flows from graphite electrodes straight through the packed carbon. 4 coal/charcoal + 1 sand -> 2 synthetic graphite, after the furnace reaches 2500 C. Needs 500 kW (about 10 steam engines); with less power it settles at a lower temperature and never graphitizes.

Edward Acheson found silicon carbide (carborundum) in 1891 while trying to make diamonds, and patented synthetic graphite in 1896. Heated far enough, SiC loses its silicon as vapour and leaves graphite behind - he thought the sand acted as a catalyst.

Game model: temperature rises with power in and falls with heat lost (proportional to temperature above 20 C), tuned so 500 kW settles at 2600 C. Real furnaces were tens of metres long, ran on Niagara hydroelectric power at hundreds of kW to MW, and one cycle took days. Today it is known that soft carbons (petroleum coke) graphitize without any catalyst.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: Graphite made by people. Purer than the graphite you dig up.

Made in the Acheson furnace above 2500 C. At that heat the carbon atoms rearrange into graphite layers, and impurities (ash, sulfur, metals) boil away. Machined into high-purity boats for zone refining.

Natural graphite carries the minerals it grew in (clay, iron, silica). Synthetic graphite became the standard for electrodes, crucibles and later nuclear reactor moderators (the 1942 Chicago Pile used hundreds of tonnes).

Graphitization: carbon atoms in coke are arranged in small, misaligned layers. Above about 2500 C they move enough to stack into the ordered hexagonal layers of graphite. Electrical resistance drops and the material becomes soft and slippery.
block.semiconductor-lab.reverberatory_fu: Roasting ore sends its sulfur up the chimney as smoke. It used to be poison gas; collected, it becomes sulfuric acid.

Burns coal or charcoal (1 piece = 8 roasts, 10 s each) and roasts sulfide ores in air without melting them. Galena -> lead oxide + SO2; cinnabar dust -> mercury + SO2; sphalerite -> zinc oxide + SO2, plus germanium concentrate every 4th and indium every 8th. SO2 + water -> sulfuric acid.

The fire burns in a separate firebox; the flame and hot gas sweep over the hearth and the low roof reflects ('reverberates') the heat down onto the ore. English smelters used it for lead and copper from the 1690s, and Henry Cort used it for puddling iron in 1784. The Nirayama reverberatory furnace in Japan (Egawa Hidetatsu, finished by his son Hidetoshi in 1857) cast cannons and is a World Heritage site.

Because the fuel never touches the ore, the ash and sulfur of coal do not get into the metal. Roasting itself gives off heat (sulfur burns), so little fuel is needed. Smelter smoke (SO2) once killed forests around mines, such as Ashio in Japan; today smelter gas is sent to contact-process sulfuric acid plants, and smelters are major acid producers.

Approximation: a real furnace is a large brick building (firebox, hearth, flue, chimney); shrunk to one block. Ge and In really come from zinc-refining residues (leach residue, flue dust), not straight from roasting; here they come out as roasting by-products.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note1: A white powder: old white paint (zinc white) and the white in sunscreen.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note: ZnO, made by roasting sphalerite: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Smelt it to reduce it with the fuel's carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note3: Zinc white became an artists' paint in 1834 ('Chinese white', Winsor & Newton). Unlike lead white it is not poisonous and does not darken.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note4: ZnO is itself a semiconductor (band gap about 3.3 eV). It absorbs UV, which is why it is in sunscreen, and it is used in varistors (surge protectors) and transparent electronics.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.placeh: Approximation: reducing ZnO needs about 1000 C, above zinc's boiling point (907 C), so real zinc escapes as vapour and must be condensed (distillation smelting [1-13]). Done in one furnace step here.
item.semiconductor-lab.refractory_brick_: The lime binder sets in air (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O), and on firing reacts with quartz to form calcium silicate (CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3), welding the sand grains together. Above about 870 °C quartz turns into tridymite and above about 1470 °C into cristobalite, both bulkier crystals.

Silica bricks are also called Dinas bricks, after the Dinas rock, a quartzite in Wales from which they were made in the 1820s. Because they do not shrink when hot, they were used for open-hearth and glass furnace roofs and in coke ovens.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_furnace.note: A furnace that uses an electric spark (an arc) to get hot enough to melt almost anything.

Needs 500 kW (one steam turbine). Top left: vein quartz; middle: charcoal or coal; bottom left: graphite rods (electrodes, one used up every 8 runs). 2 vein quartz + 1 charcoal or coal -> 1 metallurgical silicon (about 86 s). It stops when power is short. Modern metallurgical silicon is made in AC submerged-arc furnaces; the game approximates it with DC until AC arrives in v0.4.

A huge current between two electrodes turns the gas (and charge) into glowing plasma at 2000-3000 °C (an arc discharge). At that temperature carbon can pull oxygen even off silicon, which holds it very tightly: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO.

The arc was found by Petrov in 1802 (published 1803) and also shown by Davy around 1808-1810 ⚠️. In 1892 Henri Moissan melted many substances in his electric arc furnace, and that same year Thomas Willson made calcium carbide (CaC2) by accident in the USA. Around 1900 Paul Héroult made the arc furnace practical for melting steel.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_furnace.plac: Approximation: real furnaces are large multi-block structures and today run on AC (high current from a transformer [4-10]). Here it is one block on DC (⚠️ whether Moissan's early furnace was DC is unconfirmed). Temperature changes are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note1: Put it beside a furnace and pump it to blow air and make the fire hotter.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note2: Each right-click with an empty hand gives about a second of air. With a turning water wheel beside it, it becomes a water-powered bellows that blows all the time. Place it next to a bloomery or blast furnace.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note3: Blowing in more oxygen makes charcoal burn hard, reaching about 1200–1300 °C. An open fire (about 800 °C) can't make iron. The tomb of Rekhmire in Egypt (about 1450 BC) shows foot-operated bellows.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.note4: In AD 31 Du Shi of the Eastern Han dynasty in China drove bellows with a water wheel. The 'tatara' of Japanese iron-making was originally the name of a big foot bellows.
block.semiconductor-lab.bellows.placehol: Approximation: one pump gives about a second of air (game value)
message.semiconductor-lab.bellows.air: Air %s%% (keep pumping to keep it going)
item.semiconductor-lab.calcium_carbide.n: Grey lumps made from lime and carbon in the arc furnace. Add water and a burnable gas comes out.
CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO at about 2000 C, only reachable in an electric arc. With water: CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 (acetylene) + Ca(OH)2.

In 1892 Thomas Willson (USA) was trying to make aluminium in an arc furnace and got carbide by chance; Henri Moissan in France made it the same year. Acetylene from carbide lit miners' and bicycle lamps and became a starting material for chemicals such as vinyl acetate.

Making 1 t of carbide takes about 3000 kWh, so carbide works were built beside hydroelectric plants. Carbide reacts with moisture in the air, so it is kept in sealed steel drums. Hazard (GHS): in contact with water releases flammable gas.
block.semiconductor-lab.perkins_ice_mach: A machine that turns water into ice as you crank it. It does not make cold; it pumps heat out ('a heat pump').

4 copper + hand pump [5-01] + 3 iron. Right-click with refrigerant (diethyl ether) to charge it, with a water bucket to fill it, then right-click empty-handed to turn the crank 16 times for 1 ice. No refrigerant, no cold. Ether is very flammable and sometimes leaks and is lost (accident). CFC [2-48] also works as a refrigerant (it does not leak away, but the ozone layer shrinks).

Compress (squeeze the refrigerant gas) -> reject heat (copper pipes give heat outside; it liquefies) -> expansion valve (a narrow valve drops the pressure) -> evaporate (turning to gas it takes heat from around it: latent heat) -> compress again. The same loop as today's fridges and air conditioners.

In 1834 American-born Perkins, working in London, patented a closed-loop refrigerator using ether. The prototype made a little ice but never became a business. People often say Linde (1876) invented the fridge, but Linde made a practical ammonia machine; Perkins had the cycle first.
Approximation: temperature and pressure are not modelled; it is shown as crank turns.
message.semiconductor-lab.perkins_ice_ma: No refrigerant, so cranking does not cool anything
Fill it with a water bucket
Ice made, but the ether leaked out (flammable and dangerous)
Ice made. A little CFC leaked into the sky (ozone %s DU)
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay.note1: A pale clay that withstands great heat. Used for crucibles and furnace linings.
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay.note2: Crafting: 4 clay balls + water bucket → 2 (washing in water lets coarse iron-rich grains settle, keeping only the fine white clay; the bucket comes back). 7 make a crucible shape.
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay.note3: Clay rich in kaolinite (Al2Si2O5(OH)4) and low in iron and alkalis does not melt even at about 1500 °C; iron and alkalis make clay melt more easily.
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay.note4: Used since antiquity for copper and bronze crucibles and furnace linings ⚠️ (start date unconfirmed); the generation before firebricks ([3-12], silica brick 1822).
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ washing (levigation) is approximated at the crafting table. Clay analysis is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.fire_clay_crucibl: A pot for melting things, made of fire clay.
Crafting: 7 fire clay. Melting in it keeps the contents away from flames and fuel, so no dirt gets in (the vessel for the crucible furnace [3-07]).
Crucibles with added graphite ([1-07]) are even more heat-resistant.
Around 1740 Huntsman melted steel in crucibles to make uniform crucible steel.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_wool.note1: Fluffy insulation made by melting rock and spinning it into fibres. Heat passes through it poorly.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_wool.note2: Blast basalt in a blast furnace (melted at about 1500 °C and blown into fibres).
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_wool.note3: Air trapped between the fine fibres stops heat, and it does not burn. Hawaii's volcanoes make natural fibres of wind-stretched lava called Pele's hair.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_wool.note4: Asbestos was once the standard insulation, but it causes mesothelioma and lung cancer and was effectively banned in Japan in 2006 ⚠️; rock wool spread as its replacement. ⚠️ Asbestos cannot be made in this mod (history only).
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_wool.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ melting and blowing are approximated by the blast furnace. Diatomaceous earth needs a new ore and is on hold.
item.semiconductor-lab.thermocouple.note: A thermometer of two different metal wires joined at the tip. Right-click a block to read its temperature.
Crafting: copper + iron + soda-lime glass (glass sheath). Right-click a block for temperature (°C) and the voltage produced (mV). Copper–iron works up to about 700 °C.
A temperature difference across the junction of two metals produces a small voltage (Seebeck effect); copper–iron gives about 0.013 mV per °C ⚠️. Measure the voltage and you know the temperature.
Seebeck found it in 1821; Le Chatelier's platinum–platinum-rhodium thermocouple (1886) reached about 1600 °C. Before that, Wedgwood (1782) judged kiln heat by how much clay shrank.
item.semiconductor-lab.thermocouple.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ temperatures are typical values by block type and whether it is lit. The high-temperature Pt–Rh type is not made (no rhodium).
item.semiconductor-lab.optical_pyrometer: Measures temperature by comparing the colour of a hot object with a bulb filament. For very hot furnaces.

Crafting: crown lens + 2 iron + W wire + dry cell. Right-click something glowing for its temperature (below about 700 °C it is too dark). For arc, Acheson and crystal-pulling furnaces that melt thermocouples.
A lens images the furnace and a battery-lit filament is placed over the image. The current at which the filament vanishes into the image gives the temperature (disappearing-filament type).
Built by Holborn and Kurlbaum in Germany in 1901. The link between colour and temperature was explained by Planck's radiation law of 1900, the start of quantum theory.
Omitted: ⚠️ temperatures are typical values per machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: High-frequency current in the coil heats only the germanium itself, melting a narrow zone. Real coils are water-cooled.
