item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Turns the lead screw. Real zone refiners move a few cm per hour.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Connected cables form one network: generators and discharging batteries feed machines directly (cables store nothing). Loss is 1% per cable along the longest path; at most 1 MW flows through a network, shared in proportion to demand. Right-click: network info.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note: Magnetite that nature magnetized (lightning does it). Known since antiquity as lodestone.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note: Faraday 1831: spin a coil in a magnetic field and current flows. Early dynamos used permanent magnets; from 1866-67 (Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone, almost simultaneously) the iron core's residual magnetism was enough.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Needs FLOWING water beside it (500 W per side). Still water does nothing: power = flow x head. Early power stations were hydro.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Coal boils water, steam pushes a piston, the dynamo turns: 50 kW. Watt's engine converted only 2-5% of the coal's heat into work; ~30% only came with steam turbines. One water bucket = 2 coal's worth of steam.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note1: A glass jar wrapped in metal inside and out stores electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note: The first capacitor (Kleist and Musschenbroek, 1745): metal foil on the inside and outside of a glass jar, the glass between them as insulator. Charge piles up on the two foils. With a coil it forms the tuned circuit of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note3: Early radio transmitters used racks of Leyden jars as their capacitors. A coil (L) and a capacitor (C) together ring at one frequency, f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) - the same idea as tuning a radio.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note4: Musschenbroek got such a shock from his jar that he wrote he would not repeat it for the whole kingdom of France. Benjamin Franklin later showed the charge sits on the glass surfaces, not in the water the first jars held.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.placeh: Approximation: the foil was tin foil (tin [1-30] not implemented) - copper here (copper-foil capacitors are real too).
item.semiconductor-lab.hf_oscillator.not: The machine that makes transistors ran on vacuum tubes - the very parts transistors would replace.

Two triode tubes + coil + Leyden jar + power input. The tubes keep the coil-capacitor circuit ringing at radio frequency (hundreds of kHz) and feed it to the induction coil of the zone refining furnace, where eddy currents melt only the germanium.

A tube amplifier whose output is fed back to its own grid keeps itself oscillating (Meissner and Armstrong, 1912-1913). Induction heaters of the 1950s that melted germanium were exactly such tube oscillators, with big water-cooled triodes.

Bell Labs' zone refiners (Pfann, 1952) were heated by RF induction of a few hundred kHz to MHz. Only the material inside the coil heats, so the graphite boat and quartz tube stay cooler - a clean way to melt one narrow zone.
block.semiconductor-lab.electric_furnace: It heats things with electricity instead of fire, so no smoke gets in.

Resistance furnace: current through graphite rods turns into heat (Joule heat, P = I squared R), up to about 1500 C. 5 kW x 10 s per item. Fires refractory bricks and clay-graphite boats. With a hydrogen tube added it becomes the hydrogen furnace.
Nichrome wire (1906) needs nickel and chromium, which we don't have yet - but a graphite rod works as a heating element too. 1500 C is above the melting point of silicon (1414 C).
Omitted: hot graphite burns in air (C + O2 -> CO2), so real graphite-element furnaces run under inert gas or vacuum, and the rods are consumables. Here the rods never wear out.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: A stick of graphite. Electricity flows through it and makes it glow hot.
Heating element of the electric furnace [4-12] and electrode of the Acheson furnace [3-10]. Graphite conducts electricity but has some resistance, so current turns into heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.plac: Approximation: real carbon rods (arc lamp carbons, 19th c.) are carbon powder bound with pitch (coal tar) and baked. Pitch is not implemented, so 3 natural graphite make 2 rods.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite's resistance falls as it gets hotter (unlike metals), and it does not melt at normal pressure - it sublimes near 3600 C. That is why graphite heaters can go far above any metal wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_dyna: A dynamo with no magnet inside. It makes its own magnet out of its own electricity.

1866-67, Varley, Siemens and Wheatstone (almost simultaneously): a steel core + 4 coils. Right-click a water wheel or steam engine to swap out its permanent-magnet dynamo: output x2 (a steam engine also burns coal twice as fast — same electricity per coal, twice the power per machine).

The core keeps a little leftover magnetism. Spinning makes a weak current, which goes through the field coils and makes the field stronger, which makes more current... it builds itself up in seconds (the 'dynamo-electric principle').

Permanent magnets of the 1860s were weak, so magneto machines could only turn part of the engine's power into electricity. Electromagnet fields made big generators possible — Varley filed a patent in December 1866, and Wheatstone presented the same idea to the Royal Society on the same day as Siemens in January 1867. Energy is still conserved: double the electricity needs double the steam.
message.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_d: Installed the self-excited dynamo: output x2
This generator already has a self-excited dynamo
This generator already has an electromagnet field built in
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.no: Steam spins a fan really fast. This is how most power plants still work.

Parsons 1884. Coal + water -> 500 kW. One coal lasts 18 s (9 MJ = 30% of the coal's heat; the steam engine gets 5%). Water: a bucket in the top slot (1 bucket = 2 coal), or a water source block beside it feeds it forever. Enough to run the Acheson furnace (500 kW) by itself.

No piston going back and forth, just a wheel of blades turning in one direction — so it can spin fast (Parsons' first: 18,000 rpm) and be built huge. Power plants sit by rivers and the sea because they need lots of cooling water.

Real plants are multi-stage (steam expands through many rows of blades) and use a condenser to turn the steam back into water under vacuum, which raises efficiency. Coal plants reach about 33-40% today, combined-cycle gas plants over 60%. Your electricity is still mostly made by spinning turbines.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.pl: Simplified: blades are not machined on a lathe ([8-01] not yet implemented); single stage, no condenser; feedwater from a river is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_acid_batter: The same kind of battery as in a car. It stores electricity as a chemical change.

Planté 1859. Lead plates in sulfuric acid. Holds 1 MJ. Every face both charges and discharges (up to 10 kW each; only 85% of the charge is stored). On a cable network it charges when there is spare power and discharges when machines need more. Keeps its charge when broken. Right-click: charge level. Glows while discharging.

Charging: 2PbSO4 + 2H2O -> Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. Discharging runs it backwards, so the acid gets weaker as the battery empties — mechanics check charge by measuring the acid's density. Planté made the PbO2 plate by charging and discharging bare lead sheets over and over ('forming').

The first rechargeable battery, and still in nearly every car 160+ years later because it can give a huge current to the starter motor and is cheap and recyclable (over 95% of the lead is recycled). Pure lead plates are soft, so grids were hardened with a few % antimony ([1-43]). Overcharging splits water into H2 + O2 — battery rooms need ventilation.
Simplified: no self-discharge, no voltage (12 V etc.); the case is glass (real: glass jars, later hard rubber / plastic).
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.network: Cable network: %s cables, longest path %s (loss %s%%), %s generators, %s machines, %s batteries, %s delivered
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Joins machines into one electric grid. Long cables lose more power.

Real loss is P = I^2 R: doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power and cuts the loss to a quarter. That is why power lines run at hundreds of kV (transformer [4-10]). In this mod the whole network shares one 1 MW limit (like one trunk line) and the loss uses the longest path for every machine - both are simplifications.
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: Copper wound round and round. It heats metal without touching it - the same principle as an induction (IH) cooktop.

High-frequency AC in the coil induces eddy currents (currents swirling inside the metal), and the metal heats itself through its own resistance (P = I²R). The higher the frequency, the more the current crowds to the surface (skin effect: depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ)).

The principle is Faraday's electromagnetic induction (1831). Edwin Northrup in the USA applied for a patent on the high-frequency induction furnace in 1916 and demonstrated one in 1918. Real coils are hollow copper tubes with cooling water flowing inside, because the coil itself heats up from the current.
item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Spins using electricity. There is one in every fan and washing machine.

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (F = BIL, the Lorentz force). A coil is pushed round by it, and the commutator (a switching part) keeps flipping the current direction. It is the same machine as a dynamo, just run the other way.

In 1821 Faraday made a wire circle a magnet using current (electromagnetic rotation), an important step that did not become a practical motor right away. At the 1873 Vienna Exhibition, workers connected two Gramme dynamos and one began to spin as a motor, showing that a generator can also be a motor.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note1: A stone that grabs iron. The ancestor of the compass.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note3: Inside magnetite, small magnetic domains (regions whose magnetism points one way) face random directions. The strong field from a lightning current is thought to line them up, turning the whole stone into a magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note4: The Japanese word jishaku comes from the Chinese "loving stone", which pulls iron like a mother hugging her child. In Han-dynasty China a lodestone spoon called sinan pointed south. In 1600 William Gilbert wrote in De Magnete that the Earth itself is a great magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note1: Spin it and electricity appears, like a bicycle light.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note3: A changing magnetic flux through a coil makes a voltage: EMF = −dΦ/dt (Faraday's law). A spinning coil gives alternating voltage, but the commutator swaps the connections every half turn to give direct current, which electrolysis needs.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note4: In 1832, the year after Faraday's discovery, Pixii in Paris built a hand-cranked magnet generator. Gramme's ring dynamo of 1871 finally gave smooth direct current usable in factories.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite is carbon atoms in stacked hexagonal sheets (sp2 bonds). Electrons free to move within the sheets (π electrons) let it conduct, but with far more resistance than metals (around 1000 times), so current heats it by Joule heating, P = I²R.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: A wire's resistance is R = ρL/A (longer means more, thicker means less). Copper's resistivity is about 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, second only to silver. Wire copper is electrolytically refined to 99.99%, because even small impurities raise the resistance a lot.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Flowing water turns the wheel to make electricity.
Hydro power P = ρgQHη (ρ: water density, g: gravity, Q: flow, H: head, η: efficiency). One tonne of water per second falling 10 m gives about 98 kW, with no fuel burned and no CO2.

The world's first hydroelectric plant opened in Appleton, USA, in 1882. In Japan a spinning mill at Sankyozawa, Sendai, started one in 1888, and Kyoto's Keage plant (1891, on the Lake Biwa Canal) powered Japan's first electric tram in 1895.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Burns coal to boil water and makes electricity from the steam.

Heat engines have a ceiling (Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, in kelvin). With steam at about 150 °C (423 K) and a 40 °C (313 K) cold side the limit is about 26%; real engines lose more to leaks and friction. In this game one coal (30 MJ) gives 1.5 MJ of electricity (5%).

Newcomen's engine (1712) was about 1% efficient. In 1769 Watt multiplied that with a separate condenser (cooling the steam in another vessel). The unit of power, the watt, is named after him, and he invented "horsepower" to sell his engines.
item.semiconductor-lab.alternator.note1: Hold it and use it on a water wheel, steam engine or turbine: it now makes AC.
item.semiconductor-lab.alternator.note2: Magnets fed by a small DC exciter spin inside fixed coils; the voltage swings + and - many times a second. Only AC can be stepped up by a transformer.
item.semiconductor-lab.alternator.note3: Alternators spread in the 1880s for AC lighting and, after the transformer (1885), for long-distance power. ⚠️ the first practical year is not confirmed.
item.semiconductor-lab.alternator.note4: Power stations today are huge three-phase alternators turned by turbines. The game only marks AC or DC; frequency and synchronising are left out (decision S-007).
block.semiconductor-lab.high_voltage_lin: A power line at about 10 times the voltage. It loses only 1/100 as much as copper cable. Connect it with transformers.
Same power at 10 times the voltage needs 1/10 the current, and the wire's loss I²R is 1/100: 0.01% per block, 10 MW per network. Machines cannot plug in directly: step down with a transformer.
In 1886 William Stanley lit the town of Great Barrington (USA) with AC sent at higher voltage and stepped down by transformers. ⚠️ the game's 2000 V is a game value.
Bare wires on glass or porcelain insulators: the higher the voltage, the bigger the insulators. Today's lines run at hundreds of thousands of volts.
block.semiconductor-lab.transformer.note: Changes the voltage of AC. Back = input, front = output. Copper cable on one side and a high-voltage line on the other.
Two coils on one iron core: the voltage ratio is the turns ratio. Works only on AC (DC does not change the magnetic flux). 98% efficient.
1885: Zipernowsky, Bláthy and Déri of Ganz (Budapest) patented the closed-core transformer (ZBD). It made AC the winner for sending power far.
Large transformers waste only 1-2% (heat in the iron and copper). The hum near them is the iron core stretching 100-120 times a second.
block.semiconductor-lab.rectifier.note1: Turns AC into DC. Back = AC in, front = DC out. Needed for the electrolyser on an AC network.
block.semiconductor-lab.rectifier.note2: A glass bulb with a mercury pool (cathode) and graphite anodes. Current flows only from the hot mercury spot to the anode, so AC comes out one-way. About 95% efficient.
block.semiconductor-lab.rectifier.note3: 1902: Peter Cooper Hewitt made the mercury-arc rectifier, the first static rectifier for power (Fleming's vacuum diode came in 1904). ⚠️ the vacuum sealing is left out.
block.semiconductor-lab.rectifier.note4: Big mercury-arc rectifiers ran railways and aluminium smelters until the 1970s, when silicon diodes and thyristors replaced them. The bulb glows blue-violet.
message.semiconductor-lab.alternator.ins: Alternator installed: this generator now makes AC
message.semiconductor-lab.alternator.alr: This generator already has an alternator
message.semiconductor-lab.alternator.not: This generator does not turn (it makes DC only)
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.kind: %1$s, %2$s, loss %3$s%%, %4$s machines cannot use this current
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.current_: AC and DC generators mixed: nothing flows
block.semiconductor-lab.voltaic_pile.not: The very first battery: copper and zinc discs stacked with salt-water-soaked cloth between them.

6 copper + 3 wool. Put a zinc ingot on top and salt below and it generates (5 W at first; one zinc and one salt last 2 minutes). Output drops as you use it (polarization); fresh zinc restores it. Compare with the Daniell cell.

Zinc dissolves and gives up electrons (Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-), and hydrogen forms at the copper (2H+ + 2e- -> H2). The hydrogen bubbles coat the copper, so current flows less and less easily (polarization).

Announced by Volta in Italy in 1800: the first steady electric current. That year Nicholson and Carlisle used it to split water, and in 1820 Orsted saw a current deflect a compass needle. The volt is named after him.
block.semiconductor-lab.voltaic_pile.pla: Approximation: power is a game value (a real pair gives about 1 V); the number of stacks and voltage are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.daniell_cell.not: A battery with zinc and copper in separate liquids, divided by an unglazed pot. Its output does not fade.

6 soda-lime glass + copper + earthenware pot (porous divider). Zinc ingot on top, copper sulfate below: it generates a steady 10 W (one zinc and one copper sulfate last 2 minutes). Unlike the voltaic pile it does not fade.

Negative: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-; positive: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Copper, not hydrogen, forms at the positive side, so no bubbles build up (no polarization). The porous wall lets ions through but keeps the two liquids from mixing. About 1.1 V.
Made by Daniell in Britain in 1836. Its steady voltage made it the standard power source for the telegraph ([15-]).
block.semiconductor-lab.daniell_cell.pla: Approximation: power is a game value; the copper and zinc sulfate produced are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.dry_cell.note1: A battery that does not spill and can be carried. Put it in a cell holder to get electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.dry_cell.note2: Zinc + 2 pyrolusite + ammonium chloride + graphite rod -> 2. In a cell holder: 8 W for 2 minutes. The manganese dioxide takes up hydrogen, so unlike the voltaic pile it hardly weakens.
item.semiconductor-lab.dry_cell.note3: The zinc can is negative, the carbon rod in the middle positive, with a paste of manganese dioxide and ammonium chloride between. Leclanché's wet cell (1866) was turned into a non-spilling paste by Gassner (1886); the Columbia dry cell (1896) brought it into homes. About 1.5 V.
item.semiconductor-lab.dry_cell.note4: A 'dry' cell is not completely dry inside (the paste is moist). In Japan, Sakizo Yai is said to have made a dry cell on his own around 1887 ⚠️ (sources differ on the year). Heavy use lowers the voltage a little; resting lets it recover.
item.semiconductor-lab.dry_cell.placehol: Approximation: power and time are game values (a real cell gives about 1.5 V). The plaster thickener, pitch seal and paper separator are left out. No spent can is left over.
A box that gives electricity when you put a dry cell in it.
Made from planks and copper. One dry cell gives 8 W for 2 minutes, then it uses the next. Connect it to machines with copper cable. Direct current; it does not rotate, so no alternator or dynamo.
Copper plates (contacts) press on the cell's positive end (carbon rod) and negative can (zinc).
The flashlight (around 1899) was born once dry cells could be carried around.
block.semiconductor-lab.lithium_ion_batt: A light rechargeable battery that stores a lot. The battery in phones and electric cars.

4 MJ (4x a lead-acid battery), 20 kW charge and discharge, 95% of the charge is stored (lead-acid: 85%). Charges and discharges on every face and feeds adjacent machines directly. DC only. Keeps its charge when broken. Real weight: for the same energy it weighs about 1/3 to 1/4 of a lead-acid battery (about 35 Wh per kg vs about 90-160 Wh per kg for LFP cells).

On charging, lithium ions leave the positive electrode, cross the electrolyte and tuck into the gaps between graphite layers; discharging sends them back. No lithium metal is used, so it is safer than earlier lithium cells. Akira Yoshino made the prototype in 1985 and Sony sold it from 1991 (2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Goodenough, Whittingham, Yoshino).

⚠️ The 1991 cell used lithium cobalt oxide LiCoO2. The game has no cobalt yet, so it uses lithium iron phosphate LiFePO4 from Goodenough's lab (1997) - hard to ignite, long-lived and common in today's electric cars. ⚠ Real cells can catch fire if damaged or overheated.

Approximation: capacity, power and efficiency are game values. The electrolyte solvent (ethylene carbonate etc.) and winding into a can are left out. The cathode is the later LiFePO4 (decision Q3-13 ②).
item.semiconductor-lab.lfp_charge.note1: The mixed ingredients of a battery's positive electrode. Roast it to get the powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.lfp_charge.note2: Lithium carbonate + 2 iron + 2 phosphoric acid (bottles returned) + charcoal. Roast in a blast furnace -> 2 lithium iron phosphate.
item.semiconductor-lab.lfp_charge.note3: Iron dissolves in phosphoric acid to iron(II) phosphate, which roasted with lithium carbonate gives LiFePO4. The charcoal keeps the iron from over-oxidising and coats the grains with carbon so electricity flows.
item.semiconductor-lab.lfp_charge.note4: LiFePO4 on its own barely conducts. Making the grains tiny and coating them thinly with carbon made it a usable battery material.
item.semiconductor-lab.lfp_charge.placeh: Approximation: really fired at about 700 °C in a furnace without air (argon or nitrogen). In the game, a blast furnace.
item.semiconductor-lab.lithium_iron_phos: The material on the positive side of a lithium-ion battery.
Roast the mix in a blast furnace. A lithium-ion battery material.

LiFePO4. Charging pulls the lithium out, leaving FePO4; discharging puts it back. The crystal hardly changes shape, so it survives thousands of charges, and it holds its oxygen tightly, so it resists fire.
⚠️ Reported in 1997 by Padhi and others in Goodenough's lab. The first mass-produced cells of 1991 used lithium cobalt oxide LiCoO2 (1980, Goodenough, Mizushima and others).
A white powder of lithium and fluorine.
Lithium carbonate + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) -> 2. + red phosphorus + fluorine -> lithium hexafluorophosphate.
Li2CO3 + 2HF -> 2LiF + H2O + CO2. It hardly dissolves in water.
Lithium fluoride crystals let ultraviolet light through, so they are used for UV lenses and windows.
item.semiconductor-lab.lithium_hexafluor: The salt dissolved in a battery's liquid that carries the lithium ions.
Lithium fluoride + red phosphorus + fluorine (cylinder returned). ⚠ GHS: gives off hydrogen fluoride with water or moisture (acute toxicity, corrosive).
LiPF6. Phosphorus and fluorine form phosphorus pentafluoride PF5, which joins lithium fluoride. In a battery it is dissolved in organic solvents such as ethylene carbonate.
Water breaks it down, so battery factories assemble cells in very dry rooms (dry rooms).
Approximation: really PF5 is made first and reacted with lithium fluoride in anhydrous hydrogen fluoride. There is no electrolyte solvent yet (left out).
item.semiconductor-lab.stepping_motor.no: A small motor that clicks round by a fixed angle every time it gets one pulse of electricity.
Electromagnet + magnet + iron -> 2. It moves a quartz watch's second hand once a second.
A variable-reluctance type was patented in Britain in 1919, and around 1936 Marius Lavet in France devised a small form for clocks (the Lavet type) ⚠️. Mass production began around 1950.
Counting pulses tells you how far it has turned, so it also positions printers, 3D printers and machine tools.
item.semiconductor-lab.stepping_motor.pl: Approximation: for now only a watch part. How to play with it for positioning is not decided yet ([4-17]).
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.note1: A very bright light made by an electric spark jumping between two carbon rods. The rods burn away.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.note2: Glows on 450 W (light level 15). Feed graphite (carbon rods); one lasts 2 minutes. Crafting: 4 iron + 2 graphite + soda-lime glass + copper cable.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.note3: Works like the arc furnace [3-15]: the arc heats the carbon tips white-hot. The carbon slowly reacts with oxygen in the air.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.note4: Davy showed the arc around 1808, and from the late 1870s arc lamps lit streets and lighthouses — electric light before the bulb. In 1899 Hertha Ayrton showed the hissing came from carbon reacting with oxygen. ⚠️ Dates being checked.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.placeho: Omitted: ⚠️ power and rod burn rate are game values. The mechanism keeping the gap is omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.arc_lamp.howto: Insert graphite (carbon rods) and supply 450 W to glow brightly. One rod lasts 2 minutes.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.n: A glass bell on an iron plate. Pump the air out with a hand pump next to it.

Holds a pressure (Pa). Starts at 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. A hand pump next to it lowers the pressure each stroke (down to 1 kPa); a Sprengel mercury pump takes it down to 0.05 Pa. Air slowly leaks back in through the greased seal (about 0.1 Pa per minute). You cannot see the pressure - use a mercury gauge.

19th-century labs used a glass bell jar ground flat at the rim and greased onto a flat plate. The outside air pushes the bell down with about 1 kg on every square centimetre, which is what keeps it sealed.
Large or hot chambers later became welded mild steel, and ultra-high vacuum uses stainless steel baked at 150-250 C so gas trapped in the walls comes out first. Here only the glass stage exists.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.p: Omitted: the grease on the ground seal (tallow [2-09]).
message.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber: You can't see air pressure. Hold a mercury vacuum gauge and right-click.
block.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pump: Magdeburg hemispheres: with the air pumped out, 16 horses could not pull them apart.

Otto von Guericke's air pump (c. 1650). Place next to a vacuum chamber and right-click with an empty hand: each stroke removes 20% of the air (chamber : cylinder = 4 : 1). It never gets below about 1 kPa (1/100 atm). Costs a little hunger.

Each stroke follows Boyle's law: the chamber air spreads into the empty cylinder, the valve closes, and that share is pushed outside. The pressure falls like 0.8, 0.64, 0.51... so the first strokes do the most.

The limit comes from dead volume: air left in the gap between the piston and the valve at the end of the stroke expands back in, and the leather packing leaks. Guericke reached roughly a few hundred Pa to 1 kPa. Better vacuum needed Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) and the diffusion pump (1915).
Approximation: the real cylinder was cast brass/bronze ([1-05] not implemented) - steel here. The leather packing uses vanilla leather (rubber [2-29] not implemented).
message.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pu: Place a vacuum chamber next to the pump.
Whoosh... the piston still moves easily (lots of air left)
Whoosh... very heavy - the air outside pushes back on the piston
It won't go lower - this is the hand pump's limit (about 1 kPa)
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum_ga: Air pressure equals the weight of 76 cm of mercury.

A closed-end U-tube of mercury (Torricelli's mercury column, 1643). Right-click a vacuum chamber: the difference in mercury height is the pressure in mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa, 1 atm = 760 mmHg). Below 1 mm it can't be read by eye.
One arm is sealed with nothing above the mercury (the 'Torricellian vacuum'); the other is open to the chamber. The chamber gas pushes its side down by exactly its pressure in mm of mercury.

For lower pressures came the McLeod gauge (1874, compresses a sample of gas with mercury so it can be read), the Pirani gauge (1906, how fast a hot wire cools) and the hot-cathode ionization gauge (1916, built like a vacuum tube).
message.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum: The mercury levels are within 1 mm - too low to read (below %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Everything is inside the glass, but it is still full of air. Seal it on a sealing station.
Glass bulb + tungsten wire filament + iron wire grid + iron plate. With air inside, the hot filament would burn out at once. Put it in a sealing station next to a pumped-down vacuum chamber.
Approximation: grid and plate are iron (nickel [1-37] not implemented). The lead-in wires through the glass (platinum / Dumet wire, glass-metal seal [5-12]) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note1: Add one more electrode to a light bulb and you can control the flow of electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note: Lee de Forest's Audion (1906). The hot tungsten filament boils off electrons; the plate collects them; a small voltage on the grid between them controls a large current - an amplifier. Part of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note3: Fleming's diode (1904) used Edison's discovery that a hot filament gives off current. De Forest added the zig-zag grid. Before transistors, every radio, telephone repeater and early computer amplified with tubes like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note4: De Forest's first Audions were 'soft' - gas left inside made them erratic. Langmuir and Arnold (c. 1913) showed that a hard vacuum (about 10^-4 Pa) makes tubes stable, which needed diffusion pumps and getters (the silver film inside a tube is the getter that ate the last gas).
Pump the air out of the bulb, then melt the glass neck shut.

Place next to a vacuum chamber (it is the exhaust manifold). Tube assembly + chamber at 0.1 Pa or lower + 500 W x 10 s (filament heated to drive out gas) -> triode vacuum tube. A hand pump cannot reach 0.1 Pa - you need a Sprengel mercury pump. Each tube lets some air back into the chamber (5% of the gap to 1 atm) - wait for it to pump down again.

Real tube factories pumped each bulb through a glass tube at its top, heated the parts to drive out gas, then melted that tube shut with a flame. The little glass tip on old tubes and light bulbs is where it was sealed off.

Gas hides in the metal and glass surfaces. While pumping, the filament is run hot and the plate heated (later by induction) so the gas comes out before sealing; finally the getter is flashed to absorb what is left.
Approximation: the sealing-off flame (gas burner) is represented by electric power.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Tungsten only emits electrons (thermionic emission) above about 2000 °C. At that temperature in air it burns at once: 2W + 3O2 → 2WO3 (yellow smoke). Gas molecules would also get in the electrons' way.

De Forest's 1906 triode, the Audion, still held some gas (a "soft" vacuum) and behaved erratically. Around 1913 Langmuir and others pumped tubes to a high vacuum and made them stable. The silver mirror inside later tubes is the getter (barium) that soaks up leftover gas.
block.semiconductor-lab.sprengel_pump.no: A pump that carries air away bit by bit with falling drops of mercury.

Place it next to a vacuum chamber and load 4 mercury: it keeps pumping every second (no power, mercury is not used up). It reaches 0.05 Pa; at 0.1 Pa or below the sealing station can seal vacuum tubes. Roughing to 1 kPa with the hand pump first is a little faster.

Mercury drops falling down a narrow glass tube trap pockets of gas between them and push them down like little pistons. With no moving parts and no dead space it reaches pressures about ten thousand times lower than a hand pump - though the mercury's own vapour (about 0.2 Pa at 20 °C) remains.

Invented by Hermann Sprengel in London in 1865; his first pump emptied a half-litre vessel in about 20 minutes. In 1879 Swan and Edison exhausted their carbon-filament lamps with it, so the filaments glowed for a long time instead of burning out. Crookes ran several in series to study cathode rays in his discharge tubes - a path that led to the discovery of the electron.
Not enough mercury (%s / %s). Right-click with mercury
No vacuum chamber next to it
Mercury drops are falling: pumping the chamber next to it (down to 0.05 Pa)
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.note: A pump that spins a rotor with a motor and pushes air out steadily. Place it next to a vacuum chamber.

250 W electric. Pumps the adjacent vacuum chamber down to 1 Pa (about 17 s from 1 atm). It can also pump a chamber beyond an adjacent diffusion pump (as its backing pump). Recipe: rotor + 2 steel + motor + 2 mercury.

In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that carried air in pockets sealed by mercury on a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a motor-driven machine. Oil-sealed rotary pumps followed soon after (⚠️ around 1907).

As the off-centre (eccentric) rotor turns, the space between it and the casing grows to draw gas in and shrinks to push it out. Sealing the gaps with a liquid (mercury, oil) is the key. The lab's 'hum' is this pump.
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.plac: Approximation: stage 1 (mercury-sealed). Gaede's rotary mercury pump also used a separate backing pump; here it pumps directly from atmosphere. The 1 Pa limit is a game value. Oil stages (castor oil, silicone oil) come later.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.n: A pump that knocks the remaining air away with a wind of mercury vapor. No moving parts.

400 W heater. Place it next to both a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump (backing). It starts once the chamber is below 10 Pa and brings it down to about 0.004 Pa, where it balances the leak (high vacuum, enough for evaporation). Recipe: 3 soda-lime glass + 2 iron + 2 mercury + tungsten wire (heater).

In 1915 Gaede boiled mercury in an iron pot and blew the vapor through glass tubes: the diffusion pump. In 1916 Langmuir cooled the walls with water to condense the vapor (the condensation pump) and made it much faster. Now vacuum tubes and lamps could reach high vacuum.

A fast downward jet of mercury vapor knocks any gas molecules that wander into it downwards. At atmospheric pressure there are too many molecules and the jet breaks up, so a backing pump must lower the pressure first. From 1928, low-vapor-pressure oils replaced mercury [5-06].
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.p: Approximation: Gaede heated with a Bunsen burner (here an electric heater). The cold trap that stops mercury vapor drifting into the chamber, the cooling water and the warm-up time are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note1: A machine that heats metal in a vacuum into vapor and coats glass with a thin layer of it.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note2: 300 W electric (tungsten wire heater). Place it next to a vacuum chamber; it runs only while the chamber is below 0.01 Pa (needs a diffusion pump [5-05]), 20 s per run. Crown glass + silver nugget -> half-silvered mirror; lens + fluorite -> coated lens [7-22]. Each run opens the chamber, so the pressure rises a little. Recipe: 2 W wire + 2 iron + copper cable + soda-lime glass.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note3: In 1912 Pohl and Pringsheim evaporated metals in vacuum to make mirror films (there were earlier attempts). In the 1930s John Strong evaporated aluminum onto telescope mirrors, making mirrors that tarnish less. The aluminum wiring of 1960s ICs was made the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.note4: Leftover air scatters the evaporated metal atoms. The distance a gas molecule travels before the next collision (mean free path) is about 6.6 mm divided by the pressure in Pa. At 0.01 Pa that is about 66 cm, longer than the bell jar, so atoms fly straight to the substrate.
block.semiconductor-lab.evaporator.place: Omitted: film thickness control (the later quartz crystal thickness monitor [8-15]) and sputtering. For now silver and CaF2 can be deposited (aluminum, chromium and others once their prerequisites exist).
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note1: A pump that spins a bladed rotor extremely fast to bat gas molecules away. No oil or mercury, so the vacuum stays clean.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note2: 6 aluminium + 2 steel + motor. 300 W. With an adjacent vacuum chamber, a running rotary pump next to it (backing), the chamber at 10 Pa or less and a precise ball bearing (grade 2+, right-click with a bearing), it pumps down to 1e-6 Pa.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note3: In 1958 Becker at Pfeiffer in Germany presented the turbine-type molecular pump (its ancestor is Gaede's 1913 molecular pump). It needed precise ball bearings to carry blades spinning tens of thousands of times a minute.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.note4: The blade tips move nearly as fast as the molecules (hundreds of m/s) and knock them downward. With no oil or mercury vapor backstreaming to dirty films, most semiconductor tool vacuums became turbomolecular.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.place: Approximation: blade stages and speed are skipped. No cold trap (which would stop a diffusion pump's vapor).
item.semiconductor-lab.methyl_chloride.n: A gas made from methanol and hydrogen chloride. Raw material for silicones.
Silicone reactor: methanol + dry hydrogen chloride (alumina catalyst) → methyl chloride. 2 per metallurgical silicon.
CH3OH + HCl → CH3Cl + H2O, with both gases passed over alumina at about 300 °C.
Flammable and harmful to the nerves if breathed (GHS: flame, health hazard). Plants keep it in closed piping. It was once a refrigerant, dropped because leaks were dangerous.
item.semiconductor-lab.dimethyldichloros: A liquid: silicon with two methyl groups and two chlorines. Water turns it into silicone.
Silicone reactor: 1 metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride (copper catalyst) + empty glass bottle → this (direct process). With distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid.
Si + 2CH3Cl → (CH3)2SiCl2. The 'direct process' found around 1940 by Rochow at GE and Müller in Germany independently. Most silicone is still made this way.
Even moist air makes it fume white hydrogen chloride (GHS: flame, corrosive). The real direct process also gives methyltrichlorosilane and others, separated by distillation.
Omitted: ⚠️ by-products (methyltrichlorosilane etc.) are not made; main product only.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicone_oil.note: An oil of linked silicon and oxygen that hardly evaporates. Used in oil diffusion pumps.
Silicone reactor: dimethyldichlorosilane + distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid. Material for the oil diffusion pump.
A chain of repeating -Si(CH3)2-O- (polydimethylsiloxane). Heat-resistant, hard to burn, low vapour pressure.
Found in shampoo, cosmetics and water-repellent sprays. ⚠️ Real diffusion-pump oils are silicones with benzene rings (phenyl groups, e.g. DC-704) that evaporate even less.
item.semiconductor-lab.silicone_oil.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ phenyl silicones for diffusion pumps are not made; one dimethyl silicone oil stands in.
block.semiconductor-lab.silicone_reactor: Makes silicone oil in three reactions. What you put in picks the reaction.

2 kW, 15 s each. ① methanol + dry hydrogen chloride + alumina (catalyst) → methyl chloride ② metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride + copper (catalyst) + empty bottle → dimethyldichlorosilane ③ dimethyldichlorosilane + distilled water → silicone oil + hydrochloric acid. Catalysts are kept.
Silicones are organic compounds of silicon. Kipping studied them in the 1900s; the direct process of about 1940 made mass production possible.
During the Second World War they were rushed into production as insulation for aircraft electrics and heat-resistant oils (Dow Corning, 1943).
Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Water from ① is discarded. By-products and distillation in ② are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.oil_diffusion_pu: A diffusion pump that boils an oil that hardly evaporates instead of mercury.
1 kW. Like the mercury diffusion pump, place it next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump; it starts below 10 Pa. Reaches 10⁻⁵ Pa and leaves 30% each second (mercury: 50%) = faster.
In 1928 Burch in Britain replaced mercury with a low-vapour-pressure oil distilled from petroleum; in the 1930s Hickman at Kodak made the fractionating type. Steel bodies allow large pumps.

No poisonous mercury vapour. Some oil vapour still creeps back into the chamber (backstreaming), so turbomolecular pumps are used when films must be clean. Letting air onto hot oil scorches it, so cool it before venting.
Omitted: ⚠️ real oils are phenyl silicones or petroleum oils. Cooling water, baffles and warm-up time are omitted; ultimate pressure and speed are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.mercury_baromete: A glass tube of mercury stood upside down. Right-click to read the air pressure at its height.
Crafting: 2 soda-lime glass + mercury (the iron flask comes back) + 2 planks. Right-click for the column height (mmHg) and pressure (hPa). The higher you place it, the lower it reads.
Mercury stops about 760 mm up the tube with a Torricellian vacuum above, where its weight balances the push of the air. 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 1013 hPa.

Torricelli made it in 1643; in 1648 Pascal's brother-in-law Périer showed the column is lower on a mountain. The hPa of weather forecasts honours Pascal. Mercury vapour is toxic, so such barometers fell out of use.
Omitted: ⚠️ weather and temperature changes are not modelled. The height scale (1/e per about 8400 blocks) is a game approximation.
Mercury column %s mmHg (%s hPa)  height Y=%s
block.semiconductor-lab.oil_diffusion_pu: Place next to both a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump. Once the chamber is below 10 Pa it pumps to 10⁻⁵ Pa. 1 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.silicone_reactor: By combination: methanol + hydrogen chloride (alumina) → methyl chloride; metallurgical silicon + 2 methyl chloride (copper) + bottle → dimethyldichlorosilane; that + distilled water → silicone oil. 2 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.diffusion_pump.h: Place next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump, then connect power. The rotary pump must pump first. Nothing is used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.rotary_pump.howt: Place next to a vacuum chamber and connect power. It slowly pumps the air out, and also backs diffusion and turbo pumps.
block.semiconductor-lab.turbo_pump.howto: Place next to a vacuum chamber and a running rotary pump, right-click it with precise ball bearings, then connect power. A clean vacuum without oil or mercury.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Put sulfuric acid or salt in the lower-left slot. (1) Water + sulfuric acid (not used up): 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, 572 kJ = 115 s at 5 kW. (2) Water + 2 salt [6-05]: 2NaCl + 2H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH, about 640 kJ = 128 s. The + electrode gives oxygen from water, chlorine from brine.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: H2, made by splitting water. One bag ≈ 1 mol (≈24 L at 25 °C, 1 atm). 19th-century labs carried gases in rubberised-cloth bags. Store large amounts in a Gas Holder [6-02]. Later used as a protective furnace atmosphere and for ammonia (Haber–Bosch).
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note: O2, from the + electrode of the electrolyzer, half the volume of the hydrogen. One bag ≈ 1 mol. Keep it in a different holder from hydrogen: mixed, they make an explosive oxyhydrogen mixture. Later used for oxidising silicon (SiO2 film).
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: The lightest gas. A balloon filled with it floats up into the sky.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note1: The gas that makes things burn. About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note1: In the age of gas lamps, gas tanks were sealed with water so the gas could not leak out.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note: A low-pressure tank: a bottomless iron bell over a tank of water (19th-century gasworks). Gas lifts the bell, and the bell's weight pushes the gas out. Holds one gas at a time (set by the first gas in, cleared when empty). Automatically takes the same gas from an adjacent electrolyzer. Capacity 1000 mol ≈ 24.5 m³ (25 °C, 1 atm). Mixing hydrogen and oxygen gives oxyhydrogen (2H2+O2→2H2O): bang.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note3: London's Gas Light and Coke Company (founded 1812) stored coal gas in water-sealed gasholders and piped it to street lamps. The huge cylindrical iron frames still stand at places like King's Cross, reused as a park and as flats.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note4: Gas pressure = bell weight ÷ bell area (a few kPa, a few % above atmospheric), so no compressor is needed, but the volume stays large. Squeezing gas small enough to carry is the job of the compressor and cylinder [6-03]. Hydrogen molecules are tiny and slowly escape through gaps in metal and dissolve a little in the seal water (ignored in game).
item.semiconductor-lab.empty_gas_cylinde: A thick steel bottle that can hold gas squeezed to 150 times air pressure.

A seamless steel cylinder (about 10 L). Put it in a compressor next to a gas holder: it is filled with 50 mol of that gas at about 150 atm. Low-pressure bags (about 1 mol) are still handy for small amounts.

Gas cylinders became practical in the 1880s: Brin's Oxygen Company in London (1886) sold compressed oxygen in metal cylinders, and the Mannesmann brothers' seamless steel tubes (late 1880s) made strong cylinders without a welded seam.
50 mol at 25 C and 150 atm takes V = nRT/P = 50 x 0.0821 x 298 / 150, about 8 L (ideal gas). Real cylinders are tested with water at 5/3 of the filling pressure and re-tested every few years.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_cylinder: In Japan, hydrogen cylinders are painted red so nobody mixes them up.
50 mol of H2 compressed to about 150 atm in a steel cylinder (about 1.2 m3 of gas at normal pressure). Flammable: 4-75% in air can explode.
Japan's High Pressure Gas Safety Act fixes cylinder colours: oxygen black, hydrogen red, carbon dioxide green, chlorine yellow, ammonia white, acetylene brown, others grey.

Hydrogen atoms are so small that they creep into steel and make it brittle (hydrogen embrittlement). Hydrogen cylinders use tougher, lower-strength steel, and modern 700-bar fuel-cell car tanks use carbon fibre with a plastic liner. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_cylinder.n: In Japan, oxygen cylinders are painted black.
50 mol of O2 compressed to about 150 atm. Pure oxygen makes things burn violently: never put oil or grease on the valve.
The first big use of bottled oxygen was the limelight of theatres (an oxy-hydrogen flame heating lime) and then welding and cutting with the oxy-acetylene torch (1903). Hospitals followed.

At high pressure, oil and grease can ignite by themselves in oxygen (adiabatic compression heats the gas when a valve is opened quickly). Oxygen valves are cleaned to remove oil and opened slowly. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note1: High-pressure cylinders were made in the 1880s, and people could carry gas around.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note: An electric piston compressor. Place it next to a gas holder with at least 50 mol: empty cylinder + 50 mol + 5 kW x 124 s -> filled cylinder of that gas. The energy (620 kJ) is the work to squeeze 50 mol from 1 to 150 atm at constant temperature, nRT ln(150).
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note3: Squeezing gas heats it, so real compressors work in stages (for example 1 -> 6 -> 30 -> 150 atm) with water coolers between them. A bicycle pump gets warm for the same reason.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note4: Isothermal work W = nRT ln(P2/P1) = 50 x 8.314 x 298 x ln150, about 621 kJ. Squeezing to 150 atm in one adiabatic stroke (no cooling) would need more work (about 1 MJ) and heat the gas to nearly 1000 C, which is why multi-stage cooling matters.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note1: Salt that turned into stone. It used to be a sea.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note2: Halite, NaCl 95-99%. Found in evaporite beds under deserts and badlands. Crush it in the crafting grid to get salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note3: When an ancient sea was cut off and dried up, its salts settled in layers. Salt beds can be hundreds of metres thick. Poland's Wieliczka mine has been worked since the 13th century and even has a chapel carved out of salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.note4: Seawater precipitates salts in order as it evaporates: calcite -> gypsum -> halite -> potassium/magnesium salts. That is why rock salt beds often sit on top of gypsum. Salt is soft and flows slowly under pressure, forming salt domes that trap oil.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt.placeho: Approximation: crushing gives salt 1:1. Removing impurities (gypsum, clay) by dissolving and recrystallising is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note1: The same salt you eat. Rock salt and sea salt are both NaCl.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note2: Sodium chloride NaCl. Raw material for chlor-alkali electrolysis [6-05] (brine -> chlorine + hydrogen + caustic soda).
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note3: Salt was so valuable that Roman soldiers were said to receive a salt allowance - the word 'salary' is often linked to it. In Japan, salt was made from seawater because there is no rock salt.
item.semiconductor-lab.salt.note4: Today about 40% of the salt mined worldwide goes to the chemical industry, mostly to chlor-alkali plants. Japan has no rock salt, so it imports solar salt from Mexico and Australia for that.
block.semiconductor-lab.rock_salt_ore.no: A layer of salt deep under the desert. Long ago this was a sea.
Evaporite bed. Generates only under deserts and badlands (y0-48), replacing stone in large lenses. Soft (Mohs 2.5): any pickaxe drops rock salt; silk touch keeps the block.
Rock salt is 'a sea turned into stone'. The Zechstein sea dried up about 255 million years ago and left salt under much of northern Europe.
Salt mines are dry and stable, so some old ones store nuclear waste or archives. Salt also conducts heat well and seals cracks by slowly flowing.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.pla: Simplified (brine mode): the diaphragm / mercury cell / ion-exchange membrane that keeps chlorine away from the caustic soda is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_gas.note: A yellow-green, poisonous gas. Salt and electricity make it.

Cl2, from the + electrode when brine is electrolysed [6-05]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Store it in a gas holder (mixing with hydrogen explodes: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl). Burn it with hydrogen to make hydrochloric acid [6-06].

Scheele made chlorine in 1774 from hydrochloric acid and manganese dioxide but thought it contained oxygen. In 1810 Davy showed it was an element and named it after the Greek 'chloros' (yellow-green).

Chlorine is heavier than air (2.5x), so it sinks into hollows. It became the first large-scale chemical weapon at Ypres in 1915 - and also the chlorination of drinking water (from 1908) that saved far more lives.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorine_cylinder: In Japan, chlorine cylinders are painted yellow.
50 mol of Cl2 filled by the compressor [6-03] from a gas holder.
Chlorine turns into a liquid at only about 7 atm at room temperature, so real chlorine cylinders contain liquid chlorine with gas on top - much more fits than in a hydrogen cylinder.

Cylinder colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard: hydrogen red, oxygen black, chlorine yellow. Dry chlorine does not attack steel, but wet chlorine does (it forms HCl), so cylinders must be kept dry.
Caustic soda. Strong enough to dissolve skin - handle with care.
NaOH, collects at the - electrode in brine electrolysis [6-05] (2 per run). Strong base: later used in the Bayer process for alumina [1-14] and for soap.
Chlorine and caustic soda always come out together in a fixed ratio (1 t Cl2 : 1.1 t NaOH). Plants must find buyers for both - this is called the 'chlor-alkali balance'.
Before electrolysis (1890s), caustic soda was made by boiling soda ash with slaked lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3. Castner and Kellner's mercury cell (1892) made electrolysis practical.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note1: Burns hydrogen in chlorine and dissolves the smoke in water to make hydrochloric acid.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note2: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl (burns at about 2000 C), then HCl gas is absorbed in water. 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 + 1/4 bucket of water (5 s) -> 1 hydrochloric acid. Gas from bags (1 mol), cylinders (50 mol) or an adjacent gas holder. No electricity needed. With no water (water slot empty), the HCl stays as dry gas: 1 mol H2 + 1 mol Cl2 -> 2 bags of hydrogen chloride gas, for trichlorosilane [1-16].
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note3: Burning hydrogen in chlorine gives a pale flame and white fumes of HCl. This 'synthetic hydrochloric acid' became the main use for the chlorine and hydrogen that chlor-alkali plants produced from the 1890s on.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.note4: The burner nozzle is made of quartz (later graphite) because hot HCl eats metals. The mixture is only safe because the gases meet at the nozzle: premixed H2 + Cl2 explodes in sunlight. Earlier, HCl came from the Leblanc process (salt + sulfuric acid) and was simply vented as a pollutant until the 1863 Alkali Act.
block.semiconductor-lab.hcl_burner.place: Approximation: one-block burner with a built-in absorber. Gas amounts are stoichiometric; cooling water is not needed.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrochloric_acid: A strong acid that dissolves metals. Your stomach makes a weak version of it.
HCl dissolved in water (about 25%, 2 mol HCl per bottle). Made in the HCl synthesis burner [6-06]. Used for tungstic acid [1-28] and germanium tetrachloride [1-34].
Alchemists called it 'spirit of salt' (made by heating salt with sulfuric acid). Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off HCl gas that fumes in moist air. Gastric juice is about 0.1 mol/L HCl.

HCl gas dissolves enormously in water: about 450 L of gas per litre at 20 C, so you cannot make it more than about 38%. In semiconductor fabs, dilute HCl with hydrogen peroxide (RCA clean SC-2, 1965) removes metal contamination from wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: Burning makes only water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, releasing about 286 kJ per bag (1 mol), exactly the electricity the electrolyzer spent splitting it. Mixed with air at 4-75% it explodes when lit.

Cavendish discovered it in 1766 as the "inflammable air" given off when acid meets metal. In 1783 Lavoisier named it hydrogène, "water-maker"; the Japanese name suiso (water element) translates that. The same year Charles flew in a hydrogen balloon.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note3: In sulfuric-acid electrolysis, + electrode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; − electrode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H2. Four electrons give one O2 and two H2, so the oxygen is half the hydrogen's volume.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note4: Scheele and Priestley each discovered it in the 1770s. Lavoisier thought every acid contained it and named it oxygène, "acid-maker". That was wrong (hydrochloric acid, HCl, has no oxygen), but the Japanese name sanso (acid element) keeps the mistake alive.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: Uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Pure water barely conducts, so sulfuric acid is added to supply ions (charged particles that carry current); the acid itself is not used up. Splitting water needs 1.23 V in theory, but about 2 V in practice because of losses at the electrodes.

In 1800, just after news of Volta's pile arrived, Nicholson and Carlisle electrolyzed water. In 1834 Faraday found the laws of electrolysis and coined (with Whewell's help) the words electrode, anode, cathode, ion and electrolyte.
block.semiconductor-lab.air_separation_u: Freezes air into a liquid and splits it into nitrogen, oxygen and argon.

Runs on electricity alone (the raw material is the air around it). 5 kW x 16 s separates 10 mol of air: about 8 bags of nitrogen, 2 of oxygen, and one bag of argon every ~11 runs. A gas holder next to it pulls from the outputs automatically.

Air is compressed to about 200 atm, cooled in a heat exchanger and then expanded through a small valve, which cools it (the Joule-Thomson effect). Repeating this liquefies it at about -194 °C. Distilling the liquid air stage by stage in a rectifying column sends low-boiling nitrogen (-196 °C) up and oxygen (-183 °C) down, while argon (-186 °C) collects in the middle.

Carl von Linde liquefied air in 1895 and separated oxygen with a rectifying column in 1902. Argon had been found in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, because nitrogen from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made chemically. Its name is Greek for 'lazy' (it reacts with nothing). It later filled light bulbs and the furnaces that pull silicon crystals. Early plants used far more electricity than today's.
Omitted: the insulated cold box (real ones were wooden boxes packed with wool etc.), hours of cool-down at start-up, a separate argon column. Power uses the modern value (1900s plants used more).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_gas.note: Four fifths of the air is this gas. Breathing it in does nothing to your body.

N2. Comes from the air separation unit [6-07]. 1 bag = about 1 mol. Works with gas holders and the compressor (nitrogen cylinder). It reacts with almost nothing, so it is used to blanket things you do not want oxidized.

The two atoms of N2 are held by a triple bond (N≡N, about 945 kJ/mol), so it hardly reacts at ordinary temperatures. Above about 1200 °C, though, it reacts with silicon to form silicon nitride (Si3N4) - so molten silicon is blanketed with argon instead.

Discovered in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford as air in which neither a candle nor a mouse could live. Lavoisier called it azote, 'lifeless' (still its French name). Plants cannot use nitrogen from the air directly; until the Haber-Bosch process [6-09] turned it into fertilizer, it set the limit on food.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note1: A gas that reacts with nothing, about 1% of the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note2: Ar. The air separation unit gives one bag per about 108 mol of air. Works with gas holders and the compressor (argon cylinder). Planned use: filling the furnace that pulls silicon crystals (CZ).
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note3: Argon is a noble gas (group 18): its outer electron shell is exactly full, so it bonds with almost nothing. Molten silicon (1414 °C) reacts with nitrogen and oxygen, but not with argon. It is about 1.4 times denser than air and lingers even in an open container.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_gas.note4: Discovered in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, who noticed that 'nitrogen' left after removing oxygen etc. from air was about 0.5% heavier than nitrogen made by chemical reactions. It is 0.93% of the air, yet nobody had noticed. Almost all argon on Earth comes from the decay of potassium-40 in rocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitrogen_cylinder: In Japan, nitrogen cylinders are painted grey.
50 mol of N2 from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Nitrogen cannot be liquefied at room temperature however hard you squeeze it (it stays gas above its critical temperature, -147 °C). So the cylinder holds high-pressure gas; liquid nitrogen travels in insulated vacuum flasks.

The Japanese rules fix the colours for oxygen (black), hydrogen (red), liquefied CO2 (green), liquefied ammonia (white), liquefied chlorine (yellow) and acetylene (brown). Every other gas, nitrogen and argon included, is grey with the contents written on it.
item.semiconductor-lab.argon_cylinder.no: Argon cylinders are grey too - read the lettering to tell them apart.
50 mol of Ar from a gas holder, filled by the compressor [6-03].

Argon's critical temperature is -122 °C, so like nitrogen it is high-pressure gas, not liquid, in a room-temperature cylinder. It is the most common shielding gas that protects metal from air during welding.

Argon comes out of air separation alongside oxygen and nitrogen, so it is by far the cheapest noble gas. It is inside light bulbs too: it slows the evaporation of the tungsten filament (Langmuir filled bulbs with nitrogen in 1913, later argon).
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth_bloc: Soft earth with white crystals in it, deep in limestone caves.
Only in dripstone caves (inside dripstone blocks). Dig with a shovel for 2 nitre earth; silk touch keeps the block.
During the War of 1812, saltpeter was mined from the cave earth of Mammoth Cave in the USA. Wooden pipes and vats from that time still remain in the cave.
Cave nitrates form when bacteria break down nitrogen from things like bat droppings (nitrification). They build up over centuries in dry cave earth that rain cannot wash out.
Approximation: placed only in dripstone caves (in reality it also came from old stable floors and walls; domestication [0-17] and nitre beds [6-10] come later).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note1: Earth containing nitrates. Soak it in water and they dissolve out.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note2: 4 + wood ash + water bucket -> nitre liquor (the bucket comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note3: Old saltpeter diggers are said to have tasted the earth of stable floors and old walls: a bitter, cool taste meant plenty of saltpeter (⚠️ a tradition).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_earth.note4: Most of the nitrate in the earth is calcium nitrate Ca(NO3)2, which absorbs moisture and hardly crystallizes on its own.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_liquor.note: The clear liquid from soaking nitre earth in water with wood ash. Boil it down and white crystals appear.
4 nitre earth + wood ash + water bucket (the bucket comes back). Boil it down in a furnace for saltpeter.
Adding wood ash is old wisdom: its potassium carbonate settles the calcium out as calcium carbonate and turns the nitrate into potassium saltpeter.
Ca(NO3)2 + K2CO3 -> 2KNO3 + CaCO3(s). Saltpeter dissolves well in hot water but poorly in cold, so boiling down and cooling makes it crystallize first (recrystallization purifies it).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitre_liquor.plac: Approximation: made before the container system (IMP-33), so no bottle. The settled calcium carbonate is discarded.
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note1: White crystals. The raw material for nitric acid, and a fertilizer. ⚠ Helps things burn (oxidizer).
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note2: Potassium nitrate KNO3, made by boiling down nitre liquor in a furnace. Distilled with sulfuric acid it gives nitric acid [6-11]. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid (keep away from fire).
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note3: As a raw material of gunpowder, saltpeter changed history (China in the 9th-10th centuries, Europe around the 13th). It also has many peaceful uses: curing meat (keeping its color), fertilizer, and removing bubbles from glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.saltpeter.note4: In the 19th century Chilean desert nitre (sodium nitrate) was exported worldwide as fertilizer. From 1913 the Haber-Bosch process made ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen, which could be oxidized to nitric acid [6-09].
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note1: A very strong acid that dissolves silver and copper. Kept in a glass bottle. ⚠ On skin it turns yellow and burns.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note2: Distil saltpeter + sulfuric acid (bottle) + an empty glass bottle with the quartz still (returned): KNO3 + H2SO4 -> HNO3 + KHSO4. The sulfuric acid bottle comes back empty. React with silver for silver nitrate. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing liquid, corrosive to metals, skin corrosion, toxic if inhaled (industrial material only).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note3: Its old name was aqua fortis ('strong water'). It dissolves silver but not gold, so it was used to part gold from silver (and test gold's purity). The first recipes appear in alchemical books of the late 13th-early 14th century; in the mid-17th century Glauber described making it from saltpeter and sulfuric acid (⚠️ the year 1648 is unconfirmed).
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.note4: Nitric acid is both an acid and an oxidizer, so it dissolves copper and silver that ordinary acids cannot (releasing NO and NO2 gas). In semiconductors it is mixed with hydrofluoric acid in etchants (such as CP-4) that dissolve and polish silicon and germanium surfaces.
item.semiconductor-lab.nitric_acid.place: Approximation: distillation in the crafting grid skips the heating. The byproduct potassium hydrogen sulfate and the brown NO2 gas are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nitrate.no: White crystals from dissolving silver in nitric acid. They turn black in light. ⚠ Leaves black stains on skin.

Silver nugget + nitric acid (the bottle comes back): 3Ag + 4HNO3 -> 3AgNO3 + NO + 2H2O. Material for photographic emulsions (silver halides) [B-02] and silver mirrors [7-05]. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid, skin corrosion, toxic to aquatic life.
It was once called lunar caustic and used in medicine, for example to burn off warts (in alchemy silver was the metal of the Moon).

Light reduces silver ions into tiny silver grains that look black. This property was the start of photography (Schulze showed in 1727 that it darkens in light ⚠️). Mixed with iodides or bromides it forms silver halides, which are far more light-sensitive.
item.semiconductor-lab.silver_nitrate.pl: Approximation: no container (in reality kept in light-proof brown bottles). Boiling down to crystals and the NO gas are omitted.
A column that extracts the tiny amounts of neon, krypton and xenon in liquid air.
Air separation unit + 4 steel + 2 copper. 2 kW, 5 s. Uses one bag each of oxygen and nitrogen per run; krypton takes 32 runs, neon 16 and xenon 250 to make one bag.
In 1898 Ramsay and Travers slowly evaporated liquid air and found neon (new), krypton (hidden) and xenon (stranger) one after another.

Air holds only 18 ppm neon, 1.1 ppm krypton and 0.09 ppm xenon. High-boiling krypton and xenon gather at the bottom of liquid oxygen and low-boiling neon above the nitrogen, so they are byproducts of air separation.
Approximation: yields are thousands of times richer than real air.
item.semiconductor-lab.neon_gas.note1: A gas that glows red when electricity passes through it: the color of neon signs.
item.semiconductor-lab.neon_gas.note2: From nitrogen in the rare gas column. Most of an excimer laser's gas (it dilutes the lasing gas and steadies the discharge).
item.semiconductor-lab.neon_gas.note3: In 1910 Claude made the neon sign. Neon's red is the set color of light from neon atoms.
item.semiconductor-lab.neon_gas.note4: Over 90% of a lithography excimer laser's gas is neon. In 2022 neon shortages worried chip fabs.
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_gas.note1: An unreactive gas found in tiny amounts in air.
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_gas.note2: From oxygen in the rare gas column (one bag per 32 runs). The lasing gas of the KrF excimer laser (248 nm).
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_gas.note3: Krypton is Greek for 'the hidden one'. From 1960 to 1983 the metre was defined by the wavelength of krypton-86 light.
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_gas.note4: Noble gases normally bond with nothing, but excited by a discharge krypton briefly forms KrF* with fluorine, which emits ultraviolet as it breaks up.
item.semiconductor-lab.xenon_gas.note1: A heavy noble gas, very scarce in air, used in bright flash lamps.
item.semiconductor-lab.xenon_gas.note2: From oxygen in the rare gas column (one bag per 250 runs). For flash lamps (ruby laser [7-13]).
item.semiconductor-lab.xenon_gas.note3: Xenon is Greek for 'stranger'. It is used in camera flashes and car headlights.
item.semiconductor-lab.xenon_gas.note4: There are only about 0.9 L in 10 million L of air, so it is very expensive.
item.semiconductor-lab.neon_cylinder.not: A steel cylinder packed with neon.
Fill it from neon bags with the compressor.
In Japan, noble gas cylinders are painted grey.
High-pressure gas. Chain it so it cannot fall over.
A steel cylinder packed with krypton.
Fill it from krypton bags with the compressor.
In Japan, noble gas cylinders are painted grey.
High-pressure gas. Chain it so it cannot fall over.
item.semiconductor-lab.xenon_cylinder.no: A steel cylinder packed with xenon.
Fill it from xenon bags with the compressor.
In Japan, noble gas cylinders are painted grey.
High-pressure gas. Chain it so it cannot fall over.
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorine_cell.no: A cell that frees fluorine with electricity. Fluorine reacts violently with almost anything; it is a very dangerous gas.

6 nickel + copper + copper cable. 2 kW, 10 s. Potassium fluoride (not used up) + graphite (anode, not used up) + hydrofluoric acid + empty cylinder -> a hydrogen bag each run and a fluorine cylinder every 5 runs. If the hydrogen outlet is full the gases mix: an accident that loses the stored fluorine and stops the cell. ⚠ Fluorine: GHS oxidizing gas, gas under pressure, acute toxicity (inhalation), skin corrosion. Handled only as an industrial material.
In 1886 Moissan in France first isolated fluorine in a chilled platinum U-tube (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1906). Several chemists before him had been injured by fluorine experiments.

Fluorine attacks most metals and glass, but nickel and copper are protected by a thin fluoride film. Fluorine forms at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode, so the two are kept apart (mixed, they react violently).
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorine_cell.pl: Approximation: real cells electrolyse molten KF·2HF (about 100 C). Voltage, temperature and amounts are not given.
item.semiconductor-lab.fluorine_cylinder: A steel cylinder filled with fluorine. Very dangerous.
Made in the fluorine cell. Lasing gas for the excimer laser [7-20]. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing gas, gas under pressure, acute toxicity (inhalation), skin corrosion. Handled only as an industrial material.
Fluorine pulls on electrons harder than any other element. It reacts with glass and even water as if burning them.
The inside of the steel cylinder is protected by the fluoride film formed when it first meets fluorine (passivation). Lithography lasers use fluorine diluted in neon.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_dioxide_ga: The gas that comes out when limestone is burned. It is also in your breath.
Roast calcite in the reverberatory furnace: quicklime comes out with CO2 in the flue slot. Gas for the CO2 laser. ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure (in cylinders). It pools in low places and can suffocate.
Lime-kiln gas is rich in CO2, and industry collected it there for fizzy drinks, dry ice and welding gas.
CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (about 900 C). CO2 is heavier than air and collects in hollows.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_catalyst.not: Black grains that help join nitrogen from the air with hydrogen into ammonia.
2 magnetite + potash + alumina. Goes in the catalyst slot of the Haber-Bosch reactor (not used up). Without it there is almost no reaction.
On fine iron made by reducing magnetite (Fe3O4) with hydrogen, the strong N≡N triple bond comes apart. Potash and alumina keep the iron grains from sintering and boost activity (promoters).
Mittasch at BASF ran about 20,000 tests and found Swedish magnetite worked best (1909-1912). Today's plants use almost the same catalyst.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_catalyst.pla: Approximation: the reduction step before use is skipped; the catalyst does not wear out.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_gas.note1: A gas with a sharp smell. The start of fertilizer made from nitrogen in the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_gas.note2: Two from 1 nitrogen + 3 hydrogen in the Haber-Bosch reactor. + sulfuric acid -> ammonium sulfate (fertilizer); + water + bottle -> ammonia water. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled), skin corrosion, flammable gas, gas under pressure, hazardous to aquatic life. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_gas.note3: N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3 (gives off heat). Higher pressure gives more NH3, but low temperature is slow, so about 450 C and 200 atm is a compromise.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonia_gas.note4: It is said that about half of the world's people are fed by crops grown with fertilizer from this process. Ammonia also makes nitric acid and so explosives (Germany kept making munitions this way in World War I).
A white powder fertilizer spread on fields. Used on tilled soil, it makes soil where crops grow well.
2 ammonia + sulfuric acid (bottle returned) make 4. Right-click farmland -> nitrogen-rich farmland (the same as soil after [0-05] peas, 3 uses). On nitrogen-rich farmland it tops it back up to 3.
2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4. Plants take up ammonium ions through their roots to make proteins.
Haber-Bosch did in a factory what root-nodule bacteria on legumes do: put air's nitrogen into the soil. Too much fertilizer washes into rivers and seas and feeds algae (eutrophication).
Approximation: differences between crops and harm from overuse are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.haber_bosch_reac: A high-pressure tower that makes ammonia, the start of fertilizer, from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen.
6 steel + compressor + copper cable. 20 kW (compression power). 1 bag of nitrogen + 3 bags of hydrogen + iron catalyst (not used up) -> 2 bags of ammonia (10 s). It will not run without the catalyst.
Nitrogen and hydrogen pass over the iron catalyst at about 200 atm and 450 C. Only about 15% reacts per pass, so the ammonia is cooled out as a liquid and the rest of the gas is sent round again.

Haber succeeded in the lab in 1909 and Bosch at BASF built the plant in 1913 (high-pressure hydrogen makes steel brittle, so he designed a double-walled reactor). Lesson: in World War I Haber led the chlorine gas attack (Ypres, 1915), and many soldiers died. The scientist who helped feed billions was also a developer of poison gas (how to make it is not in this mod).
Approximation: everything reacts in one pass; pressure and temperature are not given as numbers (standard screen).
message.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_sulfa: Nitrogen fertilizer spread: fertile farmland (3 shares of nitrogen)
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_gauze.no: A net woven from fine platinum wire. Speeds up reactions between gases.
2 platinum. Returned after crafting (a catalyst). SO2 + oxygen + this -> sulfur trioxide.
SO2 and O2 stick to the platinum surface, react, and leave as SO3; the platinum itself is unchanged (a catalyst).

In 1831 Peregrine Phillips, an English vinegar maker, patented turning SO2 into SO3 with platinum (the contact process). Arsenic and the like poison platinum, so from about 1915 vanadium pentoxide took over.
item.semiconductor-lab.platinum_gauze.pl: Approximation: really platinum on a carrier such as asbestos (no longer used), not a net. The temperature (about 450 °C) is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.sulfur_trioxide.n: White crystals. Reacts violently with water to give sulfuric acid.
Sulfur dioxide + oxygen (bag) + platinum gauze (returned) or vanadium pentoxide (returned). + sulfuric acid + iron flask -> oleum. ⚠ GHS: corrosive, reacts violently with water.
2SO2 + O2 ⇄ 2SO3. The reaction gives off heat, so high temperatures push it back and low temperatures make it slow; with a catalyst about 450 °C is the compromise between speed and yield.
Put straight into water, SO3 forms a fine mist of acid that is hard to absorb, so it is absorbed into concentrated sulfuric acid instead (oleum).
item.semiconductor-lab.oleum.note1: Very concentrated sulfuric acid that fumes. Kept in an iron flask.
item.semiconductor-lab.oleum.note2: Sulfur trioxide + sulfuric acid (bottle returned) + iron flask. + water + 2 glass bottles -> 2 sulfuric acid (iron flask returned). ⚠ GHS: corrosive (severe skin and eye damage), reacts violently with water.
item.semiconductor-lab.oleum.note3: SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7. Adding water doubles it: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4. It reacts with moisture in the air and gives off white fumes.
item.semiconductor-lab.oleum.note4: Concentrated sulfuric acid and oleum form a thin film on iron that stops further attack (passivation), so they ship in steel tanks. Dilute sulfuric acid dissolves iron and cannot.
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_bed.note1: A heap of soil, rotten meat and lime. Over time it becomes saltpetre earth.
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_bed.note2: Dirt + 2 rotten flesh + bone meal + slaked lime. Left alone, it slowly ripens into a nitre-earth block (dig with a shovel -> nitre earth -> saltpetre, as in [6-16]).
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_bed.note3: Proteins from meat and urine rot to ammonia, and soil bacteria turn it into nitric acid with oxygen (nitrification). With calcium from the lime, calcium nitrate builds up in the soil; potash from wood ash turns it into potassium nitrate (saltpetre).
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_bed.note4: Saltpetre was a gunpowder ingredient, so 18th-century European states had nitre beds built. In Gokayama and Shirakawa-go in Japan, saltpetre was cultured under house floors from silkworm droppings and grass. Saltpetre is made by bacteria.
block.semiconductor-lab.nitre_bed.placeh: Approximation: really months to over a year (tens of minutes in the game). Urine, straw and turning the heap are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_chamber.note: A large room lined with lead, where sulfuric acid is made.
8 lead. Returned after crafting. 2 SO2 + water + saltpetre + this + 2 glass bottles -> 2 chamber acid. ⚠ GHS: lead is a health hazard (wash hands after handling).
Sulfuric acid eats iron and wood, but lead grows a thin film of lead sulfate and stops dissolving, so the rooms were built of lead sheet. Inside, nitrogen oxides carry oxygen to SO2 (a catalyst).

In 1746 John Roebuck in Britain made sulfuric acid in bulk in lead chambers, and sulfuric acid became cheap for the first time. Gay-Lussac (1827) and Glover (1859) towers later recovered the nitrogen oxides.
item.semiconductor-lab.chamber_acid.note: Dilute sulfuric acid from the lead chamber. Boiling it down makes it stronger.

Two come from the lead-chamber route. + quartz still (returned) -> sulfuric acid (boiled down). ⚠ GHS: corrosive. When made, brown fumes (nitrogen dioxide) sometimes leak and make you feel sick for a while.
2SO2 + O2 + 2H2O -> 2H2SO4, with NO and NO2 acting as oxygen-carrying catalysts. It reaches only about 65%; it cannot make concentrated acid or oleum like the contact process [6-13].
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is a brown toxic gas (GHS: acute toxicity, inhalation). Fumes leaking from lead-chamber works harmed nearby fields and homes.
item.semiconductor-lab.chamber_acid.plac: Approximation: really the saltpetre's nitrogen oxides are recovered and reused (the game uses one). Glover and Gay-Lussac towers are omitted.
message.semiconductor-lab.chamber_acid.l: Brown fumes (nitrogen dioxide) leaked... you feel a little sick
block.semiconductor-lab.haber_bosch_reac: Put in 1 nitrogen bag, 3 hydrogen bags and the iron catalyst, and connect power. You get 2 ammonia bags. Without the catalyst it does nothing (the catalyst is not used up).
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.howto:
Stores one kind of gas (no power).
- Takes gas from a neighbouring electrolyzer or air separation unit
- Put bagged gas on the left to fill it; bags come out on the right
- The first gas decides the kind; empty resets it
- Mixing hydrogen and oxygen explodes and empties it
