item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note3: The gold wires are pressed onto the chip's aluminium pads with heat and pressure (thermocompression). There is one wire per pad.
item.semiconductor-lab.bonded_chip.note4: Today's bonders join more than 20 wires per second automatically.
block.semiconductor-lab.wire_bonder.note: Joins a chip to its leads with gold wire finer than a hair.

200 W (heats the stage). 1–8 chips + gold bonding wire (as many per chip as it has pads) + headers (one per chip) → bonded chips (15 s). Pads are wiring that reaches the chip edge; the NOT example has 4. Chips without pads cannot be bonded.
On a heated stage, pressing the end of the gold wire onto a pad makes gold and aluminium stick (thermocompression). The wire is led to the lead, pressed again and cut.
Thermocompression bonding was devised at Bell Labs around 1957 (⚠️ year not checked). Ultrasonic bonding was added later.
block.semiconductor-lab.wire_bonder.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Wire loop shapes and ultrasonic bonding are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note1: A small steel can that goes over a chip.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note2: Crafting: 1 steel → 8. In the package sealer [9-34] it is fitted over a bonded chip, filled with dry nitrogen and welded.
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note3: Filling the can with dry nitrogen keeps moisture off the chip surface. Transistors and early ICs came in these round cans (TO-5, TO-18 and others).
item.semiconductor-lab.can_cap.note4: The rim of the can and header is joined in an instant with a large current (resistance welding).
item.semiconductor-lab.can_packaged_chip: An IC sealed in a metal can with dry nitrogen. Resists moisture.
Made in the package sealer [9-34] from a bonded chip + can cap + nitrogen. Keeps the chip's contents (which circuit it is).
Early-1960s ICs had leads coming out of round metal cans just like transistors; the Apollo Guidance Computer's ICs started in this form too.
Hermetic cans are costly and heavy but very reliable, so they are still used in space and military equipment.
item.semiconductor-lab.plastic_packaged_: An IC wrapped in a black epoxy body: the familiar 'centipede'.
Made in the package sealer [9-34] from bonded chips + epoxy molding compound (1 per 4 chips). Keeps the chip's contents.
Epoxy compound is pressed into a heated mould around the chip (transfer molding): cheaper than cans and easy to mass-produce. Two rows of leads make a DIP (dual in-line package).

Fairchild introduced the DIP in 1964 (first in ceramic). Plastic DIPs spread from the late 1960s, and calculator and PC boards filled with these black centipedes. ⚠️ The year plastic spread is not checked.
block.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.n: Seals bonded chips inside a metal can or an epoxy body.
500 W. 1–8 bonded chips + can caps (one each) + 1 bag of nitrogen → metal-can ICs; or 1–8 bonded chips + epoxy molding compound (1 per 4 chips) → plastic ICs (20 s). Keeps the chips' contents.
Moisture or sodium on the chip surface changes its behaviour; enclosing it protects it. Cans are filled with nitrogen and welded; epoxy is pressed into a mould at about 175 °C and cured.
Early transistors and ICs were sealed in metal cans and glass. From the late 1960s cheap epoxy plastic packages (DIP and others) took over. ⚠️ Years not checked.
block.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Lead trimming and forming and post-seal testing are not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.nee: Needs chips and a can or epoxy
item.semiconductor-lab.cw_multiplier.not: Rectifiers and capacitors arranged like a ladder to multiply a voltage many times.
Crafting: 4 Leyden jars + 2 rectifiers + 2 steel + 1 copper cable → 1. With an accelerator tube it becomes the accelerator of the ion implanter [9-28] (tens to hundreds of kilovolts).
Each AC cycle charges a capacitor and passes it on to the next stage, so the voltage stacks up with the number of stages. Greinacher at the University of Bern devised the circuit in 1920.

In 1932 Cockcroft and Walton in Cambridge used it to reach hundreds of kilovolts and changed lithium nuclei with protons (1951 Nobel Prize in Physics). Such voltages spark through air and can electrocute people who merely come close, so the equipment is fenced and earthed.
item.semiconductor-lab.cw_multiplier.pla: Approximation: a part item; stage count and voltage are not modelled.
A vacuum tube of stacked glass and metal rings. Inside, ions are pushed faster by high voltage.
Crafting: 6 soda-lime glass + 3 steel → 1. With a Cockcroft–Walton multiplier it becomes the accelerator of the ion implanter [9-28].

With slightly different voltages on each metal ring, an ion gets a push at every ring and speeds up. The glass insulates the rings, and the inside is kept at high vacuum so ions do not hit air molecules.

At the same time Lawrence in the US built the cyclotron, accelerating particles round and round in an electromagnet (1930–31, 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics). Accelerators now also treat cancer and make hospital tracers. Fast ions hitting metal give off X-rays, so accelerators are shielded.
Approximation: a part item; length and vacuum level are not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.no: Turns dopant atoms into ions, speeds them up with high voltage and shoots them into wafers.

5 kW. 1–8 process wafers (with developed resist or oxide windows) + 1 dopant source (B2O3 = p-type, phosphorus = n-type) → implanted wafers (30 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.01 Pa or below. Implanting alone does nothing until annealing [9-29].

An ion source ionises the dopant, a mass-analysing electromagnet picks only the wanted ion (¹¹B⁺, ³¹P⁺), and the accelerator's high voltage drives it in. Unlike diffusion, windows stay open, ions do not spread sideways, and dose and depth can be set precisely.

Shockley filed the patent in 1954 and implantation became a production step in the 1960s–70s; every fab relies on it today. High voltage can electrocute and fast ions give off X-rays, so implanters are enclosed and shielded. Real ion-source gases, boron trifluoride and phosphine, are highly toxic and their cylinders are kept in monitored cabinets.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.pl: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Solid sources stand in for the source gases (BF3, PH3). Dose is only recorded; depth is not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.need: Needs wafers and a dopant source
block.semiconductor-lab.anneal_furnace.n: Heats wafers after ion implantation to heal the damage. Until then, the implanted atoms do nothing.

3 kW. 1–8 implanted wafers + 1 nitrogen or argon → annealed wafers (20 s). Takes nitrogen/argon from an adjacent gas holder. No wafers with resist (strip it first). Wafers without implants do not change.

Implanted ions knock silicon atoms out of place and sit in the gaps themselves. Around 1000 °C the atoms re-order (annealing) and dopants move onto lattice sites where they carry current (activation). Nitrogen or argon keeps the surface from oxidising.

The same idea as annealing iron. Since the 1980s, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) heats wafers for only seconds with lamps, because long furnace heating lets the dopants spread from where they were placed. ⚠️ Furnace temperature and time are typical values.
block.semiconductor-lab.anneal_furnace.p: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values (a real furnace takes about 30 min). No lamp RTA, furnace only. Dopant spreading by heat is not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note1: Argon ions hit a metal target and the knocked-out atoms settle on the wafer. It also coats the sides of steps.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note2: 5 kW. 1–8 process wafers + 1 aluminium (target wear) + 1 argon → wafers coated with Al (20 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.01 Pa or below. Takes argon from an adjacent gas holder. Then, as after evaporation, resist and phosphoric acid turn the film into wiring. With a tantalum target it lays the barrier film in copper-wiring trenches and holes ([9-36]).
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note3: A high voltage across low-pressure argon makes a glow discharge; Ar⁺ ions hit the target and knock atoms out (atomic billiards). Atoms arrive from many directions, so steps cast less shadow than in evaporation. A magnet behind the target traps electrons (magnetron). W, Mo, Ti and alloys can be deposited too.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.note4: In 1852 Grove recorded that a discharge tube's cathode wore away and coated the glass. The nuisance became a production tool with the magnetron in the 1970s. High voltage can electrocute, so the system is enclosed.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.placehol: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Al target only. Better step coverage is only recorded; the circuit is the same as with evaporation (for yield later). Argon pressure during the discharge (~0.5 Pa) is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_tetrafluor: A gas of carbon with four fluorines. It hardly reacts, except in a discharge, where it releases fluorine.
Fluorination reactor: 1 graphite + 1 fluorine cylinder → 8 bags. Gas for the dry etcher.
C + 2F2 → CF4. The C–F bond is very strong: CF4 does not burn and is of low toxicity. Broken up in a plasma it gives F, which turns SiO2 into gaseous SiF4.
A very long-lived greenhouse gas (about 6,500 times CO2, lasting 50,000 years). Fabs destroy it before release. ⚠️ Figures from IPCC reports.
Omitted: ⚠️ amounts are game values. Industrial CF4 is also made from HF and chlorocarbons.
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorination_rea: Burns carbon in fluorine to make carbon tetrafluoride.
500 W (cooling and control). 1 graphite (or synthetic graphite) + 1 fluorine cylinder → 8 CF4 + empty cylinder (10 s).
Fluorine attacks almost everything, so the reactor is nickel, protected by a fluoride skin. The gas is fed slowly with cooling.
Moissan, who first isolated fluorine in 1886, recorded carbon burning in it. Fluorine work has many accidents and is done in monitored rooms.
Omitted: ⚠️ amount (8 bags per cylinder) and power are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note1: Etches oxide with a discharge (plasma). Unlike liquid HF it only cuts straight down.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note2: 3 kW. 1–8 wafers with developed resist + 1 CF4 → wafers with windows (15 s). Works only when a vacuum chamber next to it is at 0.1 Pa or below. Strip the resist afterwards. With chlorine (Cl2) it cuts the silicon itself straight down, leaving thin fins under the resist (FinFET [9-37]). With dry hydrogen chloride it removes only the SiGe layers from stacked Si/SiGe fins, leaving free-standing nanosheets (GAA [9-38]).
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note3: A radio-frequency discharge breaks CF4 into F, which turns SiO2 into gaseous SiF4. The wafer electrode charges negative, so ions strike from straight above and etch only downward (anisotropic: reactive ion etching, RIE).
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.note4: From the 1970s. Liquids dissolve sideways as much as down, so lines below about 2–3 µm widen and merge. Every fine line in today's chips is dry-etched.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.place: Omitted: ⚠️ in game, on grids of 36 or finer (from the g-line stepper) wet windows widen by one cell; dry ones do not. Power and time are game values. Added O2 and discharge pressure are omitted. The FinFET high-k gate (HfO2) is added in the ALD reactor (metal gates omitted).
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_silicid: Bluish crystals made by heating magnesium with silicon. Acid turns it into silane.
Silane generator: 2 magnesium + 1 metallurgical silicon → this. React with 4 hydrochloric acid to fill a silane cylinder.
2Mg + Si → Mg2Si. With acid: Mg2Si + 4HCl → SiH4 + 2MgCl2.
In 1857 Wöhler and Buff made silane (a silicon hydride) for the first time this way. It also reacts slowly with water.
item.semiconductor-lab.silane_cylinder.n: A gas of silicon and hydrogen (SiH4) that catches fire by itself in air. Raw material for CVD films.
Silane generator: 1 magnesium silicide + 4 hydrochloric acid + empty cylinder → this. In the CVD furnace it reacts with oxygen to make the interlayer film (SiO2).
SiH4. At about 400 °C: SiH4 + O2 → SiO2 + 2H2O. Low enough that aluminium does not melt, so it insulates over the wiring.

Pyrophoric (GHS: flame, gas under pressure). Fabs keep cylinders in enclosures with leak monitors and purge lines before opening them. ⚠️ Industrial silane comes from SiHCl3 disproportionation or SiCl4 hydrogenation.
item.semiconductor-lab.silane_cylinder.p: Omitted: ⚠️ the Mg2Si-acid route turns only about 25% of the Si into silane, mixed with disilane etc. Amount per cylinder is a game value.
block.semiconductor-lab.silane_generator: Makes silane gas from magnesium and silicon. What you put in picks the reaction.
1 kW, 10 s each. ① 2 magnesium + 1 metallurgical silicon → magnesium silicide ② 1 magnesium silicide + 4 hydrochloric acid + empty cylinder → silane cylinder (acid bottles pop out on top).
① heats the two without air into an alloy. ② breaks it with acid and fills the gas into a cylinder.
Silane burns on contact with air, so the unit is purged before opening (a gas with many accidents). The magnesium chloride solution is discarded.
Omitted: ⚠️ amounts, power and time are game values. Magnesium chloride is not kept (discarded).
block.semiconductor-lab.cvd_furnace.note: Grows a film on wafers from reacting gases. Covers the first wiring layer with insulation.

2 kW. 1–8 wafers with patterned first metal + 1 silane cylinder + 1 oxygen → wafers with an interlayer film + empty cylinder (20 s). Oxygen comes from an adjacent gas holder. Then via windows (resist → etch) → second Al → etch gives the second wiring layer (METAL2). With ammonia instead of oxygen it deposits a silicon nitride protective film on finished wafers (3SiH4 + 4NH3 → Si3N4 + 12H2).

SiH4 + O2 → SiO2 + 2H2O at about 400 °C. Thermal oxidation (about 1000 °C) cannot be done over aluminium (melts at 660 °C), so insulation over metal is deposited by CVD. Vias (vertical holes) join the two metal layers.
Two wiring layers let lines cross over each other, so chips get smaller. ⚠️ Two-level metal spread in production around the 1970s (sources being checked). Today's chips have more than ten layers.
block.semiconductor-lab.cvd_furnace.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ power and time are game values. Film thickness, phosphorus doping for reflow (PSG) and planarisation (CMP) are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.cmp_polisher.not: Polishes a bumpy wafer surface flat with chemicals and fine particles.

2 kW. 1–8 wafers with an interlayer film + 1 colloidal silica → planarised wafers (30 s, bottle pops out on top). Refuses wafers with resist or a metal film. The particles leave a little dirt (clean it in the cleaning bench).

Alkaline silica slurry flows onto a pad on a rotating platen while the wafer is pressed on it. The chemistry softens the surface and the particles cut the high spots first. Flattening after each layer keeps fine lines in focus (depth of focus DOF = k2·λ/NA²).
IBM began using it in production in the 1980s ⚠️ (date being checked). Like building a skyscraper and levelling each floor before the next. Today it is also essential for copper (damascene) wiring.
block.semiconductor-lab.cmp_polisher.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ real pads are polyurethane foam; nylon felt stands in here. Power and time are game values. Depth-of-focus checks are not in yet (v0.5; steps are only recorded).
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.note1: An exposure tool that prints through a thin slit while moving the mask and the wafer together. Almost every fab exposure tool today is one.
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.note2: Stepper + 2 ball screws + motor + 4 steel + copper cable. Same slots as the stepper plus a mask-stage screw (lead or ball screw) lower right. It uses only a thin band of the lens, so the same lens prints finer lines than in the stepper. Mask-stage error enters the overlay at 1/4.
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.note3: In the 1990s step-and-scan tools, which sweep a slit across each chip, took over from steppers. The mask stage and wafer stage move in opposite directions in perfect 4:1 step.
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.note4: Printing a whole chip at once needs a large, perfect lens. With a slit only a thin central band of the lens is used, where aberrations are smallest. In exchange, two stages must move together to nanometre accuracy.
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.placehol: Approximation: the slit halves the effect of lens aberrations (game value). Stepping is by hand, one chip at a time (automatic control after [10-15]).
Grows a thin layer of crystal, lined up with the wafer below, from gases.

10 kW. 1–8 bare silicon wafers + 1 silicon tetrachloride + 2 hydrogen + 1 dopant source (B2O3 = p, phosphorus = n) → wafers with an epitaxial layer + 4 dry hydrogen chloride (30 s). Hydrogen comes from an adjacent gas holder. The layer survives oxidation. With germanium tetrachloride instead of a dopant source it stacks 3 alternating Si/SiGe pairs (for GAA [9-38]).

On wafers at about 1200 °C: SiCl4 + 2H2 → Si + 4HCl. Atoms copy the crystal below (epi = upon, taxis = arrangement). The layer can have a different type and doping from the substrate, so 1960s bipolar ICs grew an n layer on a p substrate.
Bell Labs announced the epitaxial transistor in 1960, giving faster switching. It is the same reaction that thickens polysilicon rods in the Siemens reactor, used as a single-crystal film.
Omitted: ⚠️ layer thickness and resistivity are not recorded. The effect on circuits (substrate type) depends on A's litho. Power and time are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_plater.no: Fills a wafer's trenches and holes with copper using electricity, making copper wiring.

1 kW. 1–8 wafers with holes and trenches in the interlayer + 1 copper sulfate + 1 copper → wafers with a copper film (20 s). Without a tantalum barrier first (sputter with a Ta target), copper soaks into the silicon and dirt rises sharply. Then CMP removes the top, leaving copper wires (metal 2) in the trenches and vias in the holes.

In copper sulfate solution the wafer is the cathode and a copper plate the anode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). Copper conducts about 40% better than aluminium but is hard to plasma-etch, so trenches are filled and polished back (damascene inlay).
IBM announced copper-wired chips in 1997, borrowing the name of Damascus inlay work. Copper wanders through silicon and ruins transistors, so a tantalum film seals it in.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_plater.pl: Omitted: ⚠️ real plating first sputters a thin copper seed layer and uses additives to fill from the bottom up. Power and time are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor_wafer.n: A silicon wafer with four layers, p-n-p-n. Cut it into high-current switches.
Diffusion furnace: 8 p-n junction wafers (n wafer + boron) + 1 white phosphorus → 8 of these. At a crafting table with aluminium + copper + soda-lime glass → 4 thyristors.
Diffusing boron into an n wafer without a mask makes both faces p (p-n-p). Diffusing phosphorus into one face again gives p-n-p-n.
Bell Labs studied p-n-p-n switches around 1956, and in 1957 GE sold the three-lead SCR (silicon controlled rectifier), an IEEE Milestone.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor_wafer.p: Omitted: ⚠️ real phosphorus goes into one face only (the other is protected). Layer thickness and doping are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor.note1: A semiconductor switch: one small pulse into the gate and it keeps carrying a large current.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor.note2: Thyristor wafer + aluminium (contacts) + copper (stud) + glass (seal) → 4. Material for the inverter.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor.note3: Inside the p-n-p-n, two transistors keep each other switched on (latching). It turns off only when the current falls to zero.
item.semiconductor-lab.thyristor.note4: It replaced mercury rectifiers and gas-filled tubes; the first railway and power inverters were built with thyristors, including Shinkansen controls.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_tetrachlo: A white solid of hafnium and chlorine. Raw material for the high-k gate film in the ALD reactor.
Hafnium chlorinator: hafnium oxide + 2 coke + 2 chlorine + empty glass bottle → this. In the ALD reactor it alternates with distilled water to grow HfO2.
HfO2 + 2C + 2Cl2 → HfCl4 + 2CO. It turns straight from solid to gas (sublimes) at about 317 °C and is collected on a cold surface.
Fumes hydrogen chloride in moist air (GHS: corrosive). Zirconium and hafnium are so alike that they are separated deliberately for nuclear reactors.
block.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_chlorina: Heats hafnium oxide with carbon and chlorine to make hafnium tetrachloride.
3 kW. 1 hafnium oxide + 2 coke + 2 chlorine + empty glass bottle → hafnium tetrachloride + 2 carbon monoxide (20 s).
At about 900 °C: HfO2 + 2C + 2Cl2 → HfCl4 + 2CO (carbochlorination), the same method as making TiCl4 for the Kroll process.
Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless poison (GHS: skull, flame). It is caught in bags, never released.
Omitted: ⚠️ power, time and amounts are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.ald_reactor.note: Deposits films one atomic layer at a time. Gives transistor gates a leak-resistant high-k film.
2 kW. 1–8 wafers with gate oxide + 1 hafnium tetrachloride + 1 distilled water → high-k gates (30 s, bottles pop out on top). Replaces the SiO2 stand-in used for FinFET.

HfCl4 vapour and water vapour flow in turn with purges between. Each pulse adds exactly one layer and stops (HfCl4 + 2H2O → HfO2 + 4HCl, about 300 °C). HfO2 has about six times the dielectric constant of SiO2, so a thicker film works the same and electrons tunnel through less.
High-k and metal gates entered mass production with Intel's 45 nm generation in 2007. ALD grew from 1970s work in Finland and 1960s research in the Soviet Union.
block.semiconductor-lab.ald_reactor.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ metal gates and film thickness (cycle count) are omitted. Power and time are game values.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.note1: Heats exposed chemically amplified resist so the acid made by light can work.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.note2: 300 W. 1–8 wafers with exposed chemically amplified resist → baked wafers (10 s). Then the developer bench (alkali). Developing without the bake dissolves nothing.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.note3: At about 100 °C one acid moves through the resist and removes hundreds of protecting groups (catalysis). Only those areas dissolve in alkali.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.note4: Too hot or too long and the acid spreads, blurring lines, so the temperature is set to a tenth of a degree.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.place: Omitted: ⚠️ temperature and time are game values. Acid spreading is not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.stepper.defocus: Steps exceed DOF: flatten by CMP
A light-patternable resin with red pigment mixed in. It becomes the red filters of an image sensor.
Positive resist + rouge (iron oxide). Material for the Bayer filter.
Real colour filters are made by coating pigmented resist, exposing and developing it, leaving red, green and blue over the pixels one colour at a time.
A red filter passes only red light (longer than about 600 nm).
Approximation: real red uses organic pigments such as diketopyrrolopyrrole; rouge stands in here.
item.semiconductor-lab.green_color_resis: A light-patternable resin with green pigment mixed in.
Positive resist + chromium oxide (green). Material for the Bayer filter.
Green filters cover half the pixels because eyes are most sensitive to green.
Chromium oxide (chrome green) has long been a green paint pigment.
Approximation: real green uses organic pigments such as halogenated copper phthalocyanine; chromium oxide stands in here.
item.semiconductor-lab.blue_color_resist: A light-patternable resin with blue colour mixed in.
Positive resist + copper phthalocyanine (blue pigment). Material for the Bayer filter.
Blue filters cover a quarter of the pixels; the missing colours are filled in from neighbours by calculation.
Copper phthalocyanine is a blue pigment with four rings around a copper atom (from the 1930s). Today's colour-filter blues are of this family.
Approximation: real resists grind the pigment fine and disperse it in resin; here it is simply mixed.
item.semiconductor-lab.bayer_filter.note: A film of tiny red, green and blue filters in a checkerboard. It lets an image sensor tell colours apart.
Colour resists in a 2x2 grid, green-red / blue-green -> 4. Mounted on an image sensor element it makes a colour sensor (assembly comes after the image sensor).
Devised by Bryce Bayer at Kodak in 1975 and granted a US patent in 1976. Almost every digital and phone camera uses this layout.
Pixels sense only brightness, so each gets one colour filter and the other two colours are computed from neighbours (demosaicing). Green covers half because eyes judge brightness mainly by green.
item.semiconductor-lab.bayer_filter.plac: Approximation: red and green use inorganic colours (rouge, chromium oxide); blue is the real copper phthalocyanine.
item.semiconductor-lab.image_sensor.note: A chip that turns light into electrons and counts them. Hold it to see how many electrons one pixel collects here.

Assembly bench: p-n junction wafer (photodiode) + chip that passed NOT (readout) + aluminium (wiring) + soda-lime glass (window). Held, it shows the electron count (more when brighter, saturates at 6000, scatters by ±√N). With a colour filter [9-45] it becomes a camera part.

Each photon hitting the photodiode frees one electron, which is stored in the pixel. Photons arrive at random, so the count scatters by about ±√N (shot noise) — why dark photos look grainy. Even in darkness heat frees a few electrons (dark current).

Bell Labs conceived the CCD (bucket-brigade charge transfer) in 1969; around 1993 a group at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory made CMOS sensors with an amplifier in every pixel. Phone cameras are almost all CMOS. ⚠️ Dates being checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.image_sensor.plac: Omitted: ⚠️ light-to-electron conversion, full-well capacity and dark current are game values. One pixel stands for all.
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_wafer.note1: Silicon etched deep into tiny springs and masses.
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_wafer.note2: Dry etcher: bare silicon wafer + chlorine → this. Becomes an accelerometer at the assembly bench.
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_wafer.note3: A mass hangs on springs thinner than a hair, with interlocking comb electrodes. When it moves the mass lags and the electrode gaps change (capacitance).
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_wafer.note4: Deep vertical etching (the Bosch process, 1994) alternates an etching gas (SF6) with a wall-protecting gas (C4F8).
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_wafer.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ really the Bosch process (SF6/C4F8); a chlorine plasma stands in here.
item.semiconductor-lab.mems_acceleromete: A chip that senses motion. Hold it to see acceleration and tilt.

Assembly bench: MEMS wafer + chip that passed NOT (readout) + aluminium + can cap (seal). Held, it shows acceleration in g (1.00 g standing, 0 g while falling, a spike on landing) and tilt (positive looking up).
It senses the acceleration of being held up. Standing, the floor pushes you up: 1 g. Falling freely, nothing holds you: 0 g — the same weightlessness astronauts feel.
Mass-produced for car airbags in 1993 and used in 2007 smartphones to turn the screen. ⚠️ Dates being checked.
Omitted: ⚠️ this world's gravity is taken as 1 g and values come from position changes, so vehicles give rough readings.
item.semiconductor-lab.color_image_senso: An image sensor with a Bayer colour filter on top, so it can tell red, green and blue apart.
Image sensor + Bayer filter. Held in hand it shows electrons per pixel (same as the image sensor). Material for the camera module.
Today's phone camera sensors carry red, green and blue filters and tiny microlenses over tens of millions of pixels.
Colour filters pass only about a third of the light to each pixel. Back-side illuminated sensors (from about 2009) were made to do better in the dark.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask_blank.no: A mirror that reflects EUV light, coated with a light-absorbing tantalum film. Patterning it makes an EUV mask.

Sputter: multilayer mirror (40+ pairs) + tantalum target + argon → this. In the reduction camera (C) the pattern is printed in resist and the absorber is etched with chlorine plasma to make an EUV mask.
EUV (13.5 nm) is absorbed by every material, so no transmissive mask is possible. A Mo/Si multilayer reflects it, and a tantalum compound covers what should not reflect (a reflective mask).
A single speck on the mask would print on every chip, so mask blanks are among the cleanest objects in the world.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask_blank.pl: Omitted: ⚠️ the real absorber is TaBN (reactive sputtering in Ar+N2); tantalum stands in. The Ru capping layer and back-side conductive film are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask.note1: A patterned reflective mask for the EUV exposure tool.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask.note2: Made by printing a pattern on an EUV mask blank in the reduction camera (C). The EUV exposure tool [9-40] (C) accepts only this mask.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask.note3: Light reflects off the mirror pattern and all-mirror projection optics (NA 0.33) shrink it fourfold onto the wafer.
item.semiconductor-lab.euv_mask.note4: One costs a fortune. Even the thin dust cover (pellicle) was hard to make for EUV and took years of development.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_scanner.note: The exposure tool that prints the finest patterns. The light and all the mirrors are in vacuum.

Scanner + 2 turbo pumps + electromagnet + 4 steel + copper cable. Slots as in the scanner (wafer, reflective EUV mask, EUV projection optics, stage screw, mask-stage screw, aperture). Needs an EUV source and a vacuum chamber (1 Pa or less) beside it. Ten mirrors and the mask leave about 2% of the light, and each chip needs 0.2 J, so less light means slower printing (more source lasers make it faster).
Built by a Dutch company after a long development, it began volume production of 7 nm chips in 2019 ⚠️. Each machine is bigger than a house, and only one company in the world can make them.
Even with about 250 W of EUV at the source, each of about ten mirrors loses some 30%, so only a few watts reach the wafer. Source power therefore set how many wafers per hour could be printed.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_scanner.plac: Approximation: a single block, not a multiblock. Light levels and the dose per chip (0.2 J) are game values. Pellicles, oblique mask illumination and stage speed are not modelled.
gui.semiconductor-lab.euv_scanner.need_s: The EUV source beside it is not lit
item.semiconductor-lab.foup.note1: A sealed box for carrying wafers. Put it in a load port and the machine loads and unloads itself.
item.semiconductor-lab.foup.note2: 8 HDPE (crafting). Holds up to 25 wafers of one kind. In a load port's input slot it feeds the machine; in the output slot it collects the machine's finished wafers.
item.semiconductor-lab.foup.note3: Real FOUPs are sealed, nitrogen-filled pods carried between tools on ceiling rails. No hand touches the wafers, so no dust or dirt gets on them.
item.semiconductor-lab.foup.note4: Used since the first 300 mm fabs (late 1990s ⚠️). Thousands move around a single fab every day.
item.semiconductor-lab.foup.placeholder: Omitted: ⚠️ real FOUPs are polycarbonate; HDPE stands in. Nitrogen filling is not modelled.
block.semiconductor-lab.load_port.note1: A stand placed next to a process machine. It feeds wafers from one FOUP into the machine and returns finished wafers to another.
block.semiconductor-lab.load_port.note2: 50 W, once a second. Put it next to a process machine with the input FOUP on top and the output FOUP below. It loads one batch of wafers the machine accepts and moves finished wafers into the output FOUP (same kind, up to 25). Carry the output FOUP to the next machine's load port as its input.
block.semiconductor-lab.load_port.note3: In a real fab a robot in front of the tool (EFEM) opens the FOUP and loads wafers one by one. People never touch the wafers.
block.semiconductor-lab.load_port.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ only the handover is modelled (no robot, lid handling or nitrogen).
gui.semiconductor-lab.load_port.no_machi: No process machine next to it
item.semiconductor-lab.point_contact_dio: A tiny germanium crystal touched by a fine metal needle. It lets current through one way only.
Crafting: n-type germanium + W wire (needle) + soda-lime glass (seal) → 4.
The needle-to-germanium contact passes current in one direction (rectification), pulling sound or signals out of radio waves (detection).
Mass-produced as radar detectors in the 1940s; the point-contact transistor of 1947 grew out of this work.
block.semiconductor-lab.dicing_saw.howto:
Cuts a finished wafer into chips.
- Top: a finished process wafer
- Middle: a diamond blade (wears out)
- Bottom: a ball screw (kept; higher grades chip less)
- Chips come out on the right (1.5 kW, 10 s). Dies marked by the prober are discarded
block.semiconductor-lab.drafting_table.h:
Draws circuit layouts (no power).
- + makes a new grid sheet. Pick a layer; left-click paints, right-click erases (wheel zooms)
- Take the current layer out as rubylith artwork, then a reduction camera makes the mask
- Put a circuit stamp in its slot and left-click to place that shape
block.semiconductor-lab.probe_station.ho:
Probes the circuit on a finished wafer (or chip).
- Set each pad to 0 V / 5 V / open and watch the currents
- "Probe" checks it; matching a historical invention makes a discovery and a circuit stamp
- No answers given: part names appear only after probing
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_prober.how:
Tests every die on a wafer and inks the bad ones.
- Top: a finished wafer, bottom: a ball screw
- The marked wafer comes out on the right (0.5 s per die, 500 W)
- Dicing throws away the inked dies, so only good chips come out
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_casing.note1: The outer wall of the EUV scanner. It keeps the inside under vacuum.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_casing.note2: 4 stainless steel + glass (viewport) + FKM O-ring -> 4. The 'casing' cells of the EUV scanner. Energy, item and gas ports may sit here too.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_casing.note3: EUV light (13.5 nm) is absorbed even by air, so the whole path from source to wafer is inside a vacuum box.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_casing.note4: A real EUV scanner is the size of a bus and is shipped in several aircraft. The vacuum box is stainless steel, which rusts little and gives off little gas, and the joints are sealed with fluororubber O-rings.
A box of mirrors that gathers the source light and spreads it evenly on the mask.
2 multilayer mirrors + ULE glass + vacuum casing. The I cell of the EUV scanner.
EUV cannot pass through lenses, so the illuminator is all mirrors too.
Arrays of small mirrors (fly's eyes) mix the light so the mask is evenly lit. Each mirror loses about 30% of the light.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_reticle_stag: A stage that holds the mask face-down and moves it fast and precisely.
Lead screw + 2 neodymium magnets + alumina ceramic plate + ULE glass + vacuum casing. The M cell, top middle of the EUV scanner.
Suction does not work in vacuum, so the mask is held by static electricity (an electrostatic chuck).
While scanning, the mask moves 4 times faster than the wafer, floated and driven by magnets with nothing rubbing. The electrostatic chuck is a sintered alumina ceramic plate.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_projection_b: A box for the mirrors that shrink the mask image onto the wafer.
2 ULE glass + stainless steel + vacuum casing. The P cell in the middle of the EUV scanner. The mirrors themselves (projection optics) go into the screen slot.
The mirror frame is ULE glass, which does not grow or shrink with temperature.
Mirror shapes must be right to a fraction of a nanometre; a frame that stretches even slightly blurs the image.
A stage that holds the wafer and moves it chip by chip.
Lead screw + 2 neodymium magnets + alumina ceramic plate + vacuum casing. The W cell, bottom middle of the EUV scanner (behind the controller).
The wafer is also held by an electrostatic chuck and moved on magnets.
Laser interferometers measure its position so it stops to about 1 nm. The wafer is held by a sintered alumina ceramic electrostatic chuck.
block.semiconductor-lab.ald_reactor.howt: Insert gate-oxidised wafers, hafnium tetrachloride and distilled water → wafers with a high-k gate. 2 kW. Bottles pop out on top. Needs a gate oxide.
block.semiconductor-lab.anneal_furnace.h: Insert implanted wafers and nitrogen or argon → wafers whose implant now works. 3 kW. Also takes gas from an adjacent gas holder. Strip resist first.
block.semiconductor-lab.bake_plate.howto: Insert wafers with exposed chemically amplified (or EUV) resist → baked wafers. 300 W. Then the developer bench; without baking no pattern appears.
block.semiconductor-lab.cleaning_bench.h: Insert process wafers, acid (nitric, hydrofluoric) and water → cleaned wafers (less dirt). Electric. Strip resist first.
block.semiconductor-lab.cmp_polisher.how: Insert wafers with an interlayer (or copper film) and colloidal silica → flat wafers. 2 kW. Bottle pops out. Strip resist first.
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_plater.ho: Insert wafers with holes and trenches in the interlayer, copper sulfate and copper → copper-filmed wafers (then CMP). 1 kW. Without a tantalum barrier first, dirt rises sharply.
block.semiconductor-lab.cvd_furnace.howt: Insert wafers, a silane cylinder and gas: oxygen → interlayer, ammonia → nitride, ITO glass + hydrogen → TFT glass. 2 kW. Empty cylinder comes out.
Insert wafers with exposed resist and developer (xylene for negative) → developed wafers. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.dry_etcher.howto: Pump the adjacent vacuum chamber below 0.1 Pa, then insert developed wafers and gas: CF4 → windows, chlorine → fins (bare wafers → MEMS), hydrogen chloride → remove SiGe (GAA). 3 kW.
Insert bare silicon wafers, silicon tetrachloride, hydrogen and a dopant source (or germanium tetrachloride) → epi-layer (or Si/SiGe stack) wafers and hydrogen chloride. 10 kW. Hydrogen also from an adjacent holder.
block.semiconductor-lab.etch_tank.howto: Insert wafers and a chemical (hydrofluoric acid, phosphoric acid, silicon etch) → wafers with windows or etched aluminium. Electric. HF in lead or PE containers.
block.semiconductor-lab.fluorination_rea: Insert graphite and a fluorine cylinder → 8 carbon tetrafluoride and an empty cylinder. 500 W.
block.semiconductor-lab.fz_puller.howto: Insert 2 polysilicon, a silicon seed, 2 argon (and dopant) → low-oxygen silicon crystal. 20 kW. Argon also from an adjacent holder.
block.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_chlorina: Insert hafnium oxide, 2 coke, 2 chlorine and an empty glass bottle → hafnium tetrachloride and carbon monoxide. 3 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.inverter.howto: Connect a DC cable to the back and an AC cable to the front → turns DC into AC (95%). Keep front and back on separate networks.
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_implanter.ho: Pump the adjacent chamber below 0.01 Pa, then insert process wafers and a dopant source → implanted wafers. 5 kW. They need the anneal furnace to work.
block.semiconductor-lab.load_port.howto: Place next to a process machine with the input FOUP on top and the output FOUP below. 50 W. Feeds one batch at a time and moves finished wafers to the lower FOUP.
block.semiconductor-lab.oxidation_furnac: Insert wafers and oxygen (dry) or a water bucket (wet) → oxidised wafers. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.package_sealer.h: Insert a wire-bonded chip, sealing material (can cap or epoxy) and nitrogen (for cans) → a packaged IC. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.rca_bench.howto: Insert process wafers with hydrogen peroxide, ammonia water, hydrochloric acid and ultrapure water → wafers with zero dirt. Electric.
Insert resist-coated wafers, sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide → stripped wafers. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.silane_generator: 2 magnesium + metallurgical silicon → magnesium silicide; that + 4 hydrochloric acid + empty cylinder → silane cylinder. 1 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.spin_coater.howt: Insert wafers and resist (positive, negative, chemically amplified, EUV) → coated wafers. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.sputter.howto: Pump the adjacent chamber below 0.01 Pa, then insert wafers, a target (aluminium, tantalum, Mo/Si) and argon → coated items. 5 kW. Argon also from an adjacent holder.
block.semiconductor-lab.wafer_polisher.h: Insert process wafers, abrasive (alumina or rouge) and colloidal silica → wafers with layers polished off (twice at most). 1 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.wire_bonder.howt: Insert a chip, gold bonding wire and a header → a wire-bonded chip. Electric.
block.semiconductor-lab.euv_scanner.howt: Build the 5x3x3 shape (sneak + right-click for the plan) inside a class-100 room. Give the source CO2 lasers and tin, pump the vacuum chamber low. Add an EUV-resist wafer, EUV mask, EUV optics and a lead screw, then press the button.
block.semiconductor-lab.mask_aligner.how: Add a resist-coated wafer and a photomask, connect power, pick the gap with the button and expose. A lead screw on the stage lets you align to the previous layer.
block.semiconductor-lab.scanner.howto: Same inputs as the stepper plus a lead screw for the mask stage. Mask and wafer move together while exposing, so lens errors matter less.
block.semiconductor-lab.stepper.howto: Add a resist-coated wafer, a mask, a projection lens, light (mercury lamp with i-line filter, or a laser) and a stage lead screw, connect power and press the button. It steps and exposes chip by chip.
item.semiconductor-lab.electromagnet.not: Iron wound with copper wire that is a magnet only while current flows.
Crafting: 1 iron ingot (core) + 8 copper wire (wire drawing [1-58]) → 1. A part for the magnet that sorts ions by mass in ion implantation [9-28] and more.
Current makes a magnetic field around it. Many turns add up the field and the iron core strengthens it further. Switch off the current and it is plain iron again.

In 1820 Ørsted found that a current deflects a compass needle. In 1825 Sturgeon wound copper wire on iron to make an electromagnet, and in the 1830s Henry wound many turns of insulated wire to lift heavy loads.
item.semiconductor-lab.electromagnet.pla: Approximation: wire insulation (once silk) is not modelled. It is a part item and does not act as a block.
item.semiconductor-lab.microcomputer.not: A tiny computer built from your own CPU and ROM chips. Right-click to run its program.
Chips that passed the 4-bit CPU (cpu4) and ROM (rom_program) challenges, a quartz resonator (clock) and a Nixie tube, on the assembly bench.
Intel MCS-4 (1971): the 4004 CPU, 4001 ROM, 4002 RAM and 4003 ran Busicom's 141-PF calculator. Change the program and it does another job: a general-purpose part.
Four instructions (LOAD, ADD, OUT, JUMP, one-hot), an 8-word ROM (the 4001 had 256). It runs on the reference CPU; your chips were proven by the challenges.
A helper chip for decimal maths. Right-click to work out 0.1 + 0.2.
Chips that passed the 8-bit CPU, multiplier and register challenges, plus wiring and a board, on the assembly bench. A part of the AI chip (learning uses decimals).
IEEE 754 (1985): the world rule for numbers as 'mantissa x 2 to a power'. Intel's 8087 (1980) built it first; before that, makers gave different answers.

In binary, 0.1 cannot be written exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 misses 0.3 a little (rounding error). AI usually learns in floating point (16/32 bits) and answers in integers (4/8 bits). ⚠️ The learning maths itself runs in Java.
item.semiconductor-lab.centrifugal_gover: Right-click a steam engine or turbine to fit it. When it spins too fast the balls fly out and close the valve, so it burns only the coal it needs.
The start of feedback control: watch the gap from the target and correct it. The screen shows the speed and the 100% target. With little load the valve closes and coal lasts longer.
In 1788 Watt fitted one to keep his steam engine's speed steady (adapted from windmill millstones ⚠️). As the shaft speeds up, two balls swing out and a linkage closes the steam valve.

In 1868 Maxwell's 'On Governors' used equations to explain why governors make the speed hunt, starting control theory. In 1922 Minorsky described PID control for automatic ship steering. The game's governor is P only.
Simplified: the stored energy (80-120%) stands in for the shaft speed; the valve linkage is not modelled
item.semiconductor-lab.teach_pendant.not: Teaches a robot arm: right-click the arm, then the machine to take from, then the one to put into.
In real factories people also jog the arm with pendant buttons to teach positions. Sneak + right-click the arm to make it forget.
You jog the arm with the pendant and press a button at each position to store it; the arm then joins the stored positions (as the 1961 Unimate did).
Factories today may also build motions on a 3D model in a computer and send them to the arm (offline teaching). The game only has hand teaching.
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.not: A machine that runs on electricity and freezes water. A relative of refrigerators and air conditioners.
Compressor + 2 copper + 6 iron. 1 kW, 20 s. One ammonia water in the refrigerant slot (not used up); water bucket -> ice (the bucket returns).

In 1876 the German Linde built an ammonia compression refrigerating machine, letting breweries cool without winter ice. Linde later liquefied air to separate oxygen and nitrogen ([6-07] air separation).

The compressed, heated refrigerant is cooled outside into a liquid, then expanded suddenly through a narrow opening so it evaporates and draws heat from around it. It moves heat from cold to hot, so it is also called a heat pump. Semiconductor fab air conditioning and constant temperature ([12-12], [8-07]) work the same way.
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.pla: Approximation: the real refrigerant is anhydrous ammonia (ammonia water here). Vanilla has no food spoilage, so there is no refrigerator function.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note1: A sour liquid you get by leaving alcohol open to the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note2: Put fermented wash (alcohol) in a fermentation crock and wait for 2. 2 vinegar + sodium hydroxide -> sodium acetate. About 5% acetic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note3: Acetic acid bacteria from the air turn alcohol into acetic acid with oxygen: C2H5OH + O2 -> CH3COOH + H2O.
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.note4: In 1864 Pasteur showed that vinegar is made by acetic acid bacteria (Mycoderma aceti). Vinegar is humanity's first acid, thousands of years older than acetic acid from wood vinegar [2-23].
item.semiconductor-lab.vinegar.placehold: Approximation: acetic acid strength is fixed.
Alcohol warmed a little to cut down the germs in it. It will not turn to vinegar in the crock.
Warm fermented wash briefly on a campfire. The fermentation crock refuses it (no germs, so no vinegar). Compare with unheated wash.
A few minutes at about 60 C reduces the souring and spoiling germs without changing the taste. Boiling would drive off the alcohol and change the flavour.
In 1864 Pasteur showed this prevents the 'disease' that soured French wine. 'Pasteurize' on milk cartons is his name.
Approximation: the temperature is represented by a campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note1: Sweet juice pressed from sugar cane, cleared with lime.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note2: 3 sugar cane + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note3: Lime neutralizes the juice's acids and makes proteins and other cloudiness clump and settle (clarification).
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.note4: Cane sugar has been made in India since around the start of the common era. Sanskrit 'sharkara' (grains of sand) is where 'sugar' comes from.
item.semiconductor-lab.cane_juice.placeh: Approximation: pressing and straining are skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note1: Sweet juice soaked out of sugar beet roots.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note2: 4 beetroot + slaked lime + water bucket (bucket returned). Boil down on a campfire for 2 raw sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note3: Beet sugar is exactly the same sucrose, C12H22O11, as cane sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.note4: Marggraf in Germany found sugar in beets in 1747, and Achard built the first beet sugar factory in 1801, so cold countries without cane could make sugar (it spread under Napoleon's Continental Blockade).
item.semiconductor-lab.beet_juice.placeh: Approximation: vanilla beetroot stands in for sugar beet (real sugar beet has a white root).
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note1: Brown sugar from boiling down the juice. It still holds much colour and flavour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note2: Boil juice down on a campfire for 2. 2 raw sugar + bone char + water bucket -> 2 white sugar.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note3: As the water boils off and it thickens, sucrose crystallizes. The surrounding molasses (brown liquid) carries the colour.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.note4: Okinawan kokuto is cane juice simply boiled down like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_sugar.placeho: Approximation: centrifuging off the molasses is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note1: Black grains from charred bone. They soak up colour very well.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note2: Char bones in a furnace (an approximation of heating without air). Used to turn raw sugar white (used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note3: Carbon coats the tiny pores of the bone's calcium phosphate, trapping the large colour molecules in them (adsorption).
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.note4: Used to decolourize sugar since the 19th century; activated carbon and ion exchange resins [2-17] are also used today.
item.semiconductor-lab.bone_char.placeho: Approximation: re-burning it for reuse is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note1: An iron can with a thin coat of tin. It hardly rusts.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note2: Iron + tin -> 4. Add cooked meat or fish to make a sealed can.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note3: Tinplate is iron sheet dipped in molten tin. In 1810 Peter Durand in England patented keeping food in tin cans.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_can.note4: For about 50 years after canning was invented there were no can openers; soldiers used bayonets or chisels ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note1: A filled, closed can. Not heated yet, so not canned food yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note2: Heat it in a furnace or campfire to make canned food.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note3: The key is to close it before heating: heat kills the germs inside, and the seal keeps new ones out. Heating first and closing afterwards lets germs in.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.note4: Appert did not know why it worked. The reason (germs) became clear about 50 years later through Pasteur's work in the 1860s.
item.semiconductor-lab.sealed_can.placeh: Approximation: real cans are boiled a long time in water (today at 120 °C under pressure). In the game you heat it in a furnace or campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note1: Food you can carry a long time. A little more filling than cooked meat.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note2: Heat a sealed can in a furnace or campfire. Hunger 9 (cooked beef is 8).
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note3: In 1804-10, Nicolas Appert in France found that food packed into bottles, sealed and boiled kept for a long time, winning Napoleon's army prize. Tin cans came after.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.note4: Heating kills the germs, the seal keeps new ones out. Modern cans last for years.
item.semiconductor-lab.canned_meat.place: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (real nutrition is about the same as cooked meat). No empty can is left. The game has no food spoilage.
A blue spray that protects crops like grapes from mould diseases.
Copper sulfate + slaked lime + water -> 4 (bucket returned). For now it is only crafted; there is no crop disease yet. ⚠ GHS: copper compounds harm aquatic life.

In 1885 Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet in France reported that it prevents downy mildew of grapes (a mould). Copper ions stop the spores from sprouting; the lime makes the copper stick to the leaves against rain and spares the leaves.
Bordeaux farmers painted the roadside vines with a blue mixture so passers-by would not steal the grapes - and only those vines escaped the disease. That was the clue.
Approximation: craft only. Crop disease and spraying to prevent it are not in the game (decision Q3-14 ②).
item.semiconductor-lab.superphosphate.no: A phosphorus fertilizer made from bones. Spread on a field, it gives bigger harvests.

3 bone meal + 2 sulfuric acid (bottles returned) -> 3. Use on farmland to make 'fertile farmland' (3 shares of phosphorus): each ripe crop harvested gives 1 extra. Nitrogen fertilizers (peas, ammonium sulfate/nitrate) speed growth; phosphorus adds yield. Spread both and both work.

The calcium phosphate in bone, Ca3(PO4)2, does not dissolve in water, so plants can hardly take it up. Sulfuric acid turns it into water-soluble calcium dihydrogen phosphate Ca(H2PO4)2 (plus gypsum CaSO4). Ca3(PO4)2 + 2H2SO4 -> Ca(H2PO4)2 + 2CaSO4.

John Bennet Lawes patented it in England in 1842 and built the world's first chemical fertilizer factory. His Rothamsted farm has compared fertilizers on the same fields for over 150 years - the oldest agricultural experiment in the world.
item.semiconductor-lab.superphosphate.pl: Approximation: phosphorus is counted as '3 harvests' and works as '1 extra item per harvest'. Bone meal instead of phosphate rock (the real thing also started with bones).
A nitrogen fertilizer. Spread on a field, crops grow faster.
Ammonia + nitric acid (bag and bottle returned). On farmland it gives 3 shares of nitrogen (like ammonium sulfate or peas). ⚠ GHS: oxidizing solid. Keep away from things that burn.
NH3 + HNO3 -> NH4NO3. About 34% of its weight is nitrogen (ammonium sulfate: about 21%), so it carries more nitrogen per kilogram. Half is ammonium and half nitrate, both quickly taken up by plants.

Failure record: large stores of ammonium nitrate have exploded again and again (Oppau, Germany 1921; Texas City, USA 1947; Beirut, Lebanon 2020). Storage rules are strict today. Nitrogen from the air becomes bread - and, mishandled, a disaster.
Approximation: in the game it works the same as ammonium sulfate (the higher nitrogen content is explained only).
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note1: Meat or fish rubbed with salt. Made without fire, and it keeps a long time.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note2: 2 raw meat or fish + salt -> 2. Edible as is (hunger 5). Smoke it in a smoker or campfire for smoked meat.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note3: Salt draws water out of the meat (osmosis). Bacteria cannot multiply without water, so it spoils slowly.
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.note4: Salt was once so precious it was called 'white gold'. The word 'salary' is said to come from salt (Latin sal) paid to Roman soldiers ⚠️ (not certain).
item.semiconductor-lab.salted_meat.place: Approximation: the amount of salt and the days of curing are left out. The game has no spoilage.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note1: Salted meat or fish cured in smoke. It keeps a very long time.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note2: Smoke salted meat in a smoker or campfire. Hunger 9 (cooked beef is 8). Chicken or fish fill you just as much.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note3: Phenols and other compounds in smoke kill germs and slow the fat from going rancid. The surface also dries, so it spoils even more slowly.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.note4: Until refrigerators ([11-13]) and canning ([11-12]), salted, dried and smoked food fed long sea voyages and winters.
item.semiconductor-lab.smoked_meat.place: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (with water dried out, there is more nutrition per weight).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note1: Two stones that grind grain into flour.
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note2: 3 smooth stone + stick. Use with 2 wheat in a crafting table -> 2 flour (the quern is returned).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note3: Turning the upper stone on the lower one crushes the grain between them. Earlier people pushed a hand stone back and forth over a flat stone (saddle quern).
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.note4: Grinding was one of the first jobs people gave to water wheels and windmills. In 1785 Oliver Evans in America built a mill that ran by itself from unloading the grain onwards.
item.semiconductor-lab.quern.placeholder: Approximation: the quern does not wear out (real ones did, and stone grit in the flour wore down people's teeth).
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note1: Ground grain. The stuff of bread.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note2: Quern + 2 wheat -> 2. 3 flour + wild yeast + water -> 2 bread dough.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note3: Starch and protein (gluten-forming) from the grain. Kneaded with water, gluten forms a mesh that traps the yeast's carbon dioxide, so the dough rises.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.note4: In the 1870s, roller milling with iron rollers spread from Hungary, grinding step by step and making white flour cheap.
item.semiconductor-lab.flour.placeholder: Approximation: vanilla bread is made straight from wheat (milling left out). This mod's bread starts from flour.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note1: Flour, water and yeast kneaded together. Bake it into risen bread.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note2: 3 flour + wild yeast + water (bucket returned) -> 2. Bake in a furnace, smoker or campfire.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note3: Yeast eats the sugars in flour and gives off carbon dioxide and alcohol (fermentation [2-39]). The gas bubbles are caught in the gluten mesh and the dough rises.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.note4: The holes in bread are where the yeast's carbon dioxide bubbles were. Baking drives off the alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.bread_dough.place: Approximation: the hours of rising are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.leavened_bread.no: Bread risen with yeast. More filling than vanilla bread.
Bake bread dough. Hunger 7 (vanilla bread is 5).
Risen bread is easier to digest and bigger from the same flour. Leavened bread is said to have been baked in Egypt around 4000 BC ⚠️.
Why bread rises (the work of a living thing, yeast) became clear only with Pasteur's research in 1857. For thousands of years people baked it without knowing why.
item.semiconductor-lab.leavened_bread.pl: Approximation: the extra hunger is a game rule (compare with vanilla bread as flat, unrisen bread).
message.semiconductor-lab.compost.fertil: Compost (bone meal) spread: a little nitrogen and phosphorus (1 share each)
block.semiconductor-lab.tired_farmland.n: A field that keeps growing the same crop. Too many times in a row and the harvest shrinks.

Harvesting a ripe crop on ordinary farmland makes it remember which crop and how many times in a row. After 3 of the same crop (wheat, einkorn, carrots, potatoes, beetroot), each harvest gives 1 less. To recover: grow a different crop, grow peas, spread compost or fertilizer, or leave it empty for a while (fallow).

The same crop keeps using the same nutrients, and its pests and diseases build up in the soil (continuous-cropping injury). Medieval Europe's three-field system rotated winter crop, spring crop and fallow; livestock grazed the fallow and manured it.

The Norfolk four-course rotation, spread by Charles Townshend in the 1730s, cycled wheat, turnips, barley and clover and did away with fallow. Turnips fed livestock in winter; clover, a legume, added nitrogen. With more animals kept through winter, there was more manure too.
block.semiconductor-lab.tired_farmland.p: Approximation: wear is counted as '3 of the same crop -> harvest -1' (decision Q3-15 ①). There are no turnips or clover (explained only).
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note1: A farm tool that cuts and turns the soil. Tills a wide area at once.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note2: 2 iron + 3 planks + 2 sticks (durability 250). Used on dirt or grass, it turns the 3x3 around into farmland (a hoe does one block).
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note3: The pointed share cuts the soil and the curved mouldboard turns it over, burying weeds and letting in air. Pulled by oxen or horses, it prepares far more land than people with hoes.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.note4: Around 4000 BC, wooden scratch ploughs (ards) were used in Mesopotamia. In 1837 John Deere in America made a steel plough that sticky prairie soil would not cling to, and the North American prairies became farmland.
item.semiconductor-lab.plow.placeholder: Approximation: no oxen or horses (the player uses it).
block.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland.n: A field in dry land that has been watered for years. Salt has built up and harvests shrink.

In desert, savanna and badlands, each harvest from watered (moist) farmland leaves salt behind. After 3, each harvest gives 1 less. Right-click with gypsum (calcium sulfate) to turn it back into farmland.

River and ground water carry a little dissolved salt. In dry land the water evaporates and the salt stays in the soil; with too much salt, roots cannot take up water. Calcium from gypsum swaps for sodium in the soil so it washes out more easily.

In Sumer in Mesopotamia, salt built up in long-irrigated fields, and crops are said to have shifted from salt-sensitive wheat to salt-tolerant barley ⚠️. Many irrigated fields worldwide still suffer from salinity today.
block.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland.p: Approximation: salt is counted as '3 irrigated harvests in dry land -> -1'. Drainage and rising ground water are omitted.
message.semiconductor-lab.salty_farmland: Gypsum spread: the salt washed out and the farmland is back to normal
block.semiconductor-lab.refrigerator.how: Add water buckets and ammonia water (not used up), then connect power. Ice comes out and the bucket returns.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note1: Measures how far away something is without going there. Sight the same mark from two places and the triangle tells you the distance.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note2: Telescope + vernier caliper (vernier scale) + 2 bronze + 2 sticks. Hold right-click to look, release to read the direction. 1) sight a mark and release (station A) -> 2) walk at least 3 m sideways, sight the same mark and release (station B) -> the base and two angles give the distance. Sneak + right-click clears station A.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note3: In 1615 the Dutchman Snellius measured the distance between towns with a chain of triangles (triangulation). Measure one base line carefully and angles alone do the rest of the country. In the 18th century the theodolite combined a telescope with graduated circles.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note4: Sine rule: with base c and end angles alpha and beta, distance from B = c sin(alpha) / sin(alpha + beta). The thinner the triangle (far target, short base), the more a small angle error grows. Ino Tadataka (1800-1821) mapped Japan by combining walked traverses with sightings of mountain peaks from many places.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.placeh: Approximation: the base length is taken directly as the distance between the two stations (really it was measured on the ground with chains or rods). No link to map items yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.statio: 📐 Station A recorded: bearing %s°. Walk sideways and sight the same mark
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.short_: The base is only %s m. Move at least %s m away first
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.no_cro: The two sight lines do not cross ahead. Did you sight the same mark? (station A kept)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.result: 📐 Base %s m, angle A %s°, angle B %s° -> %s m from here to the target (at %s, %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.real: The block you sighted is really %s m away (off by %s m)
A machine that holds a room's temperature and humidity steady. Precise machines grow and shrink with temperature, so air conditioning matters.

Refrigerating machine + motor + copper cable + 6 iron. Uses 2 kW the whole time it runs. Within 8 blocks the temperature swing drops from +-3 C to +-0.1 C, cutting the mask aligner's thermal overlay error (the stage growing and shrinking) from 3.3 um to 0.1 um.

In 1902 the American Carrier built air conditioning that held temperature and humidity for a printing plant where damp paper stretched and colors misregistered. Air conditioning was born for paper, not people.
Steel grows about 11 um per metre per degree, which is why lengths are measured in rooms held at the standard 20 C (CIPM 1931). Today's lithography rooms hold temperature to a hundredth of a degree.
Approximation: the temperature swings (+-3 C, +-0.1 C) and range (8 blocks) are game values. Humidity control is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note1: Glass melted and drawn out into thin threads.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note2: 4 from 2 soda-lime glass + platinum bushing (returned). 7 + 2 iron make a HEPA filter.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note3: Molten glass pulled through small holes becomes threads finer than a hair. Mass production began in the 1930s for insulation, filters and reinforced plastics.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note4: Thin glass bends without breaking easily. Optical fibre is also a thin thread of very pure silica glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note1: A filter that removes almost all the tiny dust in the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note2: 7 glass fibre + 2 iron. Goes in the air conditioner's filter slot and becomes the air inlet of a cleanroom [12-14].
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note3: Developed in the 1940s in the Manhattan Project to catch radioactive dust. It removes at least 99.97% of 0.3 um particles.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note4: Large particles hit the fibres and tiny ones wander into them (Brownian motion). Mid-sized particles around 0.3 um are the hardest to catch, so performance is rated at that size.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.place: Approximation: real HEPA media is pleated ultra-fine borosilicate glass fibre (soda-lime glass fibre here).
A platinum plate with many tiny holes. Molten glass pulled through it becomes threads.
3 platinum. With 2 soda-lime glass it makes 4 glass fibre (the bushing returns).
In the 1930s Owens-Corning and others began mass-producing glass fibre by pulling molten glass through tiny holes in platinum plates.
Platinum neither dissolves in glass above 1000 C nor corrodes. Platinum-rhodium bushings are still used today.
Approximation: the heat to melt the glass is skipped (drawn in the crafting grid).
block.semiconductor-lab.hepa_ceiling.not: A ceiling outlet that sends clean air from the top down.

HEPA filter + 2 iron -> 2. Lay them across the ceiling of an enclosed room and run an air conditioner with a HEPA filter inside to make a cleanroom. With 80% or more of the ceiling it is class 100, with 25% class 1000. Wafers exposed by a mask aligner inside stay cleaner (outside: dirt +2).
In 1962 Whitfield at Sandia Laboratories devised the laminar-flow cleanroom, sending air one way from a ceiling of HEPA filters to the floor to sweep dust away, cutting room dust hundreds of times.

Cleanroom class counts particles of 0.5 um or larger per cubic foot of air (class 100 = at most 100; US Federal Standard 209, 1963). Today's fabs are thousands of times cleaner than an operating room. People are the biggest source of dust, so workers wear full-body cleanroom suits.
block.semiconductor-lab.hepa_ceiling.pla: Approximation: the class thresholds (80% and 25% of the ceiling) are game values. A room is at most 512 air blocks.
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete.n: Concrete of lime and volcanic ash that lasts 2000 years.
Wet mix (slaked lime + 2 tuff + 2 gravel -> 4) sets when it touches water. Mine with a pickaxe.

Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 reacts in water with the silicon and aluminium of volcanic ash (pozzolana) to form insoluble stony compounds (calcium silicate hydrates and others) - the pozzolanic reaction. So it sets even underwater.

The dome of Rome's Pantheon (about AD 128) is unreinforced concrete and still among the largest of its kind. Harbour walls in the sea are said to have grown stronger from crystals formed with seawater ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete.p: Approximation: vanilla tuff stands in for volcanic ash (pozzolana) (decision). It sets instantly (real concrete gains strength over days).
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete_m: Concrete that has not set yet. It sets when it touches water.
Slaked lime + 2 tuff + 2 gravel -> 4. It falls like sand when placed. Placed next to water (poured into water) it sets into Roman concrete.
With water the lime-ash reaction starts and it hardens (hydraulic). Ordinary lime plaster sets with CO2 from the air, so it will not set underwater.
Romans sank wooden forms into the sea and poured the mix into them to build harbour walls.
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_raw_meal.n: Powder of limestone and clay. Fired, it becomes the base of cement.
3 calcite (limestone) + clay -> 2. Fire in a blast furnace -> clinker.
About 80% limestone (CaCO3) and 20% clay (oxides of silicon, aluminium, iron). If the ratio drifts, it sets poorly.
Cement works are built next to limestone quarries.
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_raw_meal.p: Approximation: calcite stands in for limestone (whose main mineral is calcite).
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_clinker.no: Grey, half-melted lumps from the kiln. Ground, they become cement.
Fire raw meal in a blast furnace. 2 + gypsum -> 4 Portland cement.
At about 1450 °C, lime and clay react to calcium silicates (alite Ca3SiO5, belite Ca2SiO4) and others, which set by reacting with water (hydration).
From the 1880s it was fired in long, slowly turning cylinders (rotary kilns). Cement-making is said to release about 8% of the world's CO2 (from the limestone and from fuel) ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.portland_cement.n: A grey powder. With water, sand and gravel it becomes concrete.
2 clinker + gypsum -> 4. + 4 sand + 4 gravel -> 8 grey concrete powder (sets when it touches water).
A little gypsum is added so it does not set the instant water goes in. Cement sets by reacting with water (not by drying), so it even sets underwater.
Joseph Aspdin in England patented it in 1824. Its set colour resembled Portland stone, hence the name.
block.semiconductor-lab.reinforced_concr: Concrete with steel bars inside. Very strong.
8 grey concrete + steel (rebar) -> 8. More than ten times as blast-resistant as ordinary concrete.

Concrete is strong in compression but very weak in tension; steel is strong in tension. They expand with heat at almost the same rate, so they do not crack apart in heat and cold, and concrete's alkali keeps the steel from rusting.
In 1867 the French gardener Joseph Monier patented flowerpots with iron mesh inside. Most of today's buildings, bridges and dams use this pairing.
Approximation: strength is shown only as blast resistance (really tensile and bending strength).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note1: A shallow tub of molten tin. Glass floats on it to become sheet.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note2: 5 tin + 4 refractory brick. Returned after crafting. 6 soda-lime glass + this -> 16 glass panes.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note3: Molten glass poured onto molten tin (about 1000 °C) floats, since it is lighter, and gravity and surface tension spread it into a perfectly flat sheet about 6 mm thick. The bottom touches tin and the top is fire-polished, so both come out mirror-flat. Nitrogen and hydrogen gas cover it so the tin does not oxidize.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note4: Alastair Pilkington in England announced the float process in 1959. Before that, sheet glass had to be ground and polished on both sides. Most window glass and phone-screen glass today is made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.placehol: Approximation: the nitrogen-hydrogen cover and annealing are omitted. The tin is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note1: A steel beam or column for the frames of tall buildings and bridges.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note2: 7 steel -> 6. Like a log, it becomes a vertical column or a horizontal beam depending on how you place it.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note3: The H-shaped section puts the material in the top and bottom flanges, making the beam stiff in bending for its weight. Steel is strong in both tension and compression, so a light frame can carry a tall building.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note4: The Iron Bridge in England (1779) was the first big cast-iron bridge. Chicago's Home Insurance Building (1885) is counted among the first steel-framed skyscrapers ⚠️. The Eiffel Tower (wrought iron, 1889) changes height by more than ten centimetres between summer and winter (thermal expansion).
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.place: Approximation: only the look and orientation; the building's loads are not calculated.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note1: A road of packed broken stone. You walk a little faster.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note2: 2 cobblestone + 2 gravel -> 4. Walking speed x1.15. + coal tar -> tar macadam.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note3: Layers of angular broken stone rolled with a heavy roller lock together and do not turn to mud in rain; the crown of the road sheds water.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note4: John Loudon McAdam of Scotland spread the method around 1820. Before that, roads turned to mud in rain and coaches could not move.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.placehol: Approximation: layer thickness and rolling are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note1: A black road of broken stone bound with coal tar. You walk even faster.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note2: 4 macadam + coal tar -> 4. Walking speed x1.3.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note3: Tar fills the gaps and glues the stones, keeping water out so car tyres do not pluck the stones loose.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note4: In 1902 Edgar Hooley in England noticed a stretch of road where tar had spilled was hard and dust-free, and patented 'tarmac' (tar + macadam). Today's asphalt comes from petroleum (not in this mod).
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.placehold: Approximation: the speed factor is a game value.
Just connect power (copper cable). Nearby temperature swings shrink, so precision machines drift less. Add a HEPA filter for clean-room air.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_thermomet: A thermometer of mercury in a thin glass tube. Right-click for air temperature; sneak and right-click for body temperature.
2 soda-lime glass + mercury (iron flask returned). ⚠ GHS: mercury - acute toxicity, organ damage (do not breathe the vapour if it breaks).
Warmed mercury expands and climbs the thin tube; the bore is so narrow that a tiny expansion moves visibly. Clinical thermometers have a constriction so the reading stays after you take it out.

Fahrenheit made the mercury thermometer in 1714. Until Thomas Allbutt in England made a short clinical thermometer in 1866, doctors' thermometers were about 30 cm long and took 20 minutes. Most today are electronic (thermistors) without mercury.
Approximation: the air temperature is a game value from the biome temperature; body temperature is approximated as 36.5-37.0 °C.
item.semiconductor-lab.marine_chronomete: A clock that keeps time even on a rolling ship. It carries the home port's (Greenwich) time so you can find your longitude.

4 bronze + crown glass + 2 crucible steel (mainspring) + ruby boule (jewel bearings) + standard screw. Right-click for Greenwich time and days since it was set. Hold it in the other hand when taking a noon sight with the sextant: longitude = (12:00 - time of noon) x 15 deg. Each one gains or loses a little every day (1 s of error = 15 arcsec of longitude).

In 1707 a British fleet lost its position in fog and ran aground with great loss of life. In 1714 Britain offered a prize for finding longitude. John Harrison, a carpenter by training, spent 40 years on his clocks, and on the 1761 voyage H4 lost only about 5 seconds in 81 days.

The Earth turns 15 deg an hour, so the gap between local noon and Greenwich time is your longitude. Pendulum clocks fail on a rolling ship, so H4 ran on a balance and mainspring compensated so heat would not change it. Its bearings used jewels such as ruby.
Approximation: the daily rate is a game value within +-0.5 s (a game day is 20 minutes).
Aluminium with a little copper and magnesium mixed in.
6 aluminium + copper + magnesium -> 6. Fired in a furnace it becomes quenched duralumin.
Duralumin is aluminium with about 4% Cu, about 0.5% Mg and some Mn.
The name comes from the German town of Düren and aluminium.
Approximation: the proportions are game values (real: about 4% Cu, 0.5% Mg).
item.semiconductor-lab.quenched_duralumi: Duralumin just heated and cooled fast, still soft. Carry it and it slowly hardens.
Duralumin charge in a furnace. After one (game) day in your inventory it turns into hard duralumin (not in chests). Right-click for its current hardness.
In 1906 Alfred Wilm in Germany left a quenched alloy over a weekend and found it had hardened (age hardening).
Quenching traps copper dissolved in the aluminium; even at room temperature copper atoms slowly gather into tiny precipitates that block deformation and harden the metal.
Approximation: about 4 days really; one day in the game, and only in your inventory.
🔩 Hardness now HV %s (about %s fully aged), %s days since quenching
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note1: An aluminium alloy that is light yet nearly as strong as steel. It framed airships and aircraft.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note2: Quenched duralumin left in your inventory for a day age-hardens into this.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note3: It framed Zeppelin airships and metal aircraft from the 1910s. Related alloys still skin aircraft today.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note4: Density about 2.8 g/cm3, about a third of steel (7.9), so its strength per weight is high.
A battery radio that fits in your pocket.

Alloy-junction transistor ×3 (amplify) + graphite (carbon resistor) + copper cable (tuning/antenna coil) + Leyden jar (capacitor) + magnet (speaker) + zinc ingot and graphite rod (zinc-carbon battery: zinc can and carbon rod). The goal of chapter 1. No redstone: every part is a real radio part.

It picks one station out of the weak signals from the antenna (tuning), extracts the audio (detection) and amplifies it with transistors to drive the speaker. Unlike tubes there is no warm-up, so it plays at once and the battery lasts.

The Regency TR-1 (USA, 1954, four transistors) was the first commercial transistor radio. Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (later Sony) released the TR-55 in 1955, and its 1957 TR-63 sold worldwide as a 'pocketable' radio.

⚠️ Approximation: the capacitor is a Leyden jar (real radios use small paper, ceramic or electrolytic capacitors). The battery is only its zinc can and carbon rod (the real zinc-carbon cell also needs MnO2 and an ammonium chloride paste, not in the game yet).
